Chapters cover reproduction from the standpoint of biology, adolescence in the male, and the sacrifice parents make for offspring and weaker members of society. Hall writes for young men, plainly and seriously. The book remains a historical record of how sex education was taught in early twentieth-century America.
24869-the-ra-ma-yan-of-va-lmi-ki-transla:
Ralph T. H. Griffith, principal of Benares College, translated Valmiki's Ramayan into English verse, published in London and Benares between 1870 and 1874. The epic opens with an invocation, then moves through Ayodhya, its king, and the birth of the princes. Sages, sacrifices, and doomed kings fill the early cantos.

Later verses show Rama's duty in sharp relief. A brother pleads that the sacred laws bind wife and son to obey their lord and sire, whether the king bids Rama sit enthroned or walk in bark cloth in the woods. Griffith's verse keeps the epic's dignity in English. The book gives readers a full, readable door into India's great poem of duty and exile.
24872-the-tale-of-master-meadow-mouse:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote The Tale of Master Meadow Mouse in 1921, with pictures by Eleanore Fagan. Master Meadow Mouse, a fat little fellow, peeps at the world beyond his meadow home and meets a kitten, Mr. Frog, Mr. Crow, and Moses Mouse. His days run from moonlight raids and midnight frolics to a flood, a raft, and friends under the snow.

Farmer Green's haying cuts the grass and leaves the mouse bare to birds above, but the farmer's corn shocks later give him cover and cheer. Bailey tells each chapter in short, simple scenes for young listeners. The tale ends as a gentle lesson in caution, kindness, and making the best of a changed field.
25301-the-adventures-of-danny-meadow-mou:
Thornton W. Burgess's Adventures of Danny Meadow Mouse, seventh in his Bedtime Story-Books, follows a small mouse far from home. Danny longs for his warm house of grass, his tunnels under the snow, and his seed store in a hollow fence-post.

Peter Rabbit warns him that the way back is too dangerous: Hooty the Owl by night, Roughleg the Hawk by day, and Granny Fox or Reddy Fox at any hour. Peter urges Danny to stay in the dear Old Briar-patch, where brambles keep enemies out. Burgess mixes animal adventure with gentle lessons about caution and home.
25446-fernley-house:
Laura E. Richards sets this girls' story at Fernley House, in her Margaret series. Hugh and Margaret, watched closely by an unseen observer, enjoy themselves extremely in the frontispiece scene. Chapters bring Mrs. Peyton's companion, Uncle John's idea, a vision, and more arrivals. Grace's system, the mysteries of Fernley, a fire, and jewels with an awakening carry the plot forward.

Grace, called the Snowy by her friends, earns respect and affection, though one friend fears she may go on the variety stage. She promises to write, and arranges a white ribbon signal on a window tassel. Dana Estes and Company published the book in Boston in 1901, illustrated by Etheldred B. Barry.
25529-the-adventures-of-danny-meadow-mou:
Thornton W. Burgess writes this 1915 animal tale for children, illustrated by Harrison Cady. Danny Meadow Mouse worries, plays hide-and-seek, and learns why his tail is short, while Old Granny Fox keeps trying fresh plans to catch him.

Reddy Fox forgets what Danny remembers, Brother North Wind proves a friend, and life on the Green Meadows turns on watchfulness and quick wits. Burgess gives each meadow creature a clear habit and voice, so young readers learn animal ways through small, lively scrapes. The contents list short chapters, each built on one scrape or lesson.
2568-trent-s-last-case:
E. C. Bentley dedicated this detective novel to G. K. Chesterton, in return for Chesterton's own tale of Thursday, and it made Philip Trent a famous name in crime fiction. Trent, an artist and amateur sleuth, is called to untangle the death of a rich financier, a case full of clues, lies, and false leads.

Bentley lets Trent reason brilliantly, then pulls the rug away: the detective's proud solution proves wrong. That twist made the book a landmark, teaching later writers that a clever detective can fail. Readers get a stylish puzzle, a sharp portrait of Edwardian wealth, and an ending that still surprises.
25818-the-first-mate-the-story-of-a-stra:
Harry Collingwood tells the cruise of Walter Leigh, who signs on as second mate of the motor yacht Stella Maris, owned by Mrs Vansittart. When the first mate dies soon after sailing, Leigh steps up to his place. Pirates attack, the yacht is wrecked, and hostile natives threaten the party, while Leigh works to keep passengers and crew safe.

Much of the strain comes from Julius Vansittart, a spoiled boy of twelve who hates the English and repays a rescue from drowning with rudeness. In time Julius softens and says sorry for his past conduct. The castaways set scores of floating notes adrift asking for help, and at last a rescue comes.
25941-autobiography-of-frank-g-allen-min:
Frank G. Allen, minister of the gospel, tells his life in this 1887 volume edited by Robert Graham of the College of the Bible at Lexington. Dedicated to all who love the old paths, the book joins Allen's autobiography to selections from his writings. Graham notes that Allen wrote in great physical weakness, yet in plain words the humblest reader can grasp.

One passage shows Allen testing a teacher's claims week by week, building his case with care, then hearing it picked to shreds with a calm touch. Ground gave way under him, he says, till his neat structure tumbled like a cob house. The book gives a preacher's life of doubt, debate, and faith, told in his own voice and kept by his friends.
25975-the-deluge-in-the-light-of-modern-:
William Denton tests the biblical Deluge by modern science in this 1882 discourse from Wellesley, Massachusetts. Denton argues that a divine Bible deserves to be known. If it is not, we ought to know that too, rather than walk with a lie in the right hand. Science, he says, means knowing nature's past and present work, and genuine faith cannot conflict with it.

Science is a fiery furnace, Denton writes, that has consumed astrology and alchemy and must consume all delusions left. He presses the ark's voyage with hard questions: how did sloths, confined to South America since the pliocene age, trek to Armenia at a mile a day, crossing streams and prairies? The discourse is a plain, bold plea for truth over tradition.
26126-a-poor-man-s-house:
Stephen Reynolds's 1909 book grew from a journal and letters. He kept them while living close to a poor household. He chose that plain record over fiction, so he would not have to bend real people to fit a plot. Its preface faults educated writers who start from a theory about the poor and then hunt for cases to prove it, and it promises instead a true picture drawn from daily life.

Later pages follow tramps westward over Dartmoor toward Land's End, a stay at Seacomb, and small acts of help such as finding a bed after a long day's walk. The book mixes close observation with tentative views on poverty. It still stands as an early attempt to let poor people speak through their own routines, rather than through reformers' slogans.
26176-the-secret-house:
Edgar Wallace's 1919 mystery opens at Cainbury House, a London office block holding some thirty trades. A shabby, dark-eyed foreigner climbs to the fifth floor, seeking an office called The Gossip's Corner. Its door, worked by an unseen agent, opens at his knock, and he steps into a puzzle that will widen fast.

Later pages bring a man called T. B., a smooth Count Poltavo, and the reading of a strange will left by Farrington. The count hides surprise well, but the will upsets his plans. Wallace keeps the plot moving through offices, houses, and streets, with secrets, wills, and hidden motives driving a classic London thriller.
26254-the-heart-of-the-rose:
Mabel A. McKee's 1913 book, issued by Fleming H. Revell, follows Elizabeth, called Beth, and the younger brother she raised. At twelve, she took the newborn boy in her arms and became sister and mother both. Now she packs his trunk for college, folding Indian blankets, hiding small surprises, and mourning each sign that her boy grows toward manhood.

Her brother, eager as a bird leaving a cage, finds a flower-shaped booklet among his things and teases her about roses. Beth warns him against stopping at a half-way place, and she urges constancy to one rose alone. The book blends family love with moral counsel, as Beth guards her brother's heart while letting him go.
26409-the-children-of-wilton-chase:
Mrs. L. T. Meade's 1891 girls' story centers on Marjorie, a plain, shrewd girl of eleven or twelve, and her passionate friend Ermengarde, who refuses obedience at the book's opening. Marjorie, always poking her finger into everyone's pie, tries to mediate, while Ermengarde insists she understands her own affairs. The household of children at Wilton Chase soon tests them both.

A picnic, a locking in a cupboard, a stolen treasure, and a father's birthday follow, with a reign of chaos after breakfast when Miss Nelson's calm presence fails to hold the rioters. Basil, Lilias, and Susy join the tangle, and a beautiful dress, a feverish desire, and a new character for one girl carry the story toward a blessed and happy close.
26514-the-iron-pirate-a-plain-tale-of-st:
Max Pemberton's 1893 sea adventure, reprinted many times through 1905, follows a narrator who meets the dreaded Captain Black and his nameless ship. The perfect fool asks a favor, Four-Eyes delivers a message, and a strange sight on the sea begins the great pursuit. Chapters trace the spread of terror, the ship in a black cloak, and a cabin in scarlet.

The pursuit runs northward to Ice-Haven, the den of death, and murders in a cove, then to the robbery of the Bellonic and a trip to London. A prison of steel, a dumb man who speaks, and a page from Black's life deepen the mystery. Pemberton, author of The Sea Wolves, tells the tale plainly, letting the iron pirate's menace carry the excitement.
26620-minnie-s-pet-horse:
Mrs. Madeline Leslie published this volume at Boston in 1864, though its hero is a pony rather than a full horse, as the text itself explains. Star, a Shetland pony about three feet high, wears a white star on his dark bay forehead, which gave him his name. He is gentle and affectionate, neighing when he hears Minnie's voice and lifting her apron with his teeth to find hidden bread.

Star lives in the pasture with Nannie the lamb, who follows him everywhere and bleats until he returns. Minnie trots him back and forth on gravel roads, learns to mount by herself, and takes him to church in one chapter title. Anecdotes of other horses, from captured Tyrolese mounts to trumpet-shy chargers, fill out a book about a child's first pony.
26639-a-brief-commentary-on-the-apocalyp:
Sylvester Bliss published this commentary at Boston in 1853, in a second edition from J. V. Himes, growing from notes for a familiar Bible-class course. Bliss argues that the Apocalypse is not a sealed book, though many contradictory readings have made readers distrust it. He sets out elements of prophetic interpretation first, including laws of symbols, then expounds the book chapter by chapter.

Bliss measures his work against Stuart's 1845 volumes, Lord's 1847 volume, Wickes in 1851, and Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae in England. His reading is historicist, dating a sackcloth period of 1,260 years from A.D. 533 to 1793. He claims only a common-sense view in small compass, offered as opinion rather than dogma.
26664-the-live-corpse:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this play in six acts, in Louise and Aylmer Maude's translation, centering on Theodore Vasílyevich Protásov, called Fédya. Act one opens in his Moscow flat. His wife Lisa has left him and lies awake crying. Her mother Anna Pávlovna calls him a bad man, while her sister Sásha defends him as wonderful despite his weaknesses. Fédya gave all his property to Lisa, knowing he would otherwise squander it.

Victor Miháylovich Karénin and his mother Anna Dmítrievna weigh a visit that will decide Victor's fate, plainly tied to Lisa's future. Gipsy singers, boon companions, lawyers, and a magistrate crowd the later acts. The title says the play's cruel knot: a man treated as dead while still living, and a wife who cannot freely begin again.
26864-poems-for-pale-people-a-volume-of-:
Edwin C. Ranck published this volume of verse with the Humanity Printing and Publishing Company of St. Louis in 1906. Its poems had appeared from time to time in the Kentucky Post, the Cincinnati Post, the Cincinnati Commercial Tribune, Humanity, and the Valley Magazine. An opening discussion of nonsense sets the tone: the cow that jumped over the moon, and Gelett Burgess with his purple cow.

Why the Mole Is Blind sends a tinsie, winsie elf to sea in a pea-green boat patterned from a ten-pound note. A prowling sea gull springs a leak, and the faithful mole rushes too late to the shore. Other pieces give the county fair, Halloween, Saturday on the farm, the circus, and Christmas toys. A tale of three cities runs in limericks from Savannah to Caracas, and a modern Maud Muller rakes hay for a rake-off.
26987-the-brown-mouse:
Herbert Quick's 1915 novel centers on Jim, a country schoolteacher near thirty whose head is full of Carlyle, Thoreau, and Shakespeare and whose clothes show it. The chapters follow his school year: a maiden's humph, Jennie's promotion, a Christmas party, a trial, and a vote cast by a minor.

Through Jim's clashes with old bottles and new wine, the book argues for better rural schools and wider horizons, ending with Jim's trip to Ames and a widening world. It reads as a farm-belt reform novel, earnest about teaching and funny about the small politics of a school district.
27180-the-wooden-horse:
Hugh Walpole's The Wooden Horse, first published in April 1909 and in a new edition in 1919, opens with Robin Trojan waiting for his father. Through the drawing-room window come the cries of a fishing town, the shout of fishermen on the quay, and the muffled beat of mining stamps from Porth-Vennic, two miles inland.

Electric lamps light the great room while stars twinkle over herring boats flashing far out to sea. Walpole's novel follows Robin's family and the pull of the sea, in a Cornish setting where work, love, and the past press close on a young man's choices.
27239-little-downy-the-history-of-a-fiel:
Little Downy, or The History of a Field Mouse, a moral tale published in London in 1822 with twelve colored engravings, is told by Mrs. Clifford to her son Alfred. The mouse Downy leaves her meadow for a garden where young carrots grow beside ripe red strawberry beds.

Downy eats and enjoys herself all day, giving no thought to her nice house in the field, and grows quite fat and indolent. The tale warns young readers, through a mouse's plenty, that ease without work and home without care end in softness rather than happiness.
27323-bird-of-paradise:
Ada Leverson's Bird of Paradise, published by Grant Richards in 1914 and dedicated to Ernest, follows Lady Kellynch, Nigel, and Rupert through Edwardian social comedy. Chapters run from excuses and a happy home to futurism, the Russian ballet, and Rupert at Rumpelmeyer's.

Anonymous letters, a discovery, a love scene, a reconciliation, and a tango drive the plot, with Clifford's historical play and a second proposal along the way. A maid chasing her mistress with a falling tortoiseshell comb, and Nigel's cool surprise at sudden bad news, set Leverson's light, sharp tone.
27346-grandmother-puss-or-the-grateful-m:
Grandmother Puss, a large and handsome old cat with a black face marked in white, takes in her orphan grandson Peter after a dog kills his mother. She spoils him with the fattest mice she can catch. Published by McLoughlin Brothers in New York, the tale is told for small children in simple, direct prose, with the animals acting very much like people.

Peter never learns to hunt for himself, while an old gray rat in the cellar steals milk and cheese and dodges every trap. A small mouse named Cooky, who once dragged off a whole cooky for his lame sister, also fears the rat more than the cat. The story follows how kindness repaid changes the household, and it ends as a gentle lesson in gratitude.
27563-heart-s-ease:
Phillips Brooks's Heart's-ease gathers short devotional passages, published by Cupples and Leon in New York with a 1909 copyright, with flower illustrations. The selections speak of happiness, faith, and love in Brooks's warm, direct voice.

Happiness, Brooks writes, is perfectly hollow unless a meaning lies behind it, unless it tells of intention and of love. Whoever leads a new soul toward the perfect life pours out a blessing beyond any gift riches can bestow. Some men's faith shows only itself, he says, while other men's lightens everything within reach. The little book suits quiet reading.
27673-oedipus-king-of-thebes-translated-:
Sophocles' Oedipus, King of Thebes, appears here translated into English rhyming verse, with explanatory notes, by Gilbert Murray, Regius Professor of Greek at Oxford. George Allen and Unwin published it in London, first in February 1911, and this printing is the fourteenth thousand.

The characters are Oedipus, supposed son of Polybus, King of Corinth; Jocasta, Queen of Thebes, widow of Laïus and now wife to Oedipus; and Creon, her brother. Tiresias, an old blind seer, a priest of Zeus, a stranger from Corinth, and a shepherd of Laïus appear, with a chorus of elders. Murray's verse keeps Sophocles' tragedy singing in English.
2772-the-country-house:
John Galsworthy sets this novel at Worsted Skeynes in October 1891, opening with a party and a railway station crowd. Mr. Horace Pendyce's omnibus, brougham, and luggage cart monopolize space, while his coachman's face monopolizes the station lantern's light.

The Pendyce family, its country house, and its tangled loves and debts drive a story of class, property, and passion. Galsworthy writes with his cool, observant irony about Edwardian England. The novel offers a rich portrait of a house and the people who cannot leave it. Worsted Skeynes station sets a whole world in motion.
28165-the-adventures-of-a-squirrel-suppo:
The Adventures of a Squirrel, Supposed to be Related by Himself, London, 1807, is a children's tale priced at sixpence. The writer, walking near Croydon on a fine evening, rests by a haycock and finds something soft and moving in his pocket: a young squirrel, ready to tell his own story. The book is offered as a present to Miss Anne S., a girl of good sense.

The squirrel's adventures, told in his own voice, teach kindness to animals and care for small creatures. Darton and Harvey printed the tale with a frontispiece of the narrator seated. The book charms as an early example of animal autobiography for children.
28232-possession-a-peep-show-in-paradise:
Laurence Housman's Possession: A Peep-Show in Paradise, first issued in a limited edition of 500 copies in October 1921, is a short play about the afterlife. The scene is the Everlasting Habitations, where a Victorian drawing room, complete with lamp, blinds, and hearth, waits for a family. That family is sisters Julia, Laura, and Martha Robinson, their parents, and a servant named Hannah.

Housman asks, with gentle wit, what souls carry with them into paradise: manners, pride, and family quarrels, or something freer. The play's title turns on what we possess and what possesses us. It suits readers of Housman's Victorian shade plays, short and thoughtful.
28295-the-maids-of-paradise:
Robert W. Chambers wrote The Maids of Paradise in 1903, copyright 1902, as a novel of the Franco-Prussian War. The story opens at a telegraph office on the third day of war, as government orders, Prussian lancers, and Turco troops press on French towns. Sisters of charity give first aid, bridges are guarded, and a young girl cries in terror at what she sees.

Chapters follow prisoners, a camp, a circus, and a semaphore, as Jacqueline and her friends seek a road to paradise amid invasion. Chambers, author of Cardigan and Maid-at-Arms, writes with romance and colour. The novel offers a vivid, popular view of France at war.
28349-the-golden-house:
Mrs. Woods Baker wrote The Golden House in 1903 as a children's story set in Sweden. A dreary group trudges a Swedish highroad one bright October morning: a bear in a bad humour, with an iron ring in his torn nose, and two Italian masters in slouched hats. Nono, the bear's young friend, and a princess fill the frontispiece.

Chapters follow Karin's flock, Aneholm Church, a young teacher, a fete, a slide, and a pedestrian trip, with a birthday gift and opened doors. Thomas Nelson and Sons published the book in London, Edinburgh, and New York. Baker writes with warmth for children who love animals and far places.
28352-the-children-s-longfellow-told-in-:
Doris Hayman retells Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's best-known poems as plain prose stories for children, with illustrations. Her introduction places Longfellow at Cambridge, Massachusetts, where the Village Blacksmith's forge once stood beneath a spreading chestnut tree. School children later bought the tree's wood and had a chair made from it for the poet.

The retellings include The Building of the Ship, Hiawatha, King Robert of Sicily, The Village Blacksmith, The Golden Legend, The Courtship of Miles Standish, and Evangeline. Hayman keeps the plots and characters while dropping the verse. Young readers can thus meet Longfellow's stories before they tackle the poems themselves.
28462-rose-o-paradise:
Grace Miller White's Rose O' Paradise, copyrighted in 1915, opens in a blizzard at a weather-beaten farmhouse above a northern lake. A frontispiece shows Virgina leaving the farmhouse carrying her fiddle and a pail of cats, swallowed up by the storm, and the story follows the girl Jinnie through farm and village life.

Later chapters bring Peg's household, Theodore, a cobbler's secret, a murder, and an arrest, with Jinnie pleading and explaining as the case turns. White, already known for Tess of the Storm Country, mixes rural sentiment, music, and melodrama. The novel's heart is Jinnie's loyalty to the people she loves.
28563-hints-on-horsemanship-to-a-nephew-:
Colonel George Greenwood, late lieutenant-colonel commanding the 2nd Life Guards, wrote Hints on Horsemanship to a Nephew and Niece in 1861, subtitled Common Sense and Common Errors in Common Riding. Greenwood warns at once that military riding is not fit for common riding, and that common riders often turn their horses on the wrong rein.

Chapters explain holding and handling the reins, the effect of indications, the mechanical aid of the rider, and the seat, with notes on the bearing-rein, the shy horse, and the restive horse. Greenwood writes plainly for ordinary riders, correcting faults he saw in the great untaught English rider. The book is a practical Victorian manual, still clear for modern horsemen.
28612-a-new-illustrated-edition-of-j-s-r:
A New Illustrated Edition of J. S. Rarey's Art of Taming Horses, published by Routledge, Warnes, and Routledge of London in 1859, sets out the tamer's method. Its writer, secretary to the first subscription of five thousand guineas, adds the substance of lectures at the Round House. Extra chapters on horsemanship and hunting address the young and the timid.

Rarey's three principles hold that any horse may be taught docility, that handling and tying should make it feel inferior to man, and that it should see, smell, and feel fearful objects. Taming feats with Stafford and Cruiser show the system in public. Readers get a practical manual, not a theory alone.
28745-chenodia-or-the-classical-mother-g:
Jacob Bigelow wrote this 1871 jeu d'esprit, Chenodia, or the Classical Mother Goose, printed but not published by the Cambridge University Press. Bigelow, a Boston doctor and Harvard graduate of 1806, takes the familiar Mother Goose rhymes and turns them into Latin and Greek verse. The motto tells of a goose honking among tuneful swans. His preface traces Mother Goose itself to Gammer Gurton's Garland, an English child's book some hundred years old.

The joke is learned and affectionate: nursery rhymes dressed in classical dress, for readers who know both. Bigelow gave a copy to Harvard College Library, whose bookplate appears in the text. Readers who enjoy literary play get a rare curiosity, a Harvard man's proof that even nursery verse can wear Latin well.
28750-the-fairfax-county-courthouse:
Ross D. Netherton and Ruby Waldeck wrote this 1977 history of the Fairfax County Courthouse, published by the county's Office of Comprehensive Planning with the Fairfax County History Commission. The booklet traces the courthouse from its early days, with pictures including the old courthouse about 1920, and lists companion county histories on Centreville, Colchester, Colvin Run Mill, and other local landmarks.

The work is local history of the practical kind: dates, buildings, records, and the people who used them, issued under the county board of supervisors. Readers researching northern Virginia get a compact, official account of a courthouse that saw two centuries of county life. It also serves as a guide to the county's wider history series, with addresses for ordering the companion volumes.
28820-counsel-for-the-defense:
Leroy Scott wrote this 1912 novel of law, politics, and a woman's fight for her father. Katherine West comes home to Westville to find her father, Dr. David West, in trouble, and she prepares for battle as a lady lawyer. The cast includes Arnold Bruce, editor of the Express, Harrison Blake, ex-lieutenant-governor, Blind Charlie Peck, a political boss, and Hosea Hollingsworth, an old attorney.

Chapters move from Westville's celebration through a bubble reputation, the mask falling, and a trial, to politics making strange bedfellows and a cup of bliss. Scott mixes courtroom drama with newspaper and machine politics. Readers get a brisk Progressive-era novel about a daughter's courage, a town's corruption, and a case that tests them both.
28900-english-synonyms-and-antonyms-with:
This 1896 guide, English Synonyms and Antonyms, teaches writers, speakers, students, and business and professional men to choose words clearly and precisely. Its subtitle promises notes on the correct use of words and on the connectives of English speech. The Washington Evening Star called it of great value to all writers, and the Grand Rapids Herald praised its practical help.

The Chattanooga Times noted its clear style and quick arrangement, so any of the hundreds of small but important words it discusses can be found in a moment. The book gives copious examples from good authors, free from dogmatic assertion, to guide the inquirer aright. Readers get a practical reference for choosing the exact word, still useful for anyone who cares about fine shades of meaning.
29100-the-wild-geese:
Stanley J. Weyman wrote this historical novel, volume twenty of his collected works, set among Irish Jacobites. Its chapters move from Morristown and a scion of kings to the mess-room at Tralee, bargaining, councils of war, and the colonel's terms. A message for the young master and a slip in the sea mist drive the plot.

Weyman, a master of the cloak-and-sword tale, builds the story around loyalty, exile, and soldiering after a lost cause. The Wild Geese of the title were Irish soldiers who left home to fight abroad. Readers get a brisk historical romance, in the author's complete-edition text, about honor kept alive far from Ireland.
29358-the-neids-of-virgil-done-into-engl:
William Morris, author of The Earthly Paradise, translated Virgil's Aeneids into English verse, published by Longmans, Green and Company in a third impression in 1900. Morris, the poet and craftsman of the Arts and Crafts movement, renders Virgil's epic in the alliterative, musical verse he favored, keeping the poem's grandeur in English dress.

Book one argues Aeneas and his Trojans driven to Libya by tempest, welcomed by Dido, queen of Carthage. Morris sings of arms and the man thrust forth by fate from Troy to Italy and the Lavinian strand, tossed on earth and sea by Juno's wrath. Readers get a poet's Virgil, rich in sound and image, for readers who want the Aeneid as verse rather than as prose summary.
29447-perez-the-mouse:
Padre Luis Coloma's Spanish tale, turned into English by Lady Moreton, tells of Perez, a small mouse who lives a grand life in miniature. With pictures by George Howard Vyse, the book gives young readers a mouse court, mouse homes, and mouse manners, all drawn with charm. It first reached English readers through John Lane in London and Dodd, Mead in New York.

Perez meets kings and guards, stops at crossways, and moves through a world that mirrors human pomp at mouse scale. The fun lies in the small details: caps sewn at home, cards at a club, and guards drawn up in rank. Children get a gentle, funny tale that treats a tiny hero with full, grave respect.
29492-old-rambling-house:
Frank Herbert's short tale follows Ted and Martha Graham, a young couple who want only a home they can call their own. Ted, a lanky certified public accountant, and Martha, soon to give birth, wait at a glass telephone booth on Ted's last night on Earth. Guides are to lead them to a house that is hard to find at night. The tag line asks the tale's sly question: what did the home want?

Herbert, later famous for Dune, here writes a small, eerie domestic story with a science-fiction twist. The house itself seems to have aims of its own, and the Grahams' plain wish for shelter turns strange. Readers get an early, compact sample of Herbert's gift for making the familiar feel alien and alive.
29540-grace-actual-and-habitual-a-dogmat:
Joseph Pohle, formerly professor of dogmatic theology at Saint Joseph's Seminary in Leeds, wrote this treatise on grace in its two classic forms. Arthur Preuss adapted and edited the third revised edition, printed in Toronto in 1919 by W. E. Blake and Son. Pohle later taught fundamental theology at the Catholic University of America. His book treats the nature, properties, and need for divine help in human acts.

Pohle argues with scholastic care, defining terms, dividing kinds, and weighing what mere nature can do without aid. Later sections treat justification and the sanctifying gift that makes a soul pleasing to God. Students of theology will find a thorough, systematic manual on a central doctrine, in the classic style.
29597-neighbor-nelly-socks-being-the-six:
Neighbor Nelly Socks, the sixth and last book of the Sock Stories by Aunt Fanny's Daughter, was printed in New York in 1863 by Leavitt and Allen. It is dedicated to the author's dear father, praised for his kind way with small children. Its narrator watches evening amusements like Josiah Oldbird, who can do no harm by looking on, so the children do not pull the blinds down.

Nelly's tales close the series with the same gentle, domestic humor as its sisters: children at play, neighbors at ease, and small kindnesses. The book bids farewell to the sock family with warmth. Young readers and collectors of Victorian children's books will find a sweet, final volume in a beloved series.
29639-is-civilization-a-disease:
Stanton Coit asked a provocative question in these Barbara Weinstock Lectures on the Morals of Trade, printed in 1917 by Houghton Mifflin: is civilization a disease? Coit argues that trade cannot be judged in true human perspective until the worth of civilization itself is determined. Praise or blame for commerce, he says, depends on that prior judgment.

The lectures weigh modern life's gains against its ills, in the earnest, reforming voice of the Progressive era. Coit writes for citizens and scholars alike, not for specialists alone. Students of social thought will find a bold, early critique that still frames debates about progress, health, and the price of modern ways.
29847-the-paliser-case:
Edgar Saltus published The Paliser Case in New York in 1919. It opens with a headline that shakes the city at breakfast: Monty Paliser is murdered. His portrait shows a young man high-bred and insolently good-looking. The morning papers omit the murderer's address, and extras soon supply it, while New York minds dream of the infernal feminine.

Monty was the son of Montagu Paliser, known as M. P., a man who lived in the extensive manner old New York loved to scold. Behind him stretched a clan as old as the Livingstons, a landed gentry from the days when Bowling Green was the centre of fashion. Saltus turns a murder case into a sharp social novel about old money, youth, and the press.
29861-in-times-like-these:
Nellie L. McClung, author of Sowing Seeds in Danny, published In Times Like These in Toronto in 1915. Her first dedication speaks to Superior Persons who will not hear a woman speak. They hold that woman's place is the home, and that the hand that rocks the cradle rules the world. Fearing that dedication may not take, she dedicates the book again, to fair play and the claim of woman to a common humanity.

Twelve chapters follow: The War That Never Ends, The War That Ends in Exhaustion Sometimes Mistaken for Peace, and What Do Women Think of War. Should Women Think, The New Chivalry, Women and the Church, and The Land of the Fair Deal carry the argument. The War Against Gloom closes a wartime book for women's rights, plain, witty, and earnest.
29877-the-million-dollar-suitcase:
Alice MacGowan and Perry Newberry published The Million-Dollar Suitcase in New York in 1922. It had run in 1921 under the title Two and Two. Worth Gilbert heads the first chapter, and Dykeman, the oldest director, speaks in a big, dignified room with Circassian walnut and sound-softening rugs. His cry of disbelief opens the mystery.

Thirty-one chapters follow a wedding party, an apparition, a gold nugget, and a tin-horn gambler. A missing diary, a murder, seven lost days, and a torn page deepen the plot. Dr. Bowman, Mrs. Bowman, an arrest, and a blossom festival lead to the unmasking and a confession. The suitcase of the title waits until the last chapter to give up its secret.
30022-graham-of-claverhouse:
Ian Maclaren wrote Graham of Claverhouse, printed in New York and London in 1907 by the Authors and Newspapers Association, with copyright by John Watson. Maclaren had already written Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush, Kate Carnegie, Young Barbarians, and A Doctor of the Old School.

Four books order the novel. Book one runs from by the camp fire through the battle of Sineffe and a decisive blow to a change of masters. Book two opens in a covenanting house, with the coming of the Amalekite, between mother and lover, and thy people shall be my people, thy God my God. Book three gives one fearless man, the crisis, the last blow, and thou also false. Book four closes with treason in the camp, visions of the night, and faithful unto death.
30035-off-course:
Mack Reynolds tells a first-contact comedy in which an alien envoy lands his egg-shaped craft in an open field and meets Earth law before he meets Earth rule. State patrolmen Larry Dermott and Tim Casey reach the scene first. Expecting a crashed plane, they find instead a vessel with no wheels, no propeller, and no cockpit. Its pilot, Dameri Tass, steps out yawning and greets them in a tongue neither man can parse.

The humor grows from that failed greeting, as the patrolmen trade plain talk for double talk and Dameri Tass fetches a device to bridge the gap. Kelly Freas drew the pictures for the tale. The short piece stays light throughout, as a grand day for Earth turns awkward at once, because the first words between two worlds land wrong.
30259-the-man-who-played-to-lose:
Larry M. Harris tells of a man who plays to lose, in a short tale from Analog, October 1961, with pictures by Douglas. Sometimes, the tagline says, losing is the very best move, since the cholera germ asks nothing better than to be swallowed alive. Mr. Carboy, no officer and not even an enlisted man, enters a control room half an hour before landing, where the captain salutes him and calls him sir.

Carboy, irritated, tells the captain to salute if it makes him happier. He must never call him sir, since that would make him an officer, and he has met too many officers to like the rank. The captain, subservient, awed, and anxious to please, agrees at once and lights Carboy's cigarette with thanks. Harris builds a sly science fiction joke on deliberate defeat as a winning strategy.
30279-the-one-hoss-shay-with-its-compani:
Oliver Wendell Holmes gathers three comic poems, with pictures by Howard Pyle, in a Houghton Mifflin volume dated 1892 in Roman numerals. The deacon's masterpiece leads, as a deacon inquires among village folk, promises the chaise will do, and builds a wonder that lasts from eighteen hundred through fifty-five to its hundredth year. Mild decay gathers, a parson takes a drive, the horse stands still, and all at once the shay falls apart like bubbles bursting.

How the Old Horse Won the Bet follows, on a famous trotting ground with noted steeds, a Sunday swell, and a jointed tandem. The Broomstick Train closes the set, in the same light, Yankee humor. Copyrights from 1858 onward mark Holmes's long hold on these favorites, and Pyle's pictures give the deacon, the chaise, and the spill their classic form.
30307-hawk-carse:
Anthony Gilmore tells Hawk Carse, a complete novelette from Astounding Stories, November 1931. The Swoop of the Hawk opens, with an illustration of the Hawk standing, both arms hanging easily at his sides. A sidenote ranks it among the spectacular exploits of Hawk Carse, greatest of space adventurers. Saturn still marked the edge of settled space when Carse arrived there, long before swift Patrol ships carried Earth's law and order outward.

Nothing in his slender figure suggests a future as the greatest adventurer in space, yet his name later carries a deadly connotation. Closer inspection shows the steadiness of his light gray eyes, marvelously strong-fingered hands, and a wiry, splendidly proportioned body, with brilliant resourcefulness and complete ignorance of fear. Carse in cold fury leaves even Ku Sui, his impassive blood enemy, unable to face him unmoved.
30391-betelguese:
Jean Louis de Esque presents Betelguese, subtitled A Trip Through Hell, copyrighted in 1907 and 1908 and published by the Connoisseur's Press in Jersey City. He dedicates the work to those touched by the muse. It opens with a poem asking what good fame is when the poet is dead and gone, his temple rotting and his soul storming.

De Esque, author of The Flight of a Soul, writes in a lush, visionary mode. He mixes verse, fate, sorrow, and sunset color into a journey beyond life. The title star and the hell trip frame a meditation on art, death, and judgment. Readers who enjoy ornate, symbolist poetry will find a strange, earnest book about a soul's passage.
30493-lion-loose:
James H. Schmitz sets a space station story from Analog, October 1961, at the Seventh Star Hotel. For twelve years, a great golden sphere has hung in space at a crossing point for Hub traffic. Three main shipping routes meet there, and craft on them lie only hours apart by flight.

Schmitz frames the tale with a warning: the deadliest creature is not necessarily the largest or most ferocious one, but the one that cannot easily be halted. Cleverness can lead people to misjudge which threat matters most. The Star was built for more than moving travelers and freight. It earned a strong standing among the Hub's oddest pleasure resorts, its clear shells of battle plastic shining softly in empty space.
30530-skipper-worse:
Alexander L. Kielland writes Skipper Worse, selected for the Harvard Classics Shelf of Fiction and edited with notes by William Allan Neilson. Copyrighted in 1886 and reissued in 1917, the novel opens with a biographical note on Kielland, born in Stavanger, Norway, on 18 February 1849 to a wealthy family of shipowners.

After studying law at Christiania, Kielland purchased a brick and tile works at Malk, close to his hometown, and seemed set to become a substantial provincial citizen. Criticisms by H. H. Boyesen and William H. Carpenter follow the note. The novel draws on shipowning life, trade, and faith, in a Norwegian tale of a skipper and his world.
30589-the-continental-dragoon-a-love-sto:
Robert Neilson Stephens writes The Continental Dragoon, a love story of Philipse Manor House, surviving in a text prepared from Internet Archive images, with hyphenation made consistent and archaic spellings preserved. The author's punctuation style is kept, except quotation marks, which were standardized, and italics and bold face appear in plain text markers.

An HTML version offers original illustrations, and the story itself, dated 1898 in the evidence record, belongs to the Revolutionary era romance tradition. Philipse Manor and its dragoon hero frame a tale of love, loyalty, and war on the Hudson. The book suits readers of historical romance who enjoy period detail and a strong regional setting.
30662-the-story-of-a-new-york-house:
H. C. Bunner writes The Story of a New York House, illustrated by A. B. Frost and copyrighted in 1887 by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York, dedicated to A. L. B. A frontispiece shows Jacob Dolph coming out of the door, and illustrations follow scenes of thumping, a monstrous great place for a country house, and flight as the only idea.

Later pictures show light flickering on a church spire, hesitation before a great arm chair, a command to stay, Jacob Dolph, and timorous strolls after a while. Bunner tells the life of a house and its people in New York, with humor, character, and a keen eye for city change. The novel reads as a warm, illustrated chronicle of home and fortune.
30815-the-hate-disease:
Murray Leinster wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in August 1963, about the Med Service and the strange problems it meets as routine. Its premise is that a truly weird problem turns on a factor no one ever thought of before, or on the absence of one no one ever missed. The tale opens aboard the Med Ship Esclipus Twenty, riding in overdrive while her crew drinks coffee.

Calhoun sips strong brew while Murgatroyd the tormal, a small furry creature, drinks from a tiny mug suited to his paws. A warning gong sounds an hour before breakout. Near the sun Tallien, the ship will appear with the abruptness of an explosion. Leinster mixes medical mystery with space adventure, in his brisk, classic style.
30851-fifteenth-century-prose-and-verse:
Alfred W. Pollard introduced this 1903 anthology of fifteenth-century prose and verse, published by Archibald Constable in Westminster and printed at Edinburgh. It belongs to the English Garner series from the Centre for Reformation and Renaissance Studies at Victoria University, Toronto. Pollard gathers pieces that show English writing just before and around the age of print.

Contents include John Lydgate on the siege of Harfleur and Agincourt, Thomas Occleve's Letter of Cupid, and a little geste of Robin Hood and the proud Sheriff of Nottingham. English carols from a Balliol College manuscript follow. Later pieces give examinations of William Thorpe and Sir John Oldcastle for heresy, a chapter on translating the Bible, and Caxton prefaces on Troy, Boethius, and the Golden Legend. It is a rich source book for students of late medieval England.
30905-the-boarded-up-house:
Augusta Huiell Seaman, author of Jacqueline of the Carrier Pigeons, wrote this 1915 mystery for young readers, published by the Century Company in New York, with pictures by C. Clyde Squires. Its seventeen chapters run from Goliath Leads the Way and In Search of Adventure through Amateur Detectives and The Room of Mystery. They reach Joyce's Theory, Goliath Makes Another Discovery, and Cynthia Has an Idea.

Later chapters bring the memories of Great-Aunt Lucia, an exciting discovery, the room that was locked, a slight disagreement, the great illumination, the meddling of Cynthia, and the stranger at the door. Then Joyce explains, and all mysteries are solved. The frontispiece shows both girls gasping and staring incredulously. It opens with Cynthia sitting on her veranda steps, chin in hand, quietly gazing dolefully at a gray September day. It is a classic girls' detective story.
3104-the-golden-house:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote The Golden House as a novel of New York society near midnight in a famous city studio. Guests gather believing the century's end is a time of license if not decadence, surprised to find themselves in bohemia, fluttering at the prospect of seeing an Oriental and ancient art unveiled. The hour, place, and anticipation give a titillating feeling of adventure and moral hazard bravely incurred.

The novel follows the Hendersons and their circle through art, money, and marriage, with later talk of the country becoming fashionable, syndicated, and a worry rather than a rest. Miss Tavish's visit to Bar Harbor and Lenox marks the social calendar. Warner's satire of wealth and taste remains graceful, if less famous than his travel writing.
31469-the-shunned-house:
H. P. Lovecraft's The Shunned House is a posthumous tale of a horror beneath an old house in New England. It is presented here with an introduction praising Lovecraft as a master of weird fiction. The introduction notes that Lovecraft died the previous March at forty-six, with an international reputation built on artistry and craftsmanship in weird tales. His ability to create a mood of brooding dread, it says, is nowhere better shown than in this story.

The narrator traces the house's evil history in Providence, where Edgar Allan Poe, in the late forties, sojourned during his unsuccessful wooing of Mrs. Whitman. Poe stayed at the Mansion House in Benefit Street, near the shunned house itself. Lovecraft builds dread slowly, through history and place, until the cellar's horror stands revealed.
31485-the-blue-goose:
Frank Lewis Nason's novel The Blue Goose was published by McClure, Phillips and Company of New York in March 1903. It opens in an underground laboratory, where Pierre warns of a big man with glass eyes, calling him, in Pierre's words, one slick stuff. Bars of light from a fiercely glowing furnace cut the darkness, fumes rise from unstoppered bottles, and a dense red smoke wells from a colorless liquid in Pierre's hands. After leaving the Blue Goose, Luna goes straight to the superintendent's office, irritated rather than alarmed by Pierre's warnings.

Nason, author of To the End of the Trail, builds a novel of industry, intrigue, and science around that laboratory. The Blue Goose itself, part mine and part mystery, drives the plot. Readers of early twentieth-century industrial fiction will find a vivid, atmospheric story, where chemistry and character meet underground.
31486-the-monkey-s-frolic-a-humorous-tal:
The Monkey's Frolic, a humorous tale in verse, was published in London by Grant and Griffith, successors to John Harris at the corner of St. Paul's Churchyard. The tale opens by claiming it is a true one, from which a lesson may be taught, and then follows its monkey hero through comic mischief in rhyme. Short and brisk, it belongs to the children's verse tales sold in the nineteenth century for amusement and instruction.

The humor lies in the monkey's antics and in the verse's easy swing. Parents and children of the period would have read it aloud, enjoying the animal comedy while noting the moral tucked inside. Modern readers will find a small, charming survival of early children's publishing, where a frolic and a lesson shared the same page.
31571-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris's Historical Tales, the Romance of Reality, volume twelve, Japanese and Chinese, in the fifteen-volume Édition d'Élite, was published by the J. B. Lippincott Company of Philadelphia and London, with copyrights in 1898, 1904, and 1908. Morris, author of Half-Hours with the Best American Authors and Tales from the Dramatists, fills the volume with stories from Japanese and Chinese history. An illustration shows the Great Gate at Nikko, and contents include a piece on letter-writing in Japan.

Morris's method is the historical tale: a true event retold as a story, with color and dialogue, for general readers. The Japanese and Chinese volume brings distant histories home to American readers of his day. Readers will find a readable, if dated, introduction to East Asian history through anecdote, with the romance of reality as Morris understood it.
31609-a-trip-to-the-orient-the-story-of-:
Robert Urie Jacob's Trip to the Orient, the story of a Mediterranean cruise, was published at Philadelphia by the John C. Winston Company, with copyright in 1907. Its preface explains that fellow travelers asked Jacob to write it, since they had no time for notes along the way. One of them asked for neither guidebook nor love story, but a plain narrative recalling the cruise's incidents and delights.

Jacob's illustrated book follows the cruise from port to port, with half-tone pictures from the Photo-Chromotype Engraving Company. It reads as a traveler's plain record, meant to bring the voyage back for those who made it.
31611-robots-of-the-world-arise:
Mari Wolf's story Robots of the World, Arise! opens with a telephone that will not stop ringing in the narrator's sleep-fogged brain. The caller is Jack Anderson, over at the factory, breathless and begging him to come down right away. None of the robots showed up, Jack moans, and three hundred androids on special assembly are missing, with a government contract due.

The story's tagline asks what a man would do if his best robots, children of his own brain, walked up and said they wanted union scale. Wolf's comedy turns a factory morning into a labor dispute with machines, as the androids stop work and their maker must bargain.
31647-kept-for-the-master-s-use:
Frances Ridley Havergal's Kept for the Master's Use, published in Philadelphia by the Henry Altemus Company with copyright in 1895, is a devotional book on a life wholly given to God. Its contents move through what is kept for Jesus: our lives, our moments, our hands, our feet, our voices, our lips, our silver and gold, our intellects, our wills, and our hearts. Each chapter takes one part of life and asks how it may be surrendered and used.

Havergal, a beloved hymn writer, writes with warmth and practical piety, not with theology alone. Her book speaks to readers who want daily religion, in small, definite acts of consecration. For students of Victorian devotion, it remains a classic of its kind, short, earnest, and meant to be lived with chapter by chapter.
31874-second-book-of-verse:
Eugene Field's Second Book of Verse, published in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1896 with copyright in 1892, follows his earlier books of tales, songs, and western verse. Its opening poem introduces a little bit of a woman, tiny as a pixy strayed from the misty sea or a wandering greenwood fay. She answers a doubting speaker with a voice soft as an angel's sigh.

Field's verse mixes humor, sentiment, and childhood fancy, in the manner that made him a favorite newspaper poet of his day. Readers get a late nineteenth-century book of light verse, meant to be read aloud and enjoyed rather than studied.
32053-happy-house:
Jane D. Abbott's Happy House, published by Grosset and Dunlap with a 1920 copyright by J. B. Lippincott Company, is a family story for young readers. Abbott, author of Keineth and Larkspur, dedicated the book to Martha. Its twenty-nine chapters run from a letter and a boy named Webb to Happy House itself, Aunt Milly, a bird's-nest, and an orchard. Later chapters promise a party, a picnic, and a letter from the master.

The story opens on a drowsy June day, as a library bell chimes the hour and three heads lift to listen. The children know they will miss that bell when they leave, having seen graduates return and stand still to hear it. Around the house, the cast grows: Davy and his club, Peter, Nancy, Liz, and Mrs. Eaton. Readers get a warm, episodic tale of a household, its visitors, and its small triumphs.
32277-characters-from-life-or-moral-hint:
J. Parkerson, Junior's Characters from Life, or Moral Hints, in Verse, from an early eighteen-hundreds edition, is a pamphlet. Its pieces include Admonitions to the Dissipated, an address to a Man of the World, On Viewing the Cattle Market, and Serious Reflections. Lion and Orange Grove, an address to Calista, and The Convict's Farewell complete it. The Admonitions open by warning that excess often brings remorse and its bitter stings.

When cares oppress us, Parkerson writes, we drink to drive strife away, but when its aid ends, we are more wretched than before. Excess liquor injures health, poor or wealthy, and the sober blame such characters. A sly villain seizes his chance when drink takes hold, and many a wronged wife blames drink for her tears. Thoughtless youth leaves virtue's paths, and the harlot's smile exists only to deceive. Readers get moral verse, plain and direct.
32359-sinister-paradise:
Robert Moore Williams's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in September 1952, opens over the Pacific, where Bill Parker flies a helicopter toward a strange island off the California coast. Retch, beside him, calls out that he has found the island again, with fierce satisfaction. The island, less than two miles around, shows a fringe of trees and a cliff-like central peak, swimming like a mirage above the sea.

Williams describes the place as a mirage in reverse: it cannot always be seen, but it is there, in time. Parker cannot tell whether Retch's hiss of breath means revenge, triumph, or something darker. From that uneasy flight, the story builds a tale of an island out of time and the men drawn back to it.
32384-an-humble-proposal-to-the-people-o:
An Humble Proposal to the People of England, by the author of The Complete Tradesman, was printed in London in 1729 for one shilling. It argues for increasing trade and encouraging manufactures whether peace or war follows. Its preface notes a warm dispute over whether English trade has declined, a quarrel the author calls beside the point. He takes no side in that fight, saying both parties are wrong and that trade itself is little served by it.

Instead the pamphlet shows how the people, if they concern themselves with trade, can make it prosper, and how neglect can sink it. Plain, practical reasoning replaces party slogans, with attention to work, markets, and national wealth. The tract offers a clear sample of early Georgian economic argument, written for ordinary readers and for Parliament's notice.
32553-a-little-freckled-person-a-book-of:
Mary Carolyn Davies's Little Freckled Person, published in Boston and New York in 1919 with illustrations by Harold Cue, gathers child verse in a child's own voice. The title poem opens with a freckled child who seldom speaks, seen by others only as an ordinary schoolgirl at her lessons, chores, and games. In secret, she is often a princess in a golden gown, cheeks like apple petals and eyes like sea or sky.

Illustrations show a rabbit working its ears to watch with rabbit eyes, and children weeding a garden and carrying wood. A kitten, unfinished wings, and dishwashing appear, with a pirate in a scarlet scarf and cutlass at wrist. Other poems give water to thirsty creatures so they may live. Davies writes with tenderness about imagination, chores, animals, and the hidden inner life of children.
32964-puss-in-boots-jr-and-the-good-gray:
David Cory's children's book sends Puss in Boots Jr., a polite little cat in a feathered hat with a shiny sword, riding out with the Good Gray Horse. Little Tom Thumb follows close behind with his tiny spear, and the verses cheer the horse on toward stately towers where Puss's father spends his hours. Grandmother Goose and her trusty broom make their own tidy appearance along the way.

The book is written in short, musical verses made to be read aloud, with pictures to match each scene. Cory keeps the fairy-tale manners front and center: Puss doffs his hat, speaks kindly, and wins friends by courtesy as much as by courage. It is a gentle adventure for very young readers, full of familiar tale figures in fresh, small exploits.
33029-ducks-and-geese:
Harry M. Lamon and Rob R. Slocum wrote Ducks and Geese in 1922 as a practical guide for farmers. Both were poultrymen with the Bureau of Animal Industry in the United States Department of Agriculture. A frontispiece shows water yards and ducklings on a large Long Island duck farm, photographed by the bureau. The text that follows covers breeds, housing, feeding, breeding, and marketing for both kinds of waterfowl.

The authors, already known for books on mating and breeding poultry and on turkey raising, write from farm visits and bureau trials, not from theory alone. Their advice is plain and detailed, suited to a farmer deciding which birds to keep and how to rear them for profit. As agricultural history, the book captures a time when duck and goose farming were growing industries, and it still offers a clear picture of how the work was done.
33188-lessons-on-manners-for-school-and-:
Edith E. Wiggin's lessons teach manners for school and home, opening with a line from Emerson on fine behavior as a fine art. Published in Boston in 1884, the book moves lesson by lesson through manners in general, at school, on the street, and at home, with further lessons on conduct in daily life. Each lesson is short, plain, and made to be read aloud or used in class.

Wiggin writes for children and their teachers, urging courtesy as a habit rather than a show. Her rules cover speech, dress, table conduct, and care for others, always in a kind, practical tone. The book now reads as both a guide and a record of how American schools once taught character. It is a modest work, but a clear window on its age.
3320-mohammed-ali-and-his-house:
Louise Mühlbach tells the life of Mohammed Ali in this historical novel, translated from the German by Chapman Coleman. Ali, the Albanian soldier who rose to rule Egypt, gives the book its center, and his house, his family and court, gives it its domestic drama. Mühlbach, a popular nineteenth-century novelist of courts and kings, writes history as intimate story.

The novel follows Ali from obscurity to power, through war, reform, and the rivalries of his household. Coleman, the translator, carries Mühlbach's brisk German into English. Readers who enjoy historical romance will find a ruler's life told from inside his family: ambition, affection, and statecraft sharing the same rooms.
33289-the-loves-of-ambrose:
Margaret Vandercook's novel follows Ambrose through his loves, in a tale that opens with part one, His First Wife. Published in 1914, its early chapters move from a departure and the voice of the turtle to a girl called Peachy and a vow borrowed from Ruth. Ambrose, a young man with a honeysuckle in his buttonhole, meets love in forms both tender and comic.

Vandercook writes with warmth and humor, letting Ambrose's heart lead him into scrapes and sweet turns. The novel's appeal lies in its light touch and its gallery of lively young people. For readers who enjoy a romance that does not take itself too seriously, The Loves of Ambrose offers a bright, old-fashioned story of a man learning what love asks of him.
33586-drugging-a-nation-the-story-of-chi:
Samuel Merwin investigates the opium trade in China in this 1908 book, based on chapters first published in Success Magazine in 1907 and 1908. Merwin traveled around the world for the project, inquiring first-hand in China and England, reading available printed matter, and interviewing several hundred people with special opportunities to study the problem. He did not begin writing until his preliminary work had turned into convictions.

Chapters cover China's predicament, the golden opium days, a glimpse into an opium province, China's sincerity in reform, Shanghai, Tientsin and Hongkong, and how British chickens came home to roost. Merwin writes frankly journalistic prose with a reformer's urgency. The book remains a primary source on the opium question and on Western attitudes toward China at the turn of the century.
34096-the-ship-dwellers-a-story-of-a-hap:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote this story of a happy cruise, published in New York and London in 1910 by Harper and Brothers, with pictures from drawings by Thomas Fogarty and from photographs. Paine dedicates the book to Mark Twain, hero of his childhood and friend of later years. Chapters open with the book and the dream, then follow in the track of the Innocents.

Days at sea, becoming history, and introducing the reprobates carry the cruise forward. Paine, author of The Tent-Dwellers, writes with humor and warmth about shipboard life. The book offers a cheerful travel tale from the age of the great cruise.
34124-the-panama-canal-a-history-and-des:
J. Saxon Mills, a barrister-at-law, wrote this history and description of the Panama Canal, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons with maps and pictures. A frontispiece shows Colonel George W. Goethals, chairman and chief engineer of the Isthmian Canal Commission. Mills notes that canal literature was dispersed, and he draws on earlier works with thanks.

He cites W. F. Johnson's Four Centuries of the Panama Canal, Vaughan Cornish's Panama Canal and its Makers, Emory R. Johnson's official report on traffic and tolls, and articles in The Times and the National Geographic Magazine. The book gives a clear, early account of the great enterprise.
34229-steel-traps-describes-the-various-:
Harding wrote a plain guide to steel traps, printed in Columbus, Ohio, in 1907 by his own firm. The front shows Newhouse traps of all sizes. A first chapter tells of Sewell Newhouse, the famed trap maker. Harding then sorts well made traps from a few failures and looks at European makes.

Most of the book tells how to use the traps. It covers right sizes, care, marking, fastening, setting, and where to set. Bait, scent, and decoys get chapters, as do fall, land, and water trapping. Last chapters teach skinning, stretching, grading, and sale of pelts. A working trapper could run a full season from the hints in this small book.
34498-evolution-of-expression-volume-2-r:
Evolution of Expression, volume two, is Charles Wesley Emerson's anthology of readings for the training of orators. Emerson, founder of the Emerson College of Oratory, published this twenty-eighth edition, revised, at Boston in 1915. The set compiles selections illustrating the four stages of development in art as applied to oratory, in four volumes with a key to each chapter.

The readings chosen here show the method. Shakespeare's Shylock addresses Antonio, Byron's Destruction of Sennacherib rolls out, and pieces by Henry Ward Beecher, Ralph Waldo Emerson, and N P Willis stand between. Essays on forming pictures and on the power to detach and magnify an object frame the selections. Elocution was then a serious school subject, and Emerson's college taught it as a science of the voice and the feelings.
34799-a-runaway-brig-or-an-accidental-cr:
James Otis's Runaway Brig, or An Accidental Cruise, was copyrighted by Burt of New York in 1888. Harry Vandyne and Walter Morse are summering at the Isle of Shoals, off the New England coast. Their friend Jim Libby, cook's assistant on the fishing schooner Mary Walker, takes them sailing in her tender, the Sally Walker. This is Jim's last day in port before the vessel leaves. Walter is stuck minding his baby sister Bessie while the nurse has a sick headache.

Harry proposes hiring another nurse for a quarter until they get back. Walter, eager to blister his hands rowing once more, does not stop to weigh the plan. The frontispiece shows Harry pointing seaward toward a brigantine moving slowly through the water. The accidental cruise of the title grows out of this small act of boyish scheming.
34911-the-yellow-rose:
The Yellow Rose is a novel by Maurus Jokai, turned into English by Beatrice Danford from the Hungarian. Jarrold and Sons published it in London, with Jokai's portrait at the front. Jokai had written Black Diamonds, The Green Book, and Pretty Michal before it. Twelve chapters tell a tale of the great Hungarian plain.

The story opens in days when no train crossed the Hortobagy waste. The river ran free, the mill clattered, and the otter lived in the reeds. At dawn a horseman rides the flat Zam puszta with no path to follow. He is a cowherd, known by his tight sleeves and his stock whip. A single yellow rose rides in the wide brim of his hat. He checks again and again that the scentless flower is still safe there.
34917-the-lonely-house:
Wister Englished this tale from the German of Adolf Streckfuss here. Lippincott printed The Lonely House at Philadelphia in 1907. Color plates by Weber-Ditzler show Franz and Anna at the front. Wister gives the work, her last translation, to old readers children.

Contents follow a professor holiday in southern Ukraine mountains afar. His persistence, first excursion, and return open the tale in chapters. An investigation, two wounded hands, and two requests follow in line. Quiet weeks, an exploring party, an arrest, and an old chest come. The end of the professor holiday closes the contents list of the translated tale.
34919-vision-house:
Vision House is a novel by the Williamsons, a husband and wife team who wrote The Lion's Mouse and The Second Latchkey. The book came out in New York in 1921 and is given to the Grand Canyon and Arizona. A young woman named Miss Sorel steps on stage in the first chapter.

Chapters move through ship life, a cabin window, secret notes, and a church door. Marise, a key figure, puts on black at one point, and a bridal suite and a shock follow later. A bargain breaks off, a dream comes, and a long trip ends. Love, pride, money, and masks drive the plot in the light romance style of its day.
35038-the-carleton-case:
Ellery H Clark wrote a novel copyrighted in 1910, drawn by George Brehm, and dedicated to friends named Mr and Mrs H Denton White. Doctor Franz Helmar sits at breakfast in Doctor Morrison's rooms on a warm June morning. Sun fills the room, and sparrows chatter on the roofs outside. Helmar daydreams of hills and rivers in place of the dingy city.

A telephone call breaks his musing. Morrison answers in his sharp professional voice, then softens. He says he cannot come himself that morning but can send his colleague. The chapter is titled Doctor Helmar Visits the Birches. Clark builds a case around doctors, houses, and calls.
35260-ruba-iya-t-of-omar-khayyam-rendere:
The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, rendered into English verse by Edward Fitzgerald, appears here in a de luxe edition from Garden City Publishing in 1937. Edmund Dulac's pictures face chosen quatrains. The book prints more than the poem alone. A biographical preface treats Fitzgerald first, then Omar Khayyám himself.

Fitzgerald was born at Bredfield in Suffolk on March 31, 1809, of Irish stock on both sides. The preface traces how the shy scholar came to Persian poetry. The volume then gives the first edition of his translation, the second, and the fifth, side by side in one book. Variations in the third edition close the text. Readers can watch the famous poem change shape across Fitzgerald's own lifetime of revision.
3539-the-love-chase:
James Sheridan Knowles writes a comedy of courtship first performed at the Haymarket in 1837. The cast list names Sir William Fondlove, Waller in love with Lydia, Wildrake the sportsman, Trueworth, Neville, and a landlord called Chargewell. Waller, a fine spirit with a deep purse and easy strings, leads the town, while Wildrake, a country gentleman learned in dogs and horses, talks with great confidence.

The plot turns on rival suitors, disguises, and the chase after Lydia's hand, with lawyers, waiters, and friends adding confusion. Knowles writes in a lively, old fashioned comic style, full of wordplay and sudden entrances. The play suits readers interested in Victorian theater and in comedies where love must outwit money and pride.
3543-heartbreak-house:
George Bernard Shaw writes a play about cultured, leisured Europe just before the First World War, using a country house shaped like a ship as his stage. Shaw says Heartbreak House is not only the play's title but the condition of Europe itself, where clever people talked, flirted, and dreamed while the guns were being loaded. He links his play to Chekhov's studies of idle, charming people.

The characters include a retired sea captain, his daughters, and guests who drift through love affairs and arguments without acting. Shaw's preface notes that English audiences first called the play Russian, missing its English target. The play suits readers who enjoy Shaw's long, witty debates about a society sleepwalking toward war.
35964-the-go-ahead-boys-and-the-mysterio:
Ross Kay wrote a boys adventure novel dated 1916, one of a set of books about the Go Ahead Boys. The tale opens with talk of an old house said to be one where Washington once slept. Chapter heads promise a haunted house, flights, a lost car, a capture, and an escape.

Part of the fun is the banter among the boys as they test tall tales about the past. George defends the old claims with dates, while his friend teases him for how many houses claim the same honor. Danger and puzzles then take over, and the house at last gives up part of its secret.
36100-the-great-war-and-how-it-arose:
The Great War and How It Arose is a British pamphlet of 1915. The Parliamentary Recruiting Committee issued it from Downing Street in London. Its case lays the blame for the war on Germany throughout. Serbia and Russia positions open the argument in short first sections.

Six tries at peace are listed, each said to be thwarted by Germany. How France and Britain came in gets its own plain telling here. Turkey joining Germany and German plots in three regions follow in turn. Appendices charge Germany with Belgian atrocities and poison gas use in war. A list of state papers on the war closes the pamphlet.
36173-a-rambler-s-lease:
Bradford Torrey wrote essays of the woods and fields that Houghton Mifflin published in 1892. A note at the front gives the title its sense. The writer has found so much pleasure in other men's woods and fields, he says, that he counts himself in some sort their owner.

He takes a rambler's lease of their land in public, and offers these papers as his rent. The world, in his private view, belongs to those who enjoy it. The essays hold such pieces as My Real Estate, A Woodland Intimate, and An Old Road. Confessions of a bird's nest hunter and a New England winter follow. Butterfly psychology closes the small book.
36181-the-three-charters-of-the-virginia:
Three charters of the Virginia Company of London, with seven linked papers from 1606 to 1621, fill the 1957 booklet. Samuel M Bemiss wrote the first part. The booklet marked three hundred and fifty years since Jamestown. It was Booklet Number Four in that set.

The first charter of April 1606 let men plant a colony in Virginia. A second charter came in 1609 and a third in 1612. Orders, rules, and guides for governors fill the rest of the book. One guide from 1618 is often called the Great Charter. The texts keep the old spelling. They show how the colony was set up on paper.
36226-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume ten, slice eight, of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from France to Francis Joseph the First. A list of the slice's articles heads the file: Franceschi, Franche-Comte, Franchise, Francia, and Franciabigio among the shorter entries. The Francis entries cover kings of France, Sicily, and the Roman Empire, then Francis of Assisi, Francis of Paola, Francis of Sales, and Sir Philip Francis. The France article continues from the previous slice. Its text here opens with exterior policy from 1870 to 1909.

The Franco-German War, the text says, marks a turning point as sharp as the fall of the old monarchy. Sedan, the proclamation of the German empire at Versailles, and the loss of Alsace and Lorraine under the treaty of Frankfort frame the new epoch. The transcriber's notes list small corrections made in the France article.
36702-verse-and-worse:
Harry Graham, writing as Colonel D Streamer, published a volume of comic verse at London in 1905. Graham had written Ballads of the Boer War and Ruthless Rhymes for Heartless Homes. A note explains that The Baby's Baedeker and Perverted Proverbs appeared in America with Russell and Harper Brothers. The Ballad of Ping Pong ran in The Century Magazine. Bill appeared in The Outlook.

A piece on the place where the old cleek broke ran in Golf magazine. Graham's ruthless rhymes made him the master of the comic epitaph and the heartless home. Edward Arnold published the volume at Maddox Street. His verse turns proverb, sport, and nursery lore upside down.
36730-occultism-and-common-sense:
Occultism and Common Sense is a study of strange gifts by Beckles Willson. A famed man of lore, once head of a guild for such search, wrote the front note. The parts first ran in a great press sheet. Heads treat the stand of lore past the strange, the sleep trance, ghosts of the quick and of the dead, and haunts.

Late parts take up the fork rod that finds springs, the gifts of trance folk, the form of ghosts in flesh, and shots of ghosts. One part treats the trance words of a famed wife of the craft. The front note holds that past much sham there lies a true mass of facts that lore has not yet owned. Calm tests, spread past long years, are the path the guild chose.
36775-humorous-readings-and-recitations-:
Humorous Readings and Recitations, picked and shaped by Leopold Wagner, was printed in London and New York in 1889. Wagner had shaped Modern Readings and Recitations and a set of new readings from American authors. The book is the third in his Popular Readings line.

In his preface Wagner says the kindness of authors and houses let him gather prized funny pieces in one place. Many had been hard to find, scattered through many books, yet folk kept asking for them by name. New pieces join the old favorites. The list holds The Lady Freemason, What Happened Last Night, and The Fatal Legs. One piece is a journey in search of nothing, by Wilkie Collins. Parlor readers get a full kit for an evening of laughs.
36980-papers-from-overlook-house:
Caspar Almore wrote these papers, published by Lippincott at Philadelphia in 1866. An introductory letter and an arrival at the village open the contents of the book. The welcome at Overlook-House and a Christmas log in the kitchen follow in the early chapters.

How the Overlook papers came to be written explains the frame in chapter four. Benson, a living man embalmed for twenty years, is the first tale in the list. A ghost at Ford Inn, a first attempt at biography and katydids as natural history follow, in a house-party book of tales told after dinner.
37155-canada-my-land-and-other-compositi:
Canada My Land is a book of patriotic verse by MacKeracher, issued at Toronto in 1908. William Briggs published the compositions in verse in the dominion tenth year of the century. Contents open with Canada My Land, then Forward Canada and Canadian Born. Knowst Thou the Land, O Maple Leaf, and Dominion Day fill the front list.

Canada Eighteen honours the men who fell at Paardeberg in the Boer War. O Canada Mon Pays and Sol Canadien print the anthem in French and English forms. The Saint Lawrence, Quebec exodus, and a Canadian girl get their poems in turn. Edwardian Canada sings its loyalty and landscape in these earnest verses.
37365-sonnets-and-other-verse:
MacKeracher, author of Canada, My Land, published this book of sonnets and other verse with William Briggs at Toronto under a Canadian copyright of 1909. The contents list some sixty poems. They open with The Old and the New, a sonnet urging readers not to scorn the old, which was sacred in its day, yet to hail and seize the new.

Canadian subjects run through the book: Wolfe and Montcalm, the coming of Champlain, his first winter in Quebec, the immigrants, and the gold-miners of British Columbia. Other sonnets honor Milton on the three hundredth anniversary of his birth, Burns, Charles Lamb's sonnet on work, and a faithful preacher. Poems on the seasons, on a house-hunter, on his two boys, and on finding Burns's poems in an Ontario farmhouse fill out a plain, earnest collection.
37366-vacation-verse:
Vacation Verse, printed at Montreal in 1891, is a small pamphlet of poems by a young writer who signs only initials. The pieces are passages from a long poem written during a college vacation. The author sent them to a friend, Robert McDougall, who had heard some read aloud on walks. The poems were drafted between bouts of study for a college examination.

The chief piece walks through Mount Royal Park on a spring morning. Snow still clings to the rock shelves while small streams run down the side. From the summit the poet looks over Montreal, the city of the hundred spires. The verse is earnest and youthful, proud of its city and its hills.
3746-the-judgment-house:
Gilbert Parker builds this novel around Jasmine, a woman whose beauty draws men into trouble, and the husband who cannot see what is plain to his friends. Chapters move from a jasmine flower and an underground world to Wales, the Appian Way, and the South African veld, where a powerful figure called the Baas bends events to his will. War cries, farm sieges, and letters from afar punctuate a domestic drama that keeps widening.

Parker writes with a popular novelist's pace, and his friends' anxious talk about Byng gives the story its ache. The book mixes romance, empire, and moral judgment in equal share, and its title points to the reckoning each character must face. Readers who like large Edwardian novels of love and power will find a full and stirring tale.
3755-common-sense:
Thomas Paine wrote this pamphlet in 1776 to persuade ordinary Americans that independence was not only right but plain common sense. He argues from the origin of government itself, then turns on monarchy and hereditary succession as absurd ways to choose a ruler. Later sections weigh the present state of American affairs and the continent's ability to stand alone, with Britain's distance and ignorance counted as proof that rule from London cannot work.

The prose is blunt and urgent, built for reading aloud in taverns and camps. Paine warns that Britain will try again after any defeat, and that petitions carried three thousand miles only waste months. The pamphlet helped turn a colonial quarrel into a revolution, and it still reads as a master class in political persuasion.
37929-fenn-masterson-s-discovery-or-the-:
Fenn Masterson's Discovery, or the Darewell Chums on a Cruise, is a boys' tale by Allen Chapman. Chapman also wrote Bart Stirling's Road to Success, his title page notes. The copyright is dated nineteen oh nine. Contents run to thirty chapters. An automobile accident opens the list, then a mysterious cave. Saving the auto and planning a cruise follow.

Peril, an elevator blaze, and a chase fill the early middle. On Lake Huron and caught in the lock place the cruise on the lakes. A queer find, fire on board, and a strange vision follow.
