Fenn becomes ill, is captured, and makes an odd discovery in the late heads. Chapter one opens with Fenn's shout at the accident. In the text shown Fenn plans a fine collection of minerals.
3802-the-lerouge-case:
Emile Gaboriau opens this founding detective novel in the village of La Jonchere, where five women report that the Widow Lerouge has not been seen for two days. Her cottage stands shut, door and shutters closed, and no knock wins an answer. The commissary at Bougival, tired of their importunities, sends for gendarmes and a locksmith to force the door. A crime comes to light in a quiet riverside place where crimes are rare.

From that forced entry the inquiry spreads through Paris and the provinces, as a dead woman's past yields secrets and suspects. Gaboriau builds his case step by step, with documents, alibis, and human frailty doing the work of detection. Readers who like the origins of the genre will find a patient, absorbing puzzle, written before fingerprints and laboratories took the stage.
38275-are-these-things-so-1740-the-great:
Are These Things So, 1740, and The Great Man's Answer are paired political pamphlets from the age of Walpole. The Augustan Reprint Society at the University of California, Los Angeles, reprinted them in 1972, with an introduction by Ian Gordon. A verse attack asked a great man at court whether the charges against the government were true.

The answer, and the newspaper trail in Gordon's notes, show the pamphlet war running week by week through the autumn of 1740, with replies called Yes, They Are and What of That. The slim volume is a lesson in how print fought power before parties had whips.
38911-for-the-cause:
For the Cause is a story collection by Stanley J Weyman, author of A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe, printed at Chicago in 1897. The title tale opens in Paris on a November evening in 1589. The city had never seemed to the eye more peaceful, though many within its walls resented the fineness of the night as a mockery.

Moonlight fell on roofs and towers, on the bare open space of the Place de Greve and the dark mass of the Louvre. The Seine lay a silvery loop about the Ile de la Cite, cut by the black shadows of the bridges. For a time the red fury was over, and the channels where the mob had seethed at noon stood empty. The other tales are King Pepin and Sweet Clive, The Deanery Ball, The Professor and the Harpy, and Archdeacon Hodden's Tribulation.
39067-horace-chase:
Constance Fenimore Woolson wrote Horace Chase, a novel published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1894. Woolson had earlier written Jupiter Lights and East Angels. The story opens in a mountain village of North Carolina in the year 1873, when spring had come with its accustomed beauty.

A pure cold wind sweeps the high valley from dawn to midnight. The Franklin family, for whom comfort is a goddess, pile fresh logs on the broad old hearth. Ruth Franklin stretches at full length on the rug before the blaze, her dog beside her. She never battles disagreeable things for the sake of conquering them. Into this sheltered household comes the world of the title figure, and Woolson builds a novel of love, money, and mountain society.
39294-the-great-house:
Stanley Weyman, known for tales of old France, set The Great House in the England and Paris of the 1840s. Longmans of New York published it in 1919. The first chapter shows a girl at an attic window of the Hôtel Lambert in Paris. She looks down on the Seine from a bare dorm room lined with pallet beds.

From Paris the story moves to London and to the great house at Beaudelays. Chapter titles name a young man, John Audley, an old agent named Toft, and a girl named Mary. The Corn Law crisis and the Riddsley election bring public strife into the tale. A deed of giving up rights stands near the close. Weyman builds a long, slow plot of rank, land, and duty in a time of change.
39324-the-literary-sense:
The Literary Sense is a collection of short stories by Nesbit, published by Macmillan in New York and London in 1903. Nesbit had written The Red House and The Would-be-Goods. The book is dedicated, with the author's love, to Dorothea Deakin.

Fifteen stories include The Unfaithful Lover, The Lie Absolute, The Girl with the Guitar, and Cinderella. The first story shows a woman hurrying to meet her lover at Cannon Street Station. She fears the station will make the meeting banal and sordid. In fancy she would meet him in a green orchard in May, in a white gown. Her hands would hold bluebells against his embrace, as in the poets. She knew, the narrator says, exactly how a tryst is conducted in print.
39805-practical-boat-sailing-a-concise-a:
Practical Boat-Sailing is a manual on handling small boats and yachts, by Douglas Frazar, published in Boston by Lee and Shepard in 1879. Frazar had served as fourth officer of a steamship, master of a bark, and commander of a yacht in the northern seas of China and Japan. A short vocabulary of nautical terms supplements the treatise.

The preface states the aim plainly. Nothing new is offered to those who already sail well and safely. Instead, any person who reads the pages should feel confident of handling a boat. Chapters explain ordinary sea manoeuvres and the use of sails, helm, and anchor. Emergencies get their own advice on what is proper to be done. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
40024-rebecca-s-promise:
Frances Sterrett writes a novel in Rebecca's Promise, printed in New York and London in 1919. Appleton made the book, with plates by Caswell. Sterrett had writ Jimmie the Sixth and Mary Rose of Mifflin. She gives the book to Lilian Josepha Sterrett, who trusts in what she calls memory insurance.

The tale opens with Cousin Susan Wentworth in two minds. She should not have brought young Rebecca Mary Wyman here, she murmurs. She should have saved her cash for new kitchen curtains, a disgrace to her house. Yet life would be worth little if we never did what we should not, she smiles. Rebecca sits like a small gray mouse with bright eyes and a pink flush.
40227-the-love-letters-of-abelard-and-he:
The Love Letters of Abelard and Heloise come Englished from Latin and reprint a text of seventeen hundred twenty two. Ralph Fletcher Seymour issued the book in Chicago with a nineteen hundred three copyright. A short life of the pair runs at the front. Their tale had made both names live on in song.

Abelard came from Brittany to study in Paris and rose fast. He led the schools of thought in the town. Heloise, niece of Canon Fulbert, came to learn from him. Lodging in her uncle’s house, the two fell in love. A child was born in flight to the country. A secret church rite wed them at her long last yes. The front tale frames the grief that the letters then voice.
40318-the-book-of-cheese:
Charles Thom and Walter Fisk wrote The Book of Cheese, issued at New York in 1918 as part of the Rural Text-Book Series shaped by L H Bailey. Thom was an investigator in cheese, once at the Connecticut Agricultural College. Fisk was assistant professor of dairy industry at the New York State College of Agriculture at Cornell. A front picture shows a cheese laboratory at Cornell.

The series aimed to give farmers and students sound, tested texts on grains, soils, stock, and crops. A book on butter by Guthrie stands as its sister volume. Thom and Fisk treat the making and judging of cheese as a craft of milk, curd, salt, and time, fit for college teaching and farm use alike. The volume shows how far the science of the dairy had come by the close of the Great War.
40360-guide-to-yosemite-a-handbook-of-th:
The Guide to Yosemite is a handbook of the trails and roads of Yosemite Valley. Ansel Hall wrote it for the National Park Service. Hall was in charge of information at the park. An aeroplane view of the valley opens the book. A key names sixty-two peaks, falls, and camps.

An introduction explains the guide's making. Thousands of visitors had asked for practical information. Each trail and road is described as it is actually followed. Points of interest appear just as a traveller discovers them. Trail conditions and times required are given. Fishing, camp sites, and forage all receive data. The book aims to supply everything a hired guide would tell. A chief ranger helped prepare the original draft.
4047-the-leavenworth-case:
Anna Katharine Green's detective novel opens with a great case: a murder in the Leavenworth house, probed by a coroner's inquest, expert testimony, and chains of circumstantial evidence. A lawyer narrator follows the clues, from facts and deductions to a sudden discovery.

Mary Leavenworth stands at the center of the mystery, watched by the detective Mr. Gryce and by readers who must weigh each side light. Green, a pioneer of the American detective tale, builds suspense from documents, motives, and careful reasoning. The novel suits readers who enjoy a classic whodunit where logic, not action, cracks the case.
40490-the-white-canoe-and-other-verse:
Alan Sullivan wrote The White Canoe and Other Verse, a book of young poems. The J E Bryant Company issued it at Toronto in eighteen hundred ninety one. The title poem sings a river bride on a north stream. Spring’s first breath stirs the grey dead trees in its first lines.

At last free of its ice fetters, the river runs clear and blue. It cries with a quivering voice for the White Canoe’s launch. She is the wandering phantom bride of the stream she rides. No billow has yet risen to peril her loved white frame. Come when the moon is throned, the last verse gently bids. Peace waits on the wave when trouble crowds the shore at home. A Vision sends the soul past night to a land where Love reigns. A Question speaks to the pale moon and the sleepless stars.
40539-a-lost-cause:
A Lost Cause is a novel by Guy Thorne, printed in New York and London by Putnam Sons in 1905, at the Knickerbocker Press. Thorne had written When It Was Dark. Thirteen chapters trace a church fight in a London suburb.

The first chapter, The Interrupted Eucharist, opens at the Church of St Elwyn. The church is a building of brick that rises to a great height. It stands in the crowded district between Hornsey and Wood Green, one of the largest buildings there. Small villa houses make a brick wilderness round it. Later heads name Mr Hamlyn and son at home, Lord Huddersfield and the guests at Scarning Court, and Lucy Blantyre at the clergy house. The offices of the Luther League and a union of forces pace the close. Church tale fans get a High Church cause.
4072-songs-before-sunrise:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Songs Before Sunrise opens an hour before dawn, with the speaker asking for a staff outside a hollow house that blind men fear. He lives on life withdrawn, feeling on sightless eyes the shadow of death that clothes Antigone.

Her living body lies dead in the poem's dark vision, if life is only blood and breath and sense. Swinburne's verse runs in long, musical waves, full of classical figures and republican hope. Readers who enjoy high Victorian lyric poetry will find a passionate, sometimes difficult book, written for the dawn of a freer age.
4099-the-angel-in-the-house:
Coventry Patmore's long poem The Angel in the House celebrates married love through preludes and cantos, including a Dean's canto on perfect love. Rare is still most noble found, Patmore writes, yet most noble still most incomplete, a sad law for lovers.

A postscript tells of violets, blue and white, enclosed by sisters who had won a wagered pair of gloves, and of Purcell's glee learned to sing by tomorrow night. The poem joins domestic detail to high ideal, praising a wife as angel of the home. Readers who like Victorian verse on love and marriage will find a famous, earnest classic.
41104-the-amazing-argentine-a-new-land-o:
The Amazing Argentine paints Argentina as a new land of enterprise, by John Foster Fraser. Funk and Wagnalls published it in New York, with forty eight photographs. Twenty three chapters run from the first invaders of its ports to its problems. The Mayo Avenue in Buenos Aires fronts the book as its first plate.

Buenos Aires gets three opening chapters on its aspects and its suburbs. Railways, land settlement, and feeding the world fill the next stretch of chapters. The constitution, the country's character, and its live stock follow in the scheme. Rosario, Cordoba, Bahia Blanca, and Mendoza each get a chapter of local colour. A trip into the Andes and the sugar lands of Tucuman widen the tour. Fraser writes to draw settlers and capital to a booming republic.
41752-the-city-of-beautiful-nonsense:
The City of Beautiful Nonsense is a novel by Edward Temple Thurston. Dodd, Mead published it in New York in 1911. The copyright dates to 1900. Thurston had earlier written The Apple of Eden. He dedicated the book to Rosina Filippi, for the gift of laughter.

The novel is built in three books. The first is called The Road to the City. The second is The Tunnel. The third is simply The City. Early chapters wander Fetter Lane in London. They treat a greengrocer and a ballad-monger. Later chapters move to Venice and a palazzo. The tale ends with chapters on sacrifice and belief. The opening scene falls on the eve of Saint Joseph's day.
41761-traditions-and-hearthside-stories-:
Traditions and Hearthside Stories of West Cornwall, second series, is a folklore collection by William Bottrell. Beare and Son printed it at Penzance in 1873, for the author, with illustrations by Joseph Blight. Its epigraph, from Longfellow, speaks of legends once told or sung in many a smoky fireside nook.

The contents mix play, tale and antiquities. Duffy and the Devil, an old Christmas play, opens the volume. Celtic monuments of Boleigh follow, then the last Cardews of Boskenna and the story of Nelly Wearne. Witches appear twice, at Buryan church-town and in the tale of Madam Noy. Fairy tales include The Small People's Cow and The Changeling of Brea-Vean. Tom of Chyannor, a tin-streamer, stars in a West Country droll, and the knockers of Ballowal haunt a tinner's fireside story. Bottrell kept Cornwall's oral tradition in print.
41809-byron-the-last-phase:
Byron, the Last Phase, by Richard Edgcumbe, was printed in New York by Charles Scribner Sons in 1909. Edgcumbe gives the book to Mrs Charles Call, daughter of Edward Trelawny, Byron companion in Greece. His subject is the last years of Lord Byron, the famed poet.

The book opens at Pisa in 1821, which Shelley called a large, grim city almost without folk. Convicts in red worked the streets in chains, in pairs, and their slow clank filled the day. Byron lived at the Palazzo Lanfranchi on the Arno. Captain Thomas Medwin came in November, and Edward John Trelawny came in January 1822 to play a large part in the last scenes. Readers get Byron end told by a man close to the Trelawny kin.
41974-veronese:
Veronese, by Francois Crastre, came out in New York in 1912 in English dress. Frederic Taber Cooper turned the French text into English. The book forms part of the Masterpieces in Colour series. Eight colour plates show works by the painter. Most plates rest in the Louvre, with one in the National Gallery, London. Veronese lived from 1528 to 1588, as the title page notes.

Chapters trace his first years and his stay in Venice. The Wedding at Cana gets a chapter of its own. His clash with the Inquisition is treated next. Later pages cover the trip to Rome, the return, and work in the Ducal Palace. The short life suits readers who want the main story with fine plates.
42052-the-golden-helm-and-other-verse:
The Golden Helm and Other Verse is a book of poems by Wilfrid Wilson Gibson, published in London by Elkin Mathews in 1903. Several pieces are reprinted from magazines of the day, with thanks to their editors. The book is dedicated to Howard Pease.

The first poem, The Torch, opens on the Farne Isles. Oswald comes from his island cell at dawn. He is white-faced and worn from a night of watching for ships in peril on the reefs. Other pieces treat an unknown knight, the death of a king, and three kings. A set called The Songs of Queen Averlaine runs through the middle of the book. A Christmas mystery, The Vision, stands among them. The title poem closes the set.
42172-every-boy-s-book-a-complete-encycl:
Edmund Routledge edited a wide guide to sports and pastimes for boys, issued in London in 1869. George Routledge and Sons brought out the form with more than six hundred pictures. Twelve years had passed since the first form, so the book was all but rewritten. New games and new tastes called for fresh text throughout.

Pages treat boxing, canoeing, croquet, golf, billiards, and base ball among much else. Pets such as canaries, owls, and hedgehogs get their own short pieces. Codes, stamps, shows, and voice tricks add indoor fun. Henry Chadwick wrote the parts on American games, and many known hands helped with the rest.
4222-laperouse:
Ernest Scott wrote this life of the French navigator Jean-Francois de Galaup, comte de La Perouse, whose ships vanished in the Pacific after leaving Botany Bay in 1788. The chapters follow his family and youth, his naval career, a love story, the great voyage of exploration, and his stay at Botany Bay.

Scott also traces the mystery that followed, Captain Dillon's later discovery of wreckage, and the fame that kept La Perouse alive in Australian memory. The Sydney monument overlooking Botany Bay gives the book its starting point, and the narrative keeps returning to what that stone marks.
42534-the-narrow-house:
The Narrow House is a novel by Evelyn Scott, author of a verse book called Precipitations, published in New York in nineteen twenty one. A verse motto from William Blake on love that builds a hell in heaven's despite heads the title page. Part one opens on a hot, bright street that looks almost deserted. A builders' sign swings before a dishevelled house at the corner.

Broken plaster thrown from a window lies in a glaring heap on the sidewalk. The old house next door needs repair as badly as the one being altered. Scott, a southern modernist, sets family life inside cramped and decaying rooms. Heat, dust, and close walls press on every scene.
42771-happy-house:
The Baroness von Hutten wrote a novel copyrighted in 1920, dedicated in a letter from Penzance to Lily Betts. Three people, one in a chair and two upside down on a grass plot, decided the dedication together, the letter jokes. It recalls how they did not work on the book at Sennen Cove, and did work on it here. Richard, Hetty, and the baroness sign it.

She had written Pam, Pam Decides, Sharrow, and Kingsmead. Chapter one opens with Mrs Walbridge standing at the top of the stairs. George H Doran published the novel at New York. The house of the title is the scene of its comedy of manners.
42934-polly-s-southern-cruise:
Polly's Southern Cruise is a girls' adventure novel by Lillian Elizabeth Roy. Grosset and Dunlap published it in 1923, continuing the travels of Polly Brewster and her friend Eleanor Maynard. The opening chapter finds the two girls deep in plans for a yachting trip south. They weigh the yacht of their friend Dalken against a rented craft with a chaperone aboard. Then they lay the scheme before a general meeting of their friends.

The voyage that follows touches at Palm Beach and takes in races at Havana. It loses itself in Kingston, tours the sights and sports of Jamaica, and meets old friends again in Panama. High life at the Canal closes the trip. Roy mixes scenery, mild mishap, and shipboard society in the series manner. The book carried its first readers on a sunny tour few of them could take in person.
43066-griselda-a-society-novel-in-rhymed:
Griselda is a tale of London society told in rhymed verse, printed in London in 1893. No author is named on the title page. A motto at the front answers critics in advance. Unnatural, the poet says, yet these things are life, and life is fit matter for the muse.

Chapter one calls the tale an idle story with an idle moral. The poet asks why he tells it at all, then says truth must be sought low, in earthy human nature. Brave lives pass each day, he grants, yet most people swing between good and ill. He vows to tell plain truth and leaves the moral to others. The story then turns to a lady of high fashion in London.
43359-human-intercourse:
A book of essays by Philip Gilbert Hamerton, published at Boston in 1898. Little, Brown issued the author's edition. Hamerton wrote widely on art, landscape, and the intellectual life. He dedicates this volume to the memory of Emerson. The two men never met or corresponded. Emerson's influence on his thinking, Hamerton says, was great and persistent.

Emerson taught him two lessons above all. Trust that doing one's best is always worthwhile, reward or no reward. Trust your own convictions and gifts without echoing others. The essays apply that creed to conversation and society. Shelley supplies the epigraph: love of tranquil solitude and quiet, wise company. Hamerton, an English artist settled in France, reflects on friendship with a painter's calm eye.
4337-power-through-repose:
Annie Payson Call wrote this book on the power that comes through repose, in a new edition with additions. Its motto, from Francois Delsarte, holds that personality binds while universality expands. Call argues that a body perfectly adjusted, well supplied with force, and free from waste becomes a perfect instrument of impression, experience, and expression.

The first chapter, on the guidance of the body, notes how much has been written on food, air, clothing, and development. What is lacking, Call says, is obedience to laws already known. Her remedy is restful attention rather than effort. The book founded a popular literature of relaxation, and it still reads as a gentle manual of self-care.
4339-nerves-and-common-sense:
Annie Payson Call, author of Power Through Repose, wrote this enlarged book of articles on nerves and common sense. Many pieces first appeared in the Ladies' Home Journal, whose editor Edward Bok supplied helpful titles. Call thanks him in her preface, and the contents show his hand in chapter names.

Chapters cover habit and nervous strain, how women can keep from being nervous, irritable husbands, the trying member of the family, and quiet versus chronic excitement. Later pieces treat working restfully, imaginary vacations, and how to be ill and get well. Call's advice is plain, domestic, and humane, aimed at daily life rather than theory.
434-the-circular-staircase:
Mary Roberts Rinehart sets this mystery in a rented country house where a middle-aged spinster finds murder on her hands. Rachel Innes, tired of town quiet, takes a furnished house for the summer and soon hears steps on a circular stair. A dead man, a missing nephew, and a bank scandal tangle round her.

Rinehart writes in Rachel's brisk, comic voice, mixing fright with domestic detail. Clues hide in cuff links, telegrams, and a hole in the wall. The novel, a landmark of the had-I-but-known school, still charms as a puzzle told by a heroine who refuses to faint.
43414-rilla-of-the-lighthouse:
Rilla of the Lighthouse is a girls' novel by Grace May North. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued it at Akron and New York in 1926. A cry of Clear out, we don't want landlubbers here, fronts the tale. Chapters open with Rilla herself, then a gift from the sea. A first adventure and a shipwrecked mariner follow in quick succession.

A swim in the night, a searching party, and Cap'n Ezra's heart ensue. A secret told, a first letter, and a hoped for message build suspense. Wee Irishy cakes, neighbourliness, and a storm fill the middle heads. Blue jewels, the owner of a box, and New Year's Eve raise the close. Lighthouse life and girl friendship carry the salt air tale through.
43736-fourteenth-century-verse-prose:
Fourteenth Century Verse and Prose, shaped by Kenneth Sisam, was printed at the Clarendon Press in Oxford in 1921. Sisam chose texts to show the range of English writing in the 1300s. Spellings stay as the old scribes left them, with marks to flag odd or worn readings.

The book opens with Robert Mannyng and his Handlyng Synne, then gives the romance Sir Orfeo. Later parts hold the Ayenbyte of Inwyt, verse by Richard Rolle, and John Barbour on Bruce at Berwick. A part on the Bible in English and a map round out the helps. A mate volume by J R R Tolkien gives the word list for these texts. Students meet Middle English in its own voice here, with strong tales and faith prose side by side.
4385-as-a-matter-of-course:
Annie Payson Call wrote this book in 1894 to help remove nervous irritants from everyday life. Such irritants, she argues in her preface, cause much physical disease and block usefulness and pleasure. Her chapters treat physical care, amusements, brain impressions, moods, tolerance, sympathy, and children, with a closing summary.

Call opens with a mountain image: a climber who knows the path takes it as a matter of course, and is free to enjoy the climb. Her counsel applies the same idea to nerves: do needful things without fuss, and drop the strain that comes from fussing. The book is a plain manual of restful living, in Call's gentle, practical voice.
43878-the-grim-house:
The Grim House, by Molesworth with pictures by Warwick Goble, was published by Nisbet in an edition dated 1906. Chapter one, called Such Nice-Looking People, opens at a family breakfast table. The father folds a letter back into its envelope with care and announces that a plan is decided, the best thing to do, with no room left for debate.

The narrator notes that his yes agreed with no one but himself. Around the table, faces fall or take on quiet resignation, while mother answers mildly that he is no doubt right. Only Moore, the youngest brother at fourteen, shows a gleam of cheer at the change ahead. Molesworth tells the tale from inside the family, where a grim new house waits offstage.
44165-soldier-rigdale-how-he-sailed-in-t:
Soldier Rigdale tells how its young hero sailed in the Mayflower and served Miles Standish. Beulah Marie Dix wrote it, and Macmillan printed it in New York in 1899, with illustrations by Reginald Birch. Dix also wrote Hugh Gwyeth, a Roundhead cavalier tale.

Chapter one, Playing with Powder, opens at sunset aboard the old ship. The wind that ruffled the waves all day has died, leaving a long heaving motion that sways the Mayflower rudely. Miles Rigdale stands with legs craftily planted and head thrown back, staring at the seesawing yards until he grows dizzy. The contents promise the name of Miles, the time of the sickness, the sowing of the fields, and the captain's soldier at the end.
44342-classical-enigmas-adapted-to-every:
Classical Enigmas, printed at London in 1811 by Darton, is a verse riddle book by a lady. Its puzzles are adapted to every month. They are composed from English and Roman history, heathen myth and famous writers. The aim, the title says, is to amuse youths. At the same time, the puzzles exert their memories.

The riddle under Aries asks for monarchs in verse. Name the queen whose bigoted zeal made her subjects fear popery, it begins. Name the last sovereign of the true Stuart race, an example of goodness and grace. Name the king dethroned by the puritan party, whose faults his lost head atoned. Name the bold king who threw off the pope's yoke and brought the Bible into fashion. Take first letters, and a month stands made.
44394-the-boy-chums-in-the-gulf-of-mexic:
Wilmer M Ely wrote The Boy Chums in the Gulf of Mexico, or On a Dangerous Cruise with the Greek Spongers, held in 1913 by A L Burt Company at New York. Ely had writ Boy Chums tales on Indian River, on Haunted Island, and in the Forest. Thirty four chapters carry the cruise. A front print shows Charley level his gun and send sixteen bullets above a wheelman's head.

Chapter One opens in the Greek section of Tarpon Springs in Florida. A sturdy boy of eighteen calls it like stepping suddenly into a strange country. Mr Driver, preparations, and the start fill the early turns. Sponging, trouble, and Manuel's release build the sea plot. A diving suit, a mystery, and a close call press the pace. Wreck, castaways, a flood, and a siege mark the late turns. A rescue and conclusion close the boys adventure.
4498-miscellaneous-prose:
George Meredith gathers several short prose pieces here, rather than a single novel or story. The set opens with his introduction to Thackeray's Four Georges, tracing Thackeray's life from Calcutta and Charterhouse to Cambridge and his early writing. It then adds brief essays called A Pause in the Strife, Concession to the Celt, and a sketch of Leslie Stephen.

Last come letters Meredith wrote to the Morning Post from the seat of war in Italy, reporting a campaign as a correspondent saw it. Together the pieces show Meredith as critic, commentator, and witness, not only as a novelist. Readers get a compact sample of his nonfiction voice: learned, witty, and quick to judge character, politics, and art.
450-susan-lenox-her-fall-and-rise:
David Graham Phillips follows Susan Lenox from a farm girlhood to city streets and back toward honor in this two-part novel, published in 1917. Orphaned and wronged, Susan is cast out, then drifts through theater, marriage, and the underworld of New York. Each fall costs her dearly, yet she keeps a stubborn sense of self.

Phillips writes with frank sympathy for a woman judged harshly by a double standard. Susan's rise, when it comes, rests on work, friends, and her own will, not rescue. The novel stands as a bold, humane study of a woman fighting for a decent life on her own terms.
4513-the-rainbow-and-the-rose:
E. Nesbit wrote this book of poems in 1905, dedicating it to Iris and Rosamund. Its contents divide into four parts, opening with the things that matter, the confession, work, the jilted lover, and the will to live. The beatific vision closes the first part, and mummy wheat, the beech tree, and songs follow.

Later poems include the veil of Maya, a song to Vera, the poet to his love, and the maiden's prayer. The magic flower, bridal eve, love and life, and songs from the Italian close the book, with a final part from the fullness of the heart. Nesbit's verse is lyrical and direct, on love, children, and the passing of time.
45343-the-adventure-girls-at-happiness-h:
Clair Blank wrote this girls' school story, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron and New York under a 1936 copyright, in the Adventure Girls series. Chapter one brings six young ladies by train to Briarhurst, the little college town, where a rusty bus waits to carry them up the hill to the college grounds.

Carol Carter doubts the bus will hold them all. Janet Gordon takes her chance on the ancient vehicle, and the driver boasts it has run for nigh onto twenty years without falling apart. The contents promise a rescue, a hockey game, a mysterious stranger, and startling news, with a girl named Phyllis arriving late in the story. Chapters on the Omega Chi society and the end of the term close the book, whose frontispiece shows two figures strolling toward girls crouched in shrubbery.
45417-dorothy-dixon-solves-the-conway-ca:
Dorothy Dixon Solves the Conway Case is a tale of crime for girls by Dorothy Wayne. Her past tales of the same girl are named on the title leaf. In those tales the girl wins her wings and meets a doubt plane and a twin kin. This book was put out at Chicago in nineteen thirty three. It is sworn to a girl who calls the books of the hand neat.

Out of luck heads the parts. To the save, in the house of the name, and guests come next. The cause, in a tight place, and a rock of birds fill the first run. A house shaft, past the top, and an old man river stand past them. A man of the tale, voices from past down, and the way out fill the mid run.
45709-montrose:
A biography of James Graham, Marquis of Montrose, by Mowbray Morris. Macmillan published it in the English Men of Action series. The first edition dates to 1892, and this printing is from 1909. A portrait frontispiece shows Montrose in 1649. Gerard Honthorst painted it at the Hague. Montrose gave it to the Queen of Bohemia.

The chapters follow a civil war career at speed. Ancestry and early years lead to the Covenant. Two Bishops' Wars, a plot, and an incident follow. The king's commission sends Montrose to the Highlands. Tippermuir, Aberdeen, and Inverlochy crown his year of victories. Auldearn, Alford, and Kilsyth extend the run. Philiphaugh ends it, and a last campaign seals his fate. Morris writes compact, admiring history.
46066-manual-of-taxidermy-a-complete-gui:
Manual of Taxidermy is a full guide to bird and beast keep by Maynard. A Cassino house of Boston brought it out in eighteen eighty three. Its long name adds bird and beast take and save to the theme. A front word looks back at bird take hands of past years in this land. Lone bird men were rare and held cracked in those dim days there.

Wilson and Audubon blaze had died down in the folk mind by then. Cassin, Lawrence, Baird, and Bryant wrote on in hush wise ways there. No broad bird book came for thirty years past Audubon great work. Samuels Birds of New England of eighteen sixty seven turned the tide. Sheets and books on birds then woke the land to bird lore fast.
46178-flower-of-the-gorse:
Flower of the Gorse is a novel by Louis Tracy, published in nineteen fifteen, and set in Brittany around the artists' village of Pont-Aven. The Breton song quoted at the front names its heroine, Fleur d'Ajonc, flower of the gorse, who sings by the clear streams.

The opening climbs the Pilgrims' Way with Mere Pitou and three girls, Barbe, Yvonne, and Madeleine, on the feast of Sainte Barbe, when a deep bell promises good luck for the year. The chapters move through a wreck, a homecoming, a flight, and a tightening net, with Harvey Raymond pressing an attack and Tollemache taking charge. Tracy builds a romance of Breton custom, coast danger, and two Englishmen drawn into village secrets.
4618-words-for-the-wise:
T. S. Arthur published Words for the Wise in 1851, with a preface saying the title needs no explanation. May its lessons prove sufficient, he hopes, as warnings, incentives, and examples to hundreds and thousands of readers. The contents run from The Poor Debtor and The Sunday Christian. They go on to I Knew How It Would Be, Jacob Jones, and Starting a Newspaper, with an experience of Mr. Jones.

Later pieces include The Way of Transgressors, Just Going to Do It, and Making Haste to Be Rich. They go on to Let Her Pout It Out, A Fine Generous Fellow, Taking It for Granted, and Love and Law. The opening tale meets a rich merchant, Petron, who claims one honest man in the world, and a tailor, Moale, long under the weather. Readers get short, plain moral sketches, each with a warning or an incentive to carry into daily life.
46315-vital-records-of-the-town-of-aubur:
Vital Records of the Town of Auburn, formerly Ward, in Massachusetts is a genealogy source book collected by Franklin Rice and issued at Worcester in 1900. It runs to the end of the year 1850. With the town records stand the inscriptions from the old burial grounds. Only one hundred fifty numbered copies were printed, this copy being one of them.

The book is dedicated to a general in whose honour the town was first named, and to its first minister. A quoted aim at the front praises the work of bringing first material into a form for quick reference. Births, marriages, and deaths from the town books thus sit beside the words cut on gravestones. A transcriber warns that odd spellings and clashes in the print are kept as they stand.
46427-the-great-war-in-verse-and-prose:
The Great War in Verse and Prose is an anthology of writings on the First World War, selected and edited by Wetherell, a Toronto educator. It was printed in 1919 by order of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario and recommended for use in schools. An introduction by the Ontario minister of education heads the book, and copies sold for twenty cents.

The contents mix poems, speeches, and orders of the day. Kipling's call to arms opens the volume. Lord Kitchener's words to the British soldier follow, with Owen Seaman's verses. Asquith and Churchill speak for the statesmen. Bliss Carman writes of the man of the Marne, and a telegram stands among the poems. The book is a schoolroom monument: the war as Ontario wished its children to remember it, in the words of those who called, fought, and mourned.
46435-practical-instruction-for-detectiv:
Practical Instruction for Detectives: A Complete Course in Secret Service Study is a training manual by Emmerson Manning. Manning's National Detective Institute of Chicago sponsored it, and Drake of Chicago published it, with copyrights of 1916 and 1921. The book teaches the business as a trade that a student can learn and then practise for pay.

An early lesson treats detective agencies and how to start one. Licensing laws, Manning warns, vary in almost all the states. In some states a plain business license suffices, at rates like any other concern's. In others only the county courts grant licenses, and the applicant must prove good character, fitness, and ability through responsible sponsors. Some states demand a bond against misuse of the license. Manning also notes that a successful agency needs no grand offices: many ran from one or two modest rooms at nominal rent.
46642-sporting-dogs-their-points-and-man:
Frank Townend Barton, a veterinary surgeon, wrote this guide to sporting dogs and their keep. Barton served the Gamekeepers' Kennel Association and wrote a shelf of horse and dog books. A bloodhound champion named Sultan fronts the book in a Baker Street photo.

Points and management in health and disease state the plan in the title. Barton treats each breed's marks of worth, then the daily care of kennel and field. Sick dogs and their cures take the back of the book. Gamekeepers, shooters, and dog men of his day kept such a guide by the kennel door. His posts and his long list of like books vouch for a hand that knew dogs in work and in rest.
4698-whitefoot-the-wood-mouse:
Thornton W. Burgess tells Whitefoot the Wood Mouse for young readers, opening with a happy winter in the Green Forest. Whitefoot, Burgess says, never lets past troubles spoil present happiness, and never borrows trouble from the future. Past things are past, and future things can wait until they happen, a wisdom Burgess thinks most human beings lack.

Whitefoot has more enemies to watch than any other little person in the forest, from Buster Bear downward, yet he stays happy whenever he has a chance. Chapters follow queer sights, Farmer Brown's boy, anxious days, a careless jump, a rescue, and two timid persons meeting. Readers get a gentle animal story about courage, watchfulness, and living in the present, easy to read aloud to children.
47097-step-lively-a-carload-of-the-funni:
George Niblo wrote Step Lively, a carload of the funniest yarns that ever crossed the footlights, Number Four in the S and S Humor Library at twenty five cents. Street and Smith in New York issued the book with copyright in nineteen oh three. Niblo had earlier written B Gosh and Atchoo. A stage patter style fills the pages. The manager words open the act.

Just give them a little nonsense, Mr Niblo, the manager said, for a little nonsense now and then is relished by the best of men. Niblo calls himself the most nonsensical man the manager ever knew. I dearly love to see folk faces wreathed in smiles, he says. He once walked twenty miles to thrash a fellow just for fun, he claims. They carried him back in an ambulance, which did not bother him. Vaudeville fans get jokes, yarns, and stage banter in print.
47307-nancy-dale-army-nurse:
Nancy Dale, Army Nurse is a girls' war story by Ruby Lorraine Radford. Henry Vallely drew the illustrations for the Fighters for Freedom Series. Whitman of Racine, Wisconsin, published it with rights in 1944. A note swears all names, characters, and events are entirely fictitious. A poem addressed To Whom It May Concern fronts the tale itself.

That poem says nurses are needed, yet recruiting lags as troops advance. Every mile of ground is bought with blood, the verses insist in grief. Death has always been the price of victory when rights are defended. Nothing excuses useless sacrifice, the poem warns its girl readers at home. Whether wounded men get nursing care lies in your hands, it says.
4745-at-the-villa-rose:
A. E. W. Mason sets At the Villa Rose in Savoy, opening with Mr. Ricardo's August habit of travelling to Aix-les-Bains. For five or six weeks he pretends to take the waters in the morning, and rides in his motor-car in the afternoon. He dines at the Cercle in the evening, and spends an hour or two in baccarat rooms at the Villa des Fleurs. Summer lightning, a cry for help, and Perrichet's story soon break that smooth life.

Chapters follow the villa itself, a salon, Helene Vauquier's evidence, and a startling discovery. A ship's captain, Madame Dauvray's motor-car, news from Geneva, an unopened letter, and an aluminium flask all enter the case. Celia's story, a seance, and explanations by Helene and by Hanaud close the mystery. Readers get a classic detective novel, elegant and twisty, with a French detective whose reasoning untangles a Riviera crime.
47694-the-labour-saving-house:
Dorothy Peel wrote The Labour-Saving House, published by John Lane in London in 1918. Peel also wrote War Ration Cookery and Learning to Cook. Parts of the book first appeared as articles in The Queen and The Evening Standard. Her theme is the servant problem of the war years, and how a house can be run with far less labour.

Early chapters ask why labour-saving houses are needed and picture the house as it might be and as it can be. Peel compares the work of a labour-making house with a labour-saving one. She prints other people's experiences of labour-saving homes at length. Later chapters treat coal, coke, and gas, and then the electric house, with cooking, heating, cleaning, and lighting by electricity. Her motto stands on the title page: the greatest labour-saving apparatus we possess is the brain.
4775-theocritus-bion-and-moschus-rendere:
Andrew Lang, M.A., lately fellow of Merton College, Oxford, rendered Theocritus, Bion, and Moschus into English prose, with an introductory essay, published by Macmillan in 1889 and dedicated to Ernest Myers. Its contents open with Theocritus and His Age, then thirty idyls of Theocritus, from the first through the thirtieth, followed by his epigrams. Bion's six idyls and fragments follow, then nine idyls of Moschus.

A life of Theocritus, taken from Suidas, opens the discussion of the poet, calling him the Chian, while noting another Theocritus, son of Praxagoras and Philinna. Lang's essay places Theocritus in his age, among shepherds, fishermen, and town life of the Greek world, before the translations themselves begin. Theocritus's idyls, Bion's laments, and Moschus's shorter pieces together show Greek pastoral poetry in prose form, clear and readable. Readers get the three pastoral poets in one volume, with Lang's learned introduction.
47970-the-dwelling-house:
Dwelling House is a work on home sanitation by George Vivian Poore, a London physician. Poore was physician to University College Hospital and a fellow of the Sanitary Institute. He sat on the permanent committee of the international congress of hygiene, as the title page states. A companion work, Essays on Rural Hygiene, is praised at the front by the Glasgow Herald.

 It is full, likewise, of recommendations by which those errors may be rectified, the review adds. The Dwelling House applies the same mind to the town and suburban home in its pages. Air, water, drains, and soil are its subjects under the roof of the title. Victorian Britain was learning that fever lived in bad drains rather than in bad air alone. Poore was one of the teachers of that lesson to householders and to the sanitarians of his day.
48056-miscellaneous-pieces-in-prose:
Miscellaneous Pieces in Prose, by John Aikin and Anna Letitia Barbauld, is a book of essays and tales, shown here in its third edition of 1792. Johnson printed it at London in Saint Paul's Churchyard. The contents open with a piece on the province of comedy. The Hill of Science, a vision, comes next, then a piece on romances.

Selama imitates the manner of Ossian, and a moral essay fights inconsistency in our expectations. The Canal and the Brook tells a fable, and a long piece weighs monastic institutions. Two famed essays ask why objects of terror please us, with a fragment of a tale, Sir Bertrand, attached. A sister essay asks what kinds of distress stir pleasant feelings. Barbauld's pieces here became classics of the English essay. The book shows brother and sister writing together, in the clear, sensible style of their age.
48222-fir-flower-tablets-poems-translate:
Fir-Flower Tablets is a book of Chinese poems in English dress. Florence Ayscough made the literal translations. Amy Lowell then turned them into English poems. Houghton Mifflin published the book in 1921. A map of China faces the title page. It shows the old districts named in the poems.

Lowell's preface explains the shared method. She states plainly that she knows no Chinese. Ayscough was born in Shanghai and lived long in China. She gave Lowell the sense of each poem word by word. Lowell shaped that sense into verse. The preface argues that the pairing of scholar and poet beats either one working alone. It calls the result a pathway to a new world of poetry.
48363-the-little-grey-house:
Marion Ames Taggart wrote a girls' novel published in October 1904, drawn for the frontispiece by Ethel Franklin Betts. A picture caption shows mowing beginning, with Prue going first. Chapter one is titled Its Children, and chapter two Its Neighbors. The house of the title is the book's center. Taggart had written Loyal Blue and Royal Scarlet and The Wyndham Girls.

The dedication honors Anna Wentworth Hecker. McClure published the book at New York. Taggart wrote many wholesome novels for girls in this period. Her grey house shelters a family whose doings fill the chapters. Domestic fiction of this kind formed a staple of girls' reading.
48604-the-daughters-of-the-little-grey-h:
Marion Ames Taggart's The Daughters of the Little Grey House was published by the McClure Company of New York in October 1907. It follows Taggart's earlier book, The Little Grey House, whose name it keeps. The volume is given to her cousin, Ella Johnson, with love. Eighteen chapters, each headed by the house's own story, carry the family forward.

The contents are a household chronicle: its inmates, its guests, its old friends, its dreadful night, and its hero. A lean-to room, a separate ell, a blended romance, a deadly insult, and a first wedding follow. Chapter one opens in the girls' room, Roberta Grey at the old mahogany dressing-table, asking how you know when you are a young lady. Frances Silsby answers from the rocking-chair: she knows she is young by the record in the Bible, and a lady by the company she keeps.
4903-hilda-wade-a-woman-with-tenacity-of:
Grant Allen's Hilda Wade opens with a doctor narrator insisting that his subject's gift must be shown before it can be described. Hilda's talent is unique and extraordinary, and the episodes that follow illustrate it through her encounters with patients, colleagues, and the formidable Professor Sebastian at St. Nathaniel's Hospital.

Sebastian, fiery-eyed and past his prime, impresses the narrator with greatness of mind and force of character as much as with scientific fame. Allen builds the novel episode by episode, each testing Hilda's insight and resolve. Readers get a Victorian mystery of character, where a woman's perception becomes the story's driving power.
49632-the-love-chase:
The Love Chase is a novel by Felix Grendon, published in Boston in 1922. Small, Maynard and Company issued the book, printed at Cambridge in Massachusetts. Grendon is named on the title page as author of Will He Come Back and Nixola of Wall Street. Two mottoes, from Byron and from George Eliot, stand at the front.

The tale is told in five parts with bold titles for each. They are Rebellion, Love Among the Outlaws, Janet on her Own, Nemesis, and Hearts and Treasures. The first chapter opens in a three room flat in the Lorillard model tenement houses in New York. A young man of twenty seven, of a dashing Count dOrsay type, sits astride a chair alone. The catalogue sample names a club called the Outlaws and a quarrel at its meeting, which ties the flat scene to the outlaw part of the plot.
49830-treasures-in-heaven-fifteenth-book:
George Lambert compiled this book for young Latter-day Saints at Salt Lake City in 1914. It is the fifteenth book of the Faith Promoting Series, designed for instruction and encouragement. Lambert had originated the series some thirty-five years earlier, his letter of April 8, 1914 explains at the front.

Publication had been suspended for almost thirty years before this volume, he writes. He asks the First Presidency for fresh sanction to resume the series with this book. The sanction he had at the start, and the good the volumes did, stand in his letter, and the treasures here are tales and testimonies of faith.
50060-under-the-hill-and-other-essays-in:
Under the Hill and Other Essays in Prose and Verse, a posthumous gathering by Aubrey Beardsley, was published by John Lane at the Bodley Head in 1904. Beardsley's own drawings illustrate the book. A photograph shows him at Mentone, in the room where he died.

The title piece, Under the Hill, is an unfinished romantic novel in a rich, ornate style. It is dedicated in mock solemn form to a invented cardinal. The Three Musicians and The Ballad of a Barber give his verse. A rendering of Catullus, table talk, and two letters round out the prose. The plates include The Toilet of Helen and The Ascension of Saint Rose of Lima.
50072-fragments-of-experience-sixth-book:
Fragments of Experience is the sixth book of the Faith-Promoting Series, printed at Salt Lake City in 1882. The Juvenile Instructor Office issued it for the teaching and heartening of young Latter-day Saints. The preface says the earlier books of the series had won a warm welcome in a short time, and met a long felt want.

The makers argue that young minds turn from dry doctrine but take to truth told as story. Tales drawn from real life, they hold, plant faith in God more surely than argument. The lives of elders of the church, full of striking events, give the material. This volume gathers such tales for the children of the mountain valleys.
50274-the-little-house:
Coningsby Dawson wrote this Christmas tale told by a little house itself. John Lane printed The Little House in New York in 1920. Stella Langdale drew the plates for the small volume here. The house claims it brought the happy ending by interfering.

Houses sleep all day and wake to talk after midnight, it says. Stairs crack, windows rattle, and floors creak as they think aloud. Old houses count births and marriages on their stairs like fingers. This one has stood almost two hundred years watching families pass. More children were born under its roof than it has stairs to count them on.
50489-poems-in-prose:
Charles Baudelaire wrote these poems in prose, rendered into English by Arthur Symons and printed in London in 1913. Symons calls the Petits Poemes en Prose both trials and confessions. In his own preface Baudelaire dreams of a poetic prose, musical without rhythm and without rhyme. Symons says he has kept close to the sense, words, and rhythm of the French.

Twelve pieces stand in the contents, from The Favours of the Moon to an epilogue. Windows, Crowds, The Cake, and Evening Twilight sit among them. The first piece shows the Moon, caprice itself, slipping through a window to a child in its cradle. She leaves her colours on the child's face and a lifelong longing for tears.
50811-what-happened-at-quasi-the-story-o:
What Happened at Quasi, subtitled The Story of a Carolina Cruise, is a boys' adventure book by George Cary Eggleston. It was published in Boston in April 1911 and illustrated by Edwards. The publisher's list places it among books for boys. Each volume there is handsomely illustrated and priced at a dollar and a half.

Eggleston's other titles in the list show his ground. They include a story of the Mississippi flatboats, a camp venture among the moonshiners of Virginia, and a blockade-running adventure. A tale of George Rogers Clark's expedition stands there too. The frontispiece of this volume shows a boy tugging at a root as a keg falls to pieces. A cruise on Carolina waters and some buried secret in a keg: the front matter promises sport and adventure.
5089-boris-godunov-a-drama-in-verse:
Alexander Pushkin's Boris Godunov, a drama in verse, presents the Time of Troubles through a crowded cast. Varlaam is a wandering friar. Athanasius Pushkin is a friend of Shuisky. Feodor is the young son of Boris. Semyon Godunov serves as the tsar's secret agent. Prince Kurbsky, the Cossack Karela, Marina daughter of Mnishek, and Ksenia daughter of Boris share the stage.

At the story's center stands Dimitry the Pretender, formerly Gregory Otrepiev, claiming the throne against Boris's haunted reign. Pushkin's blank verse carries conspiracy, conscience, and crowd scenes with Shakespearean breadth. Readers get Russia's founding historical drama, compact, political, and still startling in its modernity.
50905-yesterday-house:
Yesterday House, a tale by Fritz Leiber, ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in August 1952. Ashman drew the pictures. A man sails his sloop, the Annie O, into a narrow cove in Maine. He has pushed out to the farthest island, past vague warnings. The cove lies still, as if time paused there to rest. Sneaker marks fade fast in the hot sun. A second island, hid by the first, waits across a rocky spine.

On it stands a neat white Cape Cod cottage. An old Essex touring car sits on the gravel drive. A radio aerial runs the length of the roof. The head note gives the twist: meeting a person dead for twenty years shocks any reader. Leiber builds dread from quiet and sameness.
50916-evening-incense:
Evening Incense is a book of evening prayers published at Philadelphia in 1856. Hooker issued it from Chestnut Street. Its author is named only as the writer of Morning and Night Watches and Words of Jesus. A text from Exodus fronts the book: Aaron burning incense at even. Verses turn the star lit sky into a temple arch. The preface is dated December 1855.

Frequent requests had asked the writer for a small volume of evening prayers. It was meant as a companion to the Morning Watches. The contents list prayers by the grace they seek. Communion with God, pardoning grace, and renewing grace open the set. Sanctifying grace, imputed righteousness, and the spirit of adoption follow. Prayers for gratitude, trust, guidance, and firmness in temptation continue the list. Such manuals ordered private devotion night by night in many homes.
51018-three-days-in-the-village-and-othe:
Leo Tolstoy looks at his neighbours in Three Days in the Village, and other sketches, printed in London in 1910. The Free Age Press, under Daniel, made the book. The sketches were written from September 1909 to July 1910. A rendering by the Maudes carries the text. The cover notes place the title sketch in the style of his popular stories, giving glimpses into village life in Russia.

Three days structure the sketch: a first day of tramps, a second day of the living and the dying, a third day of taxes. A conclusion is named a dream. Singing in the village, traveller and peasant, and a talk with a wayfarer follow. The first day opens baldly: something entirely new has lately shown itself in our country districts. To our village of eighty homesteads, from half a dozen to a dozen cold, hungry, tattered tramps come every day.
51257-the-furious-rose:
Dean Evans wrote the Furious Rose, a tale in a galaxy magazine. The January number of 1952 carried the story. Thorne illustrated it for that monthly's readers. The world was a setup for any man wanting to get along. Given victims enough to toss to the wolves.

A master clock blipped in an office of federal executions. Lights lowered to a neutral setting then. Long probing shadow fingers snaked across the office floor. Radek leaned back and frowned at the hour of the night. No man should go to his execution machine at that hour. Why not hang a man instead, he wonders in the tale. His grandfather talked of twelve citizens saying the word once. Radek was a safe man now, too old for the war outside. Evans gives execution a bureaucrat's uneasy night.
51306-a-dog-day-or-the-angel-in-the-hous:
A Dog Day, or the Angel in the House, by Walter Emanuel, pictured by Cecil Aldin, was printed in New York by R H Russell in 1902. Rights were held by William Heinemann. Emanuel gives the book to W W Jacobs because he liked it. The tale runs as a dog diary of one day.

The day opens at seven in the morning. The dog wakes feeling rather below par, owing to disturbed rest. He has hardly enough energy to stretch himself. In the middle of the night a strange man came in by the kitchen window. From the broken text at the front, the dog spots the bag of silver and saves the house. Humor fans get a burglar night from the dog side of the door.
51343-motor-matt-s-reverse-or-caught-in-:
Motor Matt's Reverse, or Caught in a Losing Cause, is a dime novel issued as number 25 of Motor Stories, a weekly of thrilling motor fiction. Street and Smith published it in New York on August 14, 1909, at five cents a copy. The cover picture shows the hero lifting himself from a fall while a girl asks if he is hurt.

The chapter list promises speed and treachery. Three plotters open the tale, and a new aeroplane follows. Treachery and tragedy come next, then a startling plan and an air line into trouble. Later chapters bring the hero to earth, tighten the coil around him, and reveal a door in the hillside. A siege, a broker's game, and a deserter carry the action on. The book is pure weekly fare: motors, flight, and peril in sixteen short chapters.
51497-tales-from-the-telling-house:
Blackmore, the author of Lorna Doone, gathered four tales of the West Country in this volume. Sampson Low published it at London in 1896. The telling-house gives the book its name and frame. The tales are Slain by the Doones, Frida; or, The Lover's Leap, George Bowring, and Crocker's Hole. Each is a short, complete piece of Exmoor storytelling.

The preface wanders before it settles. Blackmore dreams of his grandfather, a parson in a shovel hat, riding a tall chestnut horse up the western slope of Exmoor. His little grandson follows on a shaggy pony. Below them the autumn muster of the sheep clans converges on the rendezvous, with dogs, shepherds, and the browning heather. It is a ramble in Blackmore's ripest manner, all moor weather and memory, before the first tale begins.
51657-charity-case:
Charity Case is a science fiction story by Jim Harmon, with pictures by Dick Francis. It ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in December 1959. The tale is told in the first person by a man with a strange curse.

He swears that things unseen plague him and speak with his voice. As a small child he was blamed for acts he says he did not do. His father locked him in a dark room, where unseen things tormented a boy who looked like him. Notes in his own hand, which he denies writing, turned his mother against him. The tale keeps its grip by letting doubt grow page by page.
52169-the-inner-house:
The Inner House is a scientific romance by Walter Besant, printed at New York by Harper and Brothers in 1888. Besant also wrote All Sorts and Conditions of Men and For Faith and Freedom. A prologue at the Royal Institution opens the tale. The director rushes to meet the evening's lecturer, a great physicist, crying that the theatre is crammed. Then the great mystery is to be solved at last: tell me before you go in.

The professor whispers his secret to his friend first. He came to a conviction that he was on the true line five years ago. Only within the last six months has he demonstrated the thing to a certainty. For six months mysterious telegrams from his laboratory had appeared in the papers. Besant's romance imagines what a secret of life itself would do to society.
52255-the-brownie-scouts-and-their-tree-:
Mildred A Wirt wrote The Brownie Scouts and Their Tree House. Cupples and Leon issued it at New York in 1951. Twenty chapters carry the girls' tale. A Brownie Wish opens the action. The Tossed Stone and Surprise follow. Six Brownie Scouts hike with their leader, Miss Gordon.

A weekly walk fills a metro natural park at the start. The girls name trees as their favorite game. Connie Williams leads the Rosedale troop in smarts. A walnut tree wins her praise on the trail. Chapters run through a mysterious sack and button drives. Mrs Myles draws their help and counsel. Unwelcome visitors and lunch guests fill the middle. Captured culprits and an auction sale build the end. A wish fulfilled closes the book. Cheerful troop fiction, the tale mixes woodcraft, kindness, and small mysteries for young scout readers.
52351-square-and-compasses-or-building-t:
Square and Compasses, or Building the House, is a boys' novel by Oliver Optic, third in his Boat Builder series. It was issued at Boston with an 1884 copyright. The series follows the young people of the Beech Hill Industrial School. Earlier volumes set them afloat; this one turns them to building a house.

The preface says the same characters from the earlier story return. Optic promises incident and adventure, yet says he never rests content with those alone. His books aimed to teach skill, honesty, and steady work along with the fun. A front plate shows a collision of boats, a hint of the harbour action inside. Oliver Optic was the pen name of a tireless writer of boys' series. This volume mixes house building craft with schoolboy scrapes and rescues, in the wholesome style that made his name a household word.
52573-samuell-gorton-a-forgotten-founder:
Samuell Gorton: A Forgotten Founder of Our Liberties is a short life by Lewis G Janes. Preston and Rounds published it at Providence in 1896. The book stands third in the Rhode Island Series. Each volume in the series sold at $1.00 net. Janes presents Gorton as the first settler of Warwick, Rhode Island.

The opening chapter sets old Warwick against the busy town of Janes's own day. Mills and manufacturing villages had replaced the colonial farms. Yet the contentions of a quarter of a millennium earlier still shaped the place. Those quarrels drove Gorton and his colleagues into the Shawomet wilderness. There they founded a settlement on ideas of liberty. Bancroft's praise of Rhode Island, quoted on the title page, frames the claim. More national ideas, he said, came from the little colony than from all the other states.
52612-travels-and-adventures-in-south-an:
Travels and Adventures in South and Central America, first series, is Don Ramon Paez's Life in the Llanos of Venezuela. Charles Scribner published it in New York in 1868. Paez dedicates it to Morris Ketchum, the kind friend of the exiled author. His motto runs: nothing is arduous to mortals. The preface tells how a Venezuelan plainsman was made.

Paez was born amid the wild scenes he describes. His parents sent him to England to finish his education. At Stonyhurst he met Charles Waterton, author of Wanderings in South America. Waterton's book became his favourite study at once. Humboldt's works next fed his taste for his native land's natural history. Returning home, he turned toward the matted woods where tigers wait. The country's troubles cut his exploring short. Still, his rambles through the plains gathered enough. Travellers, he notes, had scarcely touched the llanos' life.
52872-harry-harding-s-year-of-promise:
Alfred Raymond's Harry Harding's Year of Promise was published by the Goldsmith Publishing Company of Cleveland, copyrighted by Cupples and Leon in 1917. Twenty-four chapters follow Harry and Teddy Burke through a year. Planning the year of promise, declaring war on the percolator, and Teddy Burke the avenger stand in the heads. The Martin Minute Men and Teddy's darkest hour follow, to All's Well That Ends Well.

Chapter one finds Harry under a horse-chestnut tree, reading the last page of a book. The tale he finishes is the book's own pattern: a king who turned the Kingdom of Despair into the Kingdom of New Hope by doing a queer little man's bidding. The year of promise ended, the king calls for his friend to thank him; no one comes, and no casket is found. Harry sighs with satisfaction, and the boys' year of promise begins.
5312-mother-goose-in-prose:
L. Frank Baum's Mother Goose in Prose, illustrated by Maxfield Parrish and published in New York in 1901, retells the nursery rhymes as short stories. An illustration of a little man with a little gun opens the book. Baum gives each rhyme a plot, a character, and a reason, turning verses children knew by heart into tales to read aloud.

Baum, soon to be famous for The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, writes here with humour and warmth for young readers. The book offers a charming doorway into Mother Goose, where the rhymes gain beginnings, middles, and ends. The illustrations remain among Parrish's most beloved work.
53121-love-a-treatise-on-the-science-of-:
Love: A Treatise on the Science of Sex-Attraction is a medical work by Bernard Talmey. The Practitioners' Publishing Company issued this third revised edition in New York. Copyright was taken in 1919 by Cecilia Talmey. The book addresses physicians and students of medical jurisprudence by design.

Forty-seven cuts and eighty-four drawings illustrate the text throughout. A verse of Schiller on hunger and love stands as its motto. The contents open with a wide introduction on sex in civilization. Sex-worship, temple customs, fashion, and prudery pass in review there. A second part traces the evolution of sex from the lowest organisms. Darwinism, variation, and the development of the genital system fill it. A third part gives the anatomy of sex in systematic chapters. The treatise belongs to the early literature of scientific sexology for doctors.
53333-ebony-and-crystal-poems-in-verse-a:
Clark Ashton Smith wrote the poems in Ebony and Crystal, a book of verse and prose printed in 1922. The Auburn Journal at Auburn printed the book, and George Sterling wrote the preface. Smith gives the book to Samuel Loveman. The verse runs past one hundred pieces, from short songs to long, dark works. Names such as The Hashish-Eater and The Tears of Lilith hint at the mood. Sea nymphs, lost lands, night, and death turn up again and again.

After the verse come short prose pieces with names like The Traveler and The Black Lake. Those works read as brief dreams, dense with gems, tombs, and strange lands. Smith had put out two books of poems before this one. Ebony and Crystal shows his lush, eerie style at full stretch, in both song and tale form.
53544-george-at-the-wheel-or-life-in-the:
George at the Wheel, or Life in the Pilot House, is a boys river tale by Harry Castlemon. The book stands in a roughing it set of tales for young readers. Castlemon wrote long runs of gunboat and trapper tales for the same fans. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

George learns the work of a river pilot house on great steam boats. Wheel craft, marks, and night runs on wide muddy streams fill the tale. Ads in the front list whole sets of the author past hits for boys. Pluck and quick sight earn the hero his place at the wheel. The tale fed a taste for river life in the age of steam.
54598-the-crimson-sign-a-narrative-of-th:
Crimson Sign is a historical adventure novel by Keightley, published by Harper in 1898. Its hero is Gervase Orme, sometime lieutenant in Mountjoy regiment of foot. Keightley had written The Cavaliers, another tale of the same wars, before this book. An illustration shows Gervase dropping noiselessly into the water at page 288 of the tale.

Mountjoy regiment served in Ireland in the Williamite war against the Jacobites. Siege, march, and secret service give Orme adventures their crimson sign of danger. Keightley writes Irish history into romance with a soldier narrator at centre. Boys and general readers of 1898 gained a brisk tale of the Boyne age.
54725-a-butterfly-chase:
A Butterfly Chase is a children's book translated from the French of Stahl, issued at New York in 1869. It carries twenty four illustrations by Lorenz Frolich. The story opens with little Minnie and her cousin Bertie at a desk, looking at a butterfly book. They have quite made up their minds, the first page says, to have a splendid collection of butterflies.

They have been reading all about the chase in a book, the opening adds. Their uncle, a professor at the Museum, stands behind that learning. From the desk scene the tale follows the children out after real specimens. The many pictures, one at the head of the first chapter, show the young collectors at their tools. The book mixes story with the plain lure of a nature collection.
54911-an-account-of-the-sore-throat-atte:
John Fothergill wrote An Account of the Sore Throat Attended with Ulcers. C Davis printed it at London in 1748. Fothergill signs as a doctor of medicine. The disease had shown up of late in the city, he says. Nearby towns and other parts of the nation saw it too. A preface warns the reader at length.

Plain swelling of the tonsils looks mild at first glance, he notes. Most men think it a mere trouble, not a danger. Bleeding and purging are the usual orders for it. Yet this new sickness is of a very different nature. The old method often fails here, he warns. Careful case writing like this marks early modern medicine learning to split one complaint from a deadlier twin.
55042-tar-heel-tales-in-vernacular-verse:
Tar-Heel Tales in Vernacular Verse is a book of dialect poems issued in New York in 1873. Doolady published it, and Bonar drew its illustrations. The poems appear under the name Major Jep Joslynn. That major is a made-up spokesman, as the author's preface frankly explains.

The nameless author had served as a staff officer with Sherman's army in North Carolina. In camp he listened for hours to Tar-Heel refugees from the pine woods. They came crowding in search of food, full of adventures to tell. He studied their habits and their quaint speech with real interest. Poems in the book include Little Boots and My Rerligion, spelled as spoken. The Buzzin' Bees of Berks and Bob Munn of Cape Cod stand beside them.
55076-bahama-bill-mate-of-the-wrecking-s:
Bahama Bill is a sea novel by Jenkins Hains, subtitled Mate of the Wrecking Sloop Sea-Horse. Page published it at Boston in 1908 at a dollar and a half. A colour frontispiece by Reuterdahl shows its giant hero gazing out to sea. The first chapter is called Beneath the Bulldog's Bilge.

Chapters follow the wrecker's reward, the mate of the Sea-Horse, and Barnegat Macreary. One tells what passed when the light failed at Carysfort. The trimming of a landsman named Dunn adds comedy. Hains wrote of the wreckers who lived by salvage on the Florida reefs and the Bahama banks, a hard trade between rescue and plunder.
55097-a-book-of-nimble-beasts-bunny-rabb: A Book of Nimble Beasts, subtitled Bunny Rabbit, Squirrel, Toad, and Those Sort of People, is a nature book by Douglas English. English was a fellow and medalist of the Royal Photographic Society, and the book is built on his photographs of wild animals. The full edition carries more than two hundred illustrations. Its subjects are the small beasts of the English countryside, presented for young readers.
55141-mysteries-of-washington-city-durin:
Mysteries of Washington City covers several months of the session of the Twenty Eighth Congress. Its author signs himself only as a Citizen of Ohio. The book was printed in Washington in 1844 and entered by Caleb Atwater. It is dedicated to the members of that Congress, senators and representatives alike. The author calls it the first of a planned series of three. Humbugs and Crimes of Washington City were to follow.

The preface promises no malice toward any individual. Its aim is to reform men by exposing vice and praising virtue. Parties are kept out of the account, the author insists. He claims the departments of government had grown better run over twenty years. The Treasury, the Land Office, and the Post Office get special praise. The State Department, he says, was always well enough. The volume mixes sketches of capital life with moral counsel.
55298-her-husband-s-purse:
Her Husband's Purse, by Helen R Martin, came out in 1916, with pictures by John Newton Howitt. Its first page drops to New Munich, a town in Pennsylvania, struck by sudden news. Daniel Leitzel, a rich lawyer turned forty-five, is to wed, and told no one at home.

His two spinster sisters, Jennie and Sadie, learn of it from the town paper. For twenty years they did his thinking for him off the job, and kept sly girls from his great wealth. To hear of his match in print makes it past all hope of a stop. A bride, called the Unknown, will wed him in a month. Plates name Margaret in scenes of shock and mirth. Readers get a droll tale of purse, pride, and late love in a Dutch town.
55341-up-in-maine-stories-of-yankee-life:
Holman Day's Up in Maine, stories of Yankee life told in verse, was published by Small, Maynard of Boston in 1900, with an introduction by Littlefield. Day gives the book to Winfield Thompson, his friend in the craft of letters, to whom he owes several of the stories. The poems are dialect pieces, meant to be heard.

The first section, Round Home, opens with Aunt Shaw's Pet Jug. Uncle Elnathan Shaw takes the blue jug from the pantry shelf at half-past four and trots down cellar for cider, as he has for thirty years. Aunt Shaw calls after him every time: take care, you always trip on the second stair, and that jug is the best in town, left her by her great-aunt Sue. One day he slipped on that second stair, and Aunt Shaw's cry down the stairs was not for him: did ye break my jug.
55560-the-mercer-boys-mystery-case:
Capwell Wyckoff sets a school mystery in The Mercer Boys' Mystery Case, published by the World Publishing Company in 1948 as a Falcon Book. The cover story gives the case: cadets Don and Jim Mercer and their friend Terry Mackson must gather all the school trophies at Woodcrest Military Academy. Every trophy is found except the cup awarded to the Class of 1933.

Bit by bit the boys uncover a strange story that puzzled school authorities for years. The contents promise a hunt in the swamp, a digger in the garden, and the cup at last. School honor rides on the search.
55782-the-turnpike-house:
Fergus Hume wrote The Turnpike House, a tale first run as a serial in the Cheshire Observer from January to April nineteen oh two. Hume had earlier written The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, The Crimson Cryptogram, and The Golden Idol. Chapter one is called The Convict Return. The turnpike house stands where four roads meet, a square two storey building with whitewashed walls.

The fence and trim garden have vanished with the turnpike gate, the tale says. A jungle of gooseberry bushes and brambles shuts the house from the roads. Flat reaped fields stretch on all sides, bleak in November twilight. Mists gather over ditch and hedge, and dripping sounds in tree clumps. A narrow crooked path leads to a broken threshold. Windows stuffed with rags and walls cracked with green slime show deep poverty. A mystery of crime and return follows.
55950-a-madcap-cruise:
A Madcap Cruise, by Oric Bates, was printed at Boston and New York by Houghton, Mifflin in 1905. It opens at dusk in a small, shut harbor on an isle in East Penobscot Bay. Jerrold Taberman tells his mate they are booked for fame, win or lose: heroes down the ages, or the worst pair of asses who ever botched a job. John Castleport, tall and dark, holds the glasses and takes the charge with a smile.

Both young men wear navy work dress, and an old gentleman, hard to please, waits on their care. Heads ahead name fog, winds from each point of the sky, and land at last. A Mr Wrenmarsh, a lone-hand game, and a storm fill the back run. Sail fans get a gay, rash cruise in fine salt prose.
55968-a-history-of-the-british-army-vol-:
The Honorable J W Fortescue wrote A History of the British Army, first volume. Macmillan issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety nine. This first part runs to the close of the Seven Years’ War. Old Style and New Style dates stand side by side in its notes.

The true start of the army tale lies far back, Fortescue holds. Hastings and the old English foot host open the long account. Knight service rose, proved weak, and passed with the feudal host. The Assize of Arms and the Great Charter mark the next steps. Edward the First set deep reforms: arrays and the Winchester law. Falkirk and Bannockburn show the foot host in its pride and fall. Paid troops hired by indent then take the field for France. Welsh spears and English bows fill the ranks of those hosts.
5625-flint-and-feather-collected-verse:
E. Pauline Johnson gathered her verse in Flint and Feather, a collection inscribed by gracious permission to the Duke of Connaught. A memoir introduction recalls that Johnson, on her deathbed, wished the writer of that introduction, living far away in the mother country, to write something about her. The poems themselves span her career as a Mohawk poet and performer.

Johnson's verse moves between Indigenous subjects, Canadian landscape, and lyric feeling, in the voice that made her famous on stage. Readers get the collected poems of a pioneering Indigenous Canadian writer, passionate, musical, and rooted in two cultures.
56302-the-source-and-mode-of-solar-energ:
The Source and Mode of Solar Energy Throughout the Universe is a work of speculative astronomy by I W Heysinger. J B Lippincott published it in Philadelphia in 1895. Heysinger states the problem plainly at the start. The sun pours out heat and light without visible fuel. What feeds that fire, and how does its energy travel?

The chapters move from the constitution of the sun to its mode and source of energy. Heysinger argues an electrical theory of the solar system. His plates show planetary electricity flowing to the sun and sun-spots forming under it. Later chapters treat the stars, meteors, and comets. The nebular hypothesis gets a chapter of difficulties. A final chapter takes up the Mosaic cosmogony. The book tries to reconcile Victorian physics, electrical theory, and Genesis in one system.
56416-john-baring-s-house:
John Baring's House, a novel by Elsie Singmaster, was copyrighted in 1920 and printed by Houghton Mifflin. Singmaster also wrote Gettysburg, Katy Gaumer, and When Sarah Saved the Day. Chapter one is titled A New Home, and opens in June twilight on the doorstep of an old house.

Elizabeth Scott leans her head against the stone wall, a hard day done. Three meals were prepared and half the large garden hoed and weeded. The gardening knowledge of herself and her brother was made up for by excess cultivation. Herbert comes round the corner with a dependent quality in his voice. Elizabeth answers briskly and firmly. Firmness is one of her most noticeable qualities, though those who oppose her call it stubbornness.
