Contents promise a puzzle in the family's life: what is the matter with us, a journey in vain, and Herbert putting two and two together.
5660-mary-louise:
Edith Van Dyne wrote Mary Louise for young readers, introducing a heroine she calls very human and much like the reader herself. Van Dyne, author of the Aunt Jane's Nieces series and The Daring Twins, presents Mary Louise as really not a fiction character at all, but a girl readers might know. Her success, the preface says, rests largely on finding such a heroine.

The novel follows Mary Louise through family troubles, friendships, and adventures, with more volumes promised about the lovable girl. Van Dyne writes for girls with warmth and directness. Young readers get a friendly series opener, centered on a kind, brave, ordinary girl.
56609-a-history-of-the-british-army-vol-:
Volume two of Fortescue's History of the British Army, the first part ending with the close of the Seven Years' War, was published by Macmillan in London in 1899. Fortescue's subject here runs from 1713 to 1763. The volume's notes warn the reader about dates: England kept the Julian calendar until 1752, eleven days behind the Gregorian, and sidenotes for the earlier years give both styles.

The contents open with the army's reduction after Utrecht. Bolingbroke and Ormonde exert a mischievous influence; Queen Anne dies and Marlborough returns; George the First takes the throne with a new ministry. Then the Jacobite rebellion of 1715: the army increased, the Ninth to Fourteenth Dragoons raised, Chelsea pensioners recalled, the Forty-first Foot raised, and the fights at Sheriffmuir and Preston. The index at the back covers both volumes of the history.
56632-two-little-women-and-treasure-hous:
Two Little Women and Treasure House, by Carolyn Wells, was published in nineteen sixteen by Dodd, Mead and Company of New York. E C Caswell illustrated the story. Wells wrote the Patty books and the Marjorie books, and this volume continues her Two Little Women series. Its heroines are Dotty Rose and Dolly Fayre.

The opening explodes with delight over a plan on Mr Rose's table. The girls are to have a real little house of their own, with fireplaces and window-seats. Both high school girls needed a quiet place to study. Their homes offered only company, sewing societies, and small sisters at play. The chapters run through a high school dance, funny Uncle Jim, and a strange intruder. A carnival queen and fortunes for all close the contents.
56974-a-london-plane-tree-and-other-vers:
Amy Levy's A London Plane-Tree and Other Verse appeared in Fisher Unwin's Cameo Series in 1889. A note records that Levy corrected the proofs about a week before her death. The epigraph, from Austin Dobson, calls hers an urban muse bound to paved ground. The book is dedicated to Clementina Black. Its first section gathers London poems: the title piece, London in July, A March Day in London, a Ballade of an Omnibus.

A second section, Love, Dreams, and Death, holds New Love New Life, Youth and Love, On the Threshold, and Last Words. Moods and Thoughts follows, with Alma Mater, In the Black Forest, The Two Terrors, and The Promise of Sleep. Odds and Ends closes the volume. Levy had earlier published A Minor Poet and Other Verse and the novels The Romance of a Shop and Reuben Sachs.
57022-a-minor-poet-and-other-verse:
A Minor Poet and Other Verse, by Amy Levy, appears in the Cameo Series from Fisher Unwin in London in a second edition of 1891. The volume reprints the issue of 1884, adding a sonnet and a translation from an earlier Cambridge book of 1881, long out of print. A portrait of Levy fronts the text. Contents mix lyrics, dramatic pieces, and translations.

Xantippe and Medea, two long poems in women's voices, anchor the book. Sinfonia Eroica, Magdalen, Christopher Found, and A Dirge follow. The opening poem, To a Dead Poet, watches strangers talk of a poet's rooms and habits. The speaker, who never saw his face, sits mute as stone and thinks she knew him best. Levy's verse is spare and bleak, much of it on fame, failure, and the wish for rest.
57138-ramshackle-house:
Ramshackle House is a mystery novel by Hulbert Footner, published by the Doran Company of New York in 1922. The scene is Broome's Point, a crescent of sand between the mouth of the Pocomico River and Chesapeake Bay.

The Broome estate runs four miles up the bay shore and a mile along the river. Its mansion, a square packing-box of a house from the sixties, has never been repainted since it was first painted. Pen Broome, the heroine, flies in and out of the big house on endless chores. The chapters promise a canoeist, a story in a newspaper, an irruption from the world, a trip to town and days of suspense. Later, Pen's hand is forced, a yacht sails away, and a postscript closes the tale. Footner specialised in polished detective fiction of exactly this kind.
57212-doctor-quintard-chaplain-c-s-a-and:
Quintard told his war story in Doctor Quintard, chaplain and second bishop of Tennessee, edited by Arthur Howard Noll. The University Press at Sewanee put it out in 1905. Noll, the church historian of Tennessee, widened the tale to cover later church work by Quintard. The book is given to friends and comrades of Quintard in the Confederate army and in the church. It runs from the start of the war in 1861 to its close in 1865.

Chapters trace Valley Mountain, Perryville, Murfreesboro, Chickamauga, Atlanta, and Franklin. A dramatic episode and the crumbling of the Confederacy close the war tale. Later parts take up the building of the church in Tennessee and the growth of Christian schools in the South. The book gives a chaplain view of war, and a bishop view of peace.
57563-queensland-the-rich-but-sparsely-p:
Queensland: The Rich but Sparsely Peopled Country is an emigration pamphlet issued by the Intelligence and Tourist Bureau at Brisbane, in its sixth edition of 1915. Its subtitle calls Queensland a paradise for willing workers. The classes who should come are listed: farmers, agricultural labourers, men accustomed to live stock, miners, and domestic servants.

Men with small capital accustomed to outdoor life are wanted, and men without capital who are not afraid of hard work. Any steady, energetic person of these classes, the pamphlet promises, should have no difficulty in earning a good livelihood. Rates of wages are printed: ordinary farm labourers get twenty to twenty-seven shillings a week with board and lodging. On sheep and cattle stations married couples receive a furnished cottage, rations, and other perquisites worth about three pounds a week besides wages.
5795-the-secret-rose:
Yeats gathers mystical tales in The Secret Rose, dedicated to AE and opening with a dedication to the rose itself. Contents include The Crucifixion of the Outcast and Out of the Rose. The Wisdom of the King and The Heart of the Spring follow. The Curse of the Fires and of the Shadows and The Old Men of the Twilight complete the set. Each tale treats the rose as a symbol of spiritual beauty and hidden truth.

Readers enter Yeats's early world of saints, kings, outcasts, and twilight figures, where earthly life touches the eternal. The prose is ornate and musical, favoring vision over action, and the stories reward slow reading. Fans of symbolist fiction and Irish mysticism will find a defining Yeats collection, short enough to read in an evening and rich enough to revisit.
57995-rose-and-rose:
Rose and Rose is a novel by Lucas, printed by Methuen in London and first published on September 15, 1921. A second edition followed the same year. The narrator, an old doctor, looks back fifty years to when he was a young medical student who spent weekends at home, at the practice he was one day to succeed.

On a certain Saturday, the only other people in his railway compartment were an artist and his wife, house hunting near Lowcester. The narrator praised a house just empty at Bullingham, five miles away, adjoining his father's. They took it, and the families became friends. He muses that the doctor who delivers a child keeps a stake in that child's whole life.
58100-words-their-use-and-abuse:
William Mathews preaches word care in Words, Their Use and Abuse, printed at Chicago in 1907. Scott, Foresman made the book; the copyrights run back to 1876 and 1884. Mathews had writ Getting On in the World and Oratory and Orators. Two mottoes front the work, and argue its whole case in advance.

Language and thought are inseparable, says the first, from Max Muller. Words without thought are dead sounds; thoughts without words are nothing. To think is to speak low; to speak is to think aloud. The word is the thought made flesh. A winged word, says the second, from Landor, has struck deep in a million hearts. On a winged word has hung the fate of nations. Words are things, the page goes on, and a small drop of ink, falling like dew upon a thought, makes thousands think. Usage is treated here as a moral art.
58510-madame-adam-juliette-lambert-la-gr:
Stephens wrote this life of Madame Adam for Dutton. Juliette Lambert, called la grande Francaise, was in her eighty-first year when the book appeared, and her life, Stephens argues, is one of the momentous chapters of French history. She lived through the revolution of 1848, the coup of 1851, the siege of Paris, the Commune, and two invasions of her country.

As mistress of a salon and founder of La Nouvelle Revue, which she edited for twenty years, she kept her finger on the nation's pulse. Gambetta, Thiers, George Sand, Flaubert, Hugo, and Daudet were her intimates. Gambetta said she was always out of the ranks. Her father, one of the ardent revolutionaries, gave her the instinct; defeat in 1871 turned it into a lifelong advocacy of nationality. Stephens writes the biography as patriotic history, France in the person of one combative woman.
58636-board-work-or-the-art-of-wig-makin:
Board-Work, or The Art of Wig-Making, by Edwin Creer, is a trade manual published in London in 1887 for hairdressers and the young men learning their work. Creer edited the Hairdressers' Chronicle and had written earlier books on hair and hairdressing.

The preface says the book answers a long-felt want among apprentices and improvers whose skill at board-work is weak. Much of the text first appeared in his journal and was then gathered, revised, and enlarged for the volume. Alongside the teaching on wig making, the book adds remarks on razors, razor sharpening, and strops, plus a set of chosen recipes for the trade. A portrait of the author and many pictures guide the learner through the work.
59379-plain-concrete-for-farm-use:
Farmers Bulletin Number 1279, Plain Concrete for Farm Use, came from the United States Department of Agriculture in October 1922. The text names T A H Miller as its author. Miller was an engineer in the Bureau of Public Roads. The aim was to help farm users new to concrete work.

The bulletin walks through each step of plain concrete work. It covers cement, sand, and stone, and how to mix them in the right parts. It then covers forms, mixing, placing, and care of fresh work. It also deals with frost, joints, lintels, finish, fire, and tight work that holds water. Cost and waste get close care all through.
59891-reginald-bateman-teacher-and-soldi:
Reginald Bateman, Teacher and Soldier, a memorial volume of selections from his lectures and other writings, was printed in 1922 for the University of Saskatchewan at Saskatoon. Henry Sotheran of London published it for the university. A prefatory note explains the book and the man.

Reginald John Godfrey Bateman was the first professor of English at the University of Saskatchewan. The governors and faculty judged that his friends and old students would value a fair selection of the lectures he gave inside and outside the university. A few poems found among his papers are added. The lectures were written for popular audiences and literary gatherings, never for print, and were hurriedly prepared in the rush of a college session. Bateman, born in Ireland, was cut off in his prime in the Great War.
59896-newfoundland-verse:
Newfoundland Verse is a poetry collection by E J Pratt, published at Toronto in nineteen twenty three. Pratt dedicates the book to his mother, and a contents page groups the poems by theme. Sea variations open the volume, with poems on bells, ground swell, ice floes, and fog. The sea is the ruling presence of the book.

A shark, a flood tide, and the loss of the steamship Florizel stand among the sea poems. Monologues and dialogues follow, then pieces called creatures of another country. An ode to December nineteen seventeen closes the main list. Pratt's early verse already shows the maritime power that made him Canada's leading poet of the sea.
59986-the-dreadnought-boys-world-cruise:
Wilbur Lawton wrote this sea tale for boys, copyrighted by Hurst in New York in 1913. Wrenn illustrated the Dreadnought Boys' world cruise for the publisher that year. A plate shows Ned shooting upward to grab the bridle of a flying beast, at page ten by its caption.

At the Golden Gate opens the contents, and an important duty follows. In Chinatown comes third, and Ned delivers the goods in chapter four of the list. Lawton had written the Boy Aviators and earlier Dreadnought Boys books on battle practice, destroyers and submarines, sending his young sailors round the world this time.
60346-i-pose:
Stella Benson wrote I Pose, a novel published by the Macmillan Company in New York in 1916. A poem opens the book, spoken by a soul that sits aloof with its Friend above the brown streets of London. The short preface gives the book its key: sometimes I pose, but sometimes I pose as posing.

The first chapter introduces a gardener, a man who, the narrator insists, is probably alive still, since the book has no death-bed scenes. Benson builds her tale on masks and play-acting: people who hide their true selves, and hide the hiding. The style is light, arch, and self-aware. I Pose was Benson's first novel, and it shows the wit that marked her later work.
60528-the-owls-house:
Crosbie Garstin wrote The Owls House, issued in New York by A L Burt Company by pact with Frederick A Stokes Company. The copyright is nineteen twenty three. John Penhale is the chief figure at the start. The tale is set in Cornwall, near Helston. Night rain, inn yards, and old streets set the scene.

Penhale leaves a Helston lawyer office late in the dusk. Fine drizzle blows down Coinage Hall Street and street lights turn puddles to gold. A chaise clatters uphill and an old soldier with a wood leg sings drunk by an inn. Penhale steps into The Angel inn and sits with the right side of his face to the wall, from habit. A scar or secret may lie behind that habit. Noise, drink, and rough sport fill the room around him.
60598-the-fireless-cook-book-a-manual-of:
Margaret J Mitchell teaches cooking without fire in The Fireless Cook Book, a manual of the construction and use of appliances for cooking by retained heat. Doubleday, Page and Company issued it, copyrighted in 1909. The title page counts 250 recipes. Mitchell had been dietitian of Manhattan State Hospital and an instructor at Drexel Institute.

The contents begin with the fireless cooker itself, then the portable insulating pail and the refrigerating box. Recipe chapters follow for cereals, soups, fish, beef, lamb, veal, pork, poultry, and vegetables. The first chapter promises dinner put on to cook, then a visit or the theatre, with no further thought.
60663-sonnets-and-verse:
H Belloc published a book of sonnets and verse in London, first issued in 1923, dedicated to John Swinnerton Phillimore. His dedication poem recalls two small boys taking delight in foolish painted toys. He asks his friend to take these imperfect toys of verse. In the heart, he hopes, they may attain the form of perfect things.

Sonnets come first, numbered in roman figures. Titles and first lines invoke the Weald, the winter moon, and youth. One sonnet begins with lifting up hearts in Gumber. Another recalls sleeping at dawn in Tuscany. Later verse follows the sonnet sequence. Belloc writes in strict forms with a Catholic and English sense of place.
61213-the-64-square-madhouse:
Fritz Leiber wrote a tale of chess and machines first printed in Worlds of If in May 1962. Reporter Sandra Lea Grayling covers a grand chess meet for the Chicago Space Mirror. For the first time, an electronic machine plays in a top world contest. The hall teems with masters, clocks, and boards of all sizes.

Talk flies about the machine's set plans and how the Russian masters may gang up on it. Leiber notes the machine can be tricked, can err, and can learn. Sandra, fresh from space news, finds chess folk stranger than crews in orbit. Fans of wit and games will enjoy the clash.
61870-the-monster-that-threatened-the-un:
The Monster That Threatened the Universe is a science fiction story by Russ Winterbotham. It appeared in Planet Stories in the spring of 1941. The headnote sets the stakes at once. A space-consuming creature reaches slimy tentacles toward trembling planets. No man of the old fighting breed remains on Earth to fight it.

The creature is Limio, a monster in a black hole of space. He lives by the dying fires of a star called Chaos. His body covers a fourth of that world. Hundreds of eyes dot his massive frame. They see by infra-red light. Limio came to Chaos as a single spore. He eats living things only to destroy rivals. A rocket ship with guns now enters his realm.
62009-the-quarterly-of-the-oregon-histor:
The Oregon Historical Society put out a quarterly of the far west's past. Volume one, number three is dated September 1900. One dollar bought a year of the sheet in that age. The Oregon Question, part two, by Joseph Wilson leads it. Tales by Hugh Cosgrove and William Case fill the next span.

Lyman took down both men's tales of the old days in full. The count and state of the native race when first seen stands there. Indian names and old print from 1812 fill the list's tail. A note by Senator Plumer of New Hampshire closes the files part. The group was set up on December 17, 1898. West past fans get gold.
62027-keeping-his-course:
Ralph Henry Barbour sends boys to sea in Keeping His Course, printed in New York and London in 1918. Appleton made the book, with copyright that year. Louderback draws the plates. A plate line fronts it: hold on, is that not a sort of a light over there? Lists of Barbour's school and sport series fill the front pages, the Purple Pennant, Yardley Hall, and Grafton books among them.

The contents open ashore and afloat. Toby resents an insult leads, then the Turnover, a boat by her name. Arnold pays his debts and friends afloat follow. Shots in the dark raise the stakes. Pursuit and capture, and the stolen launch, drive the mid run. The field here is water: a launch, a theft, and a chase, and a hero who must keep his course in more ways than one.
62109-the-star-mouse:
The Star Mouse is a science fiction story by Fredric Brown, printed in Planet Stories in the spring of 1942. Its headnote ranks the saga of Mitkey above the adventures of Robinson Crusoe, Gulliver, and Paul Bunyan.

Mitkey is at first just another mouse, living behind the floorboards of the Connecticut house of Professor Oberburger, a refugee formerly of Vienna and Heidelberg. The professor had fled the excessive admiration of powerful fellow-countrymen for a gas, the by-product of an unsuccessful rocket fuel, that might have been a highly successful something else. He had escaped, the story hints, without giving them the correct formula. A small grey mouse and a small grey man: the professor, a bachelor, talks to himself constantly while he works, and Mitkey has excellent ears.
62536-uttara-the-legend-of-the-turquoise:
Uttara, the Legend of the Turquoise, is a tale in verse and prose by Carlo de Fornaro. Both text and art come from the same hand in this small book. A New York jeweler house put the work out as its own gift book. The book bears a rights line of the year nineteen hundred and two.

Three great gods fall in love with one mortal maid in the tale. The maid is a priests child of rare and blind fair looks in the songs. A court poet goes blind from one sight of her face in the frame tale. Hymn lines from old India head the first page of the fable. The blue green stone of the title lends the tale its hue and fate.
62597-design-of-a-steel-railroad-warehou:
Louis Liston Tallyn wrote this thesis for his bachelor of science degree in civil engineering at the University of Illinois in 1901. The design covers a steel railroad warehouse at New Orleans for the Illinois Central Railroad. Ira Baker, head of the department, signed the page that approves the work in May 1901.

Tallyn opens by saying he chose a subject of practical use for the career ahead of him, since he meant to make railroad work his specialty. Warehouse design, he notes, had drawn little study so far. He argues that nearly all railroad warehouses of the day were wood, but rising timber costs made steel the plain choice for new work. The paper then works through design principles and the steel frame itself. Engineering readers get a full student design from the age when steel took over the freight house.
62644-veterinary-medicines-their-actions:
George F Korinek wrote Veterinary Medicines, Their Actions, Uses and Dose. The Veterinary Science Association of America published it, with copyright in 1917. Korinek graduated from the Ontario Veterinary College and from the University of Toronto's veterinary department. He served as registrar of the association that issued the book. Ten years of practical work in veterinary medicine and surgery stand on his title page. The front matter defines the three branches of the subject.

Materia medica treats medicines, their sources, preparation, doses, and effects. Therapeutics applies all means to the cure of disease or the relief of pain. Toxicology treats poisons, their nature, detection, and treatment. A medicine is an agent of animal, vegetable, or mineral origin. The general actions follow in order: alteratives, which change the working of nutrition, and anaesthetics among them.
62770-a-booklet-of-verse:
Rozelle Myers-Funnell wrote A Jubilee Offering, a booklet of verse printed at Ottawa in 1897 at fifty cents. She gives the book, by leave, to Her Majesty's representative in Canada and to the Countess of Aberdeen. Contents name fifteen poems. The Jubilee Song stands first, then Quinte, hope, thou art near, and farewell to the old school-house. At clinics and beyond follow. Bric-a-brac, indifference, autumn, photographed, and at even fill the rest.

The Jubilee Song, set to the air of the national anthem, calls on fair Canada to bring forth a worthy lay from her heart. It sings of the sturdy past, when brave hearts struggled with sword and pen for home and Queen. It sings the golden now of peace, and the coming years when truth alone shall stand and justice rule every land. The volume ends its song with the cry of her jubilee.
63010-verse:
Verse is the gathered poems of Adelaide Crapsey, printed by Alfred A Knopf in New York in 1926. Crapsey was born on September 9, 1878, and died on October 8, 1914, in her thirty sixth year. Her father held the rights in her work.

A short life at the front tells that she grew up in Rochester, New York, where her father led a parish. She shone at Kemper Hall school and at Vassar College, then taught history and letters. Ill health forced her to stop work in 1908. Crapsey is famed for the cinquain, a five line form she made her own. Her poems are brief, spare, and full of quiet grief. Readers meet a fine, brief talent cut off young, in her own best form.
63109-doctor-universe:
Carl Jacobi wrote a space tale called Doctor Universe, first run in Planet Stories in the fall of 1944. Its star is Grannie Annie, an old woman who writes science tales under the name Annabella Flowers. She has stumbled on a real murder plot more wild than any tale she ever made, and the gun is aimed at the narrator.

He meets her at the Spacemen's Club in Swamp City, a rest house where no women may pass the door. She storms the lounge on her green umbrella, in a black dress and a doily cap, and defies the clerk to move her. Two years have passed since they last met. The tale that follows mixes club rules, space port life, and a plot to kill.
63153-morning-in-the-west-a-book-of-vers:
Morning in the West is a book of verse by Katherine Hale, issued at Toronto by the Ryerson Press with copyright in 1923. Hale had written Grey Knitting and The White Comrade before it. She dedicates the poems to her mother, who means song to her, she says. The first part of the book takes its title from the title poem.

Cunnewabum, a ballad of Jasper Road, and Buffalo Meat stand in that first part. Return of the Trappers and Spanish Pilots keep the western theme. A second part, Women, holds portraits and dance poems. Pavlowa dancing and Calvé in blue show her range of subjects there. A third part, Going North, turns to shadow and snow country. Hale writes Canada, west and north, in singing measure.
6324-the-story-of-a-white-rocking-horse:
One by one the lights go out in the toy department, shoppers and clerks leave, and only a small light guides the night watchman. Then a Calico Clown cries that they can have fun. A Lamb on Wheels warns that they must be sure no eyes watch, and the Bold Tin Soldier agrees, glad the store is empty. Laura Lee Hope's toys talk and move only when no one sees, and the White Rocking Horse sways at the centre of their night world.

Too large for the counter with clown, monkey, rabbit, and soldier, the horse and the lamb watch days pass and nights return, with kind boys preferred to one rude chap. The story belongs to Hope's Make Believe series, beside the Sawdust Doll and the Bold Tin Soldier. It is a gentle tale for children, where toys keep their society after closing time and kindness counts most.
63418-poor-blossom-the-story-of-a-horse:
The author of Neddy and Me and Only a Ladybird wrote the story of a horse, printed at London. My place of birth fronts the tale as a picture. The book is given to all who have the management of that noble and useful animal the horse. My place of birth opens the chapters, then broken, my new master, and I am sold.

The furniture dealer, sad scenes of life, and my new master Benjamin Bunter follow. The great carnival, here and there, and my gentle mistress fill the middle. Another loss and a disappointment lead to exit Blossom at the close. The first thing I remember is a green field enclosed by a stiff fence, where I was running by my mother's side, the horse begins. Mr Bayne entered the field, and my mother ran up to be caressed and fed. Kindness and cruelty to horses are the lesson.
6345-seven-maids-of-far-cathay-being-eng:
Bing Ding compiles English notes from a Chinese class book, written by seven Chinese girls of the graduating class at the Woman's Anglo-Chinese College of Neuchang. The college president set them a game for their last six months of course, their notes were read aloud, taken down by a stenographer, and arranged alphabetically. Friends asked for publication exactly as written, and the president permitted it.

The notes, illustrated by Ai Lang, show young writers practising English with charm and frankness, from dedications to a grandmother genius of geniuses to a night rescue on rocks. A boat comes near in darkness, one lantern flashes like an insect, and Miss Sterling's voice calls through the black night asking if all are safe. The book is a rare, direct record of Chinese schoolgirls writing in a new tongue.
63677-the-recluse:
Mike Curry wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Planet Stories in the winter of 1954. Arak Miller has been alone on a planet for twenty five years when a ship appears one summer afternoon. He watches it from the mesa and thinks, from Earth. Visions of his wife, his sons, and his work rise in him.

Miller plans to light great pyres of pine and brush to signal his presence. He carries a figure called Marbach into his house and sits him on a chair. Miller crashed years before and was left for dead. He has built room after room he never uses. Curry builds the tale on longing for a human voice.
63698-biographical-catalogue-of-the-port:
Mary Boyle compiled this catalogue of portraits at Panshanger house. Elliot Stock printed it in London in 1885 with plates. Panshanger was the seat of Earl Cowper, the title page says. Boyle gives the pages to Francis Lord Cowper and his wife.

A Carlyle line on true portraits fronts the catalogue as motto. Boyle used the same system as her Hinchingbrook and Longleat books. Family members and kin get the fullest sketches in her plan. Public life details yield to private and domestic ones, she writes. Arise, pray, work stands as the house motto on the catalogue front page shown.
63707-the-primus-curse:
The Primus Curse is a science fiction story by Bill Wesley, printed in the magazine Planet Stories in May 1954. Its headnote speaks in the captain's voice: the psychology boys had been right again, and it annoyed the veteran. He had felt like a mechanical man all the time, sending men to their deaths.

Captain Evan Grimes opens the tale by dressing down his chief engineer. Manson has used the banned name Mercury for the planet Primus, three times on this trip, though the Service banned it five years ago. Recorders are spying, and the slip could cost a week's pay. Manson salutes, grinning, and pleads forgetfulness. The Academy code, the story notes, drums one lesson into cadets: your ship is your life. Every speck of meteoric dust on her hide is your responsibility, and the crew with her. Wesley builds his curse on that drilled-in obedience.
64184-the-airship-boys-in-the-great-war-:
De Lysle F Cass sends two boy airmen into the Great War in a tale issued at Chicago in 1915. Alan Hope reads war news in a newspaper and finds it touches a close friend. His chum Ned Napier, buried in blueprints, learns that they should worry after all.

The boys' ship, the Ocean Flyer, is readied while a stranger tries to buy her and a warning comes from Buck Stewart. Chapters run to Paris, the Ardennes, a firing squad at sunrise, and the rescue of Bob Russell, who tells how he was taken as a spy. Cossacks in Poland, besieged Przemysl, Vienna, and a battle with Zeppelins above the clouds follow. Young readers get wartime air adventure written while the war it describes still raged.
64262-buffalo-bill-s-big-surprise:
Colonel Prentiss Ingraham wrote Buffalo Bill's Big Surprise, or The Biggest Stampede on Record, copyright 1914 by Street and Smith at New York. A prefatory appreciation of William Cody recalls the start of the stories. Ingraham and Ned Buntline, friends of Cody, forgathered in the dingy Rose Street office of the New York Weekly and began writing Buffalo Bill's adventures. Cody was born in Scott County, Iowa, on February 26, 1846, and migrated to Kansas as a boy.

Forty-four chapters run the dime-novel course: bad news, an outlaws' ally, a forged letter, and an Indian village. A ride for help, black troopers at bay, a living tomb, Devil's Den, and a haunted hacienda follow. Black Bill works a lone hand, takes a prisoner, and escapes twice. Ingraham keeps Cody rescuing and unmasking to the final Revealed.
64474-planet-in-reverse:
Planet in Reverse is a science fiction novelette by Henry Guth, printed in Planet Stories in the spring of 1948. Its hero, Darrel Bond, pilots a million-ton freighter alone. Ships in his day fly nearly by themselves, and Bond is bored to rebellion by button-pushing.

Warned by the fleet admiral to keep to the freight lanes, Bond swings his ship outside the orbit of Uranus for relief. Something on the strange world beyond cuts off all radio contact with Earth. A love affair grows there under reversed conditions, hinted by the story's backwards-spoken cry for help. The tale is pulp work of its moment: a restless spaceman, a jumbled planet where speech and time run odd, and a romance tested by a world turned the wrong way round.
64476-panama-and-the-canal-in-picture-an:
Panama and the Canal in Picture and Prose is a big photo book by Willis Abbot. Syndicate Publishing brought it out in English and Spanish in 1913. Water-colours by Read and Gordon Grant stand among its many pictures. More than six hundred photographs were taken just for this one book. Leading men of the great work approved the whole account, it boasts.

The canal runs south from Colon for ten miles, the map note says. Then it bends east toward the Pacific, against what most folk think. Chapter one, the front door to Panama, opens at Antilla in Cuba. Colon's streets, the railroad built through swamp, and the French come next. San Blas Indians, the Chinese story, and railroad costs fill that part. Abbot had written The Story of Our Navy before this giant work.
6455-the-little-lady-of-the-big-house:
Jack London's The Little Lady of the Big House opens in darkness, with Dick Forrest waking simply, without movement save eyes opening. Unlike most, he knows himself at once in time, place, and personality, taking up the interrupted tale of his days without effort. He is master of broad acres, fallen asleep after marking Road Town with a match and pressing off his electric reading lamp, near a sleepy fountain's ripple.

Far off, faint to a keen ear, comes the throaty bawl of King Polo, his champion Short Horn bull, thrice grand champion of all. Later, Paula, the little lady, introduces the house's sages with a warning. Dar Hyal abstains wholly, Theodore Malken gets poetically drunk on one cocktail, Aaron Hancock is an expert wine bibber, and Terrence McFane can put ninety nine men under the table. London writes a California ranch novel of wealth, love, and talk.
64664-buffalo-bill-s-ruse:
Colonel Prentiss Ingraham wrote this Buffalo Bill tale for Street and Smith of New York. The rights date to 1906, and its second title is Won by Sheer Nerve. Ingraham was the famed hand of the Border Stories line of Cody tales.

Pizen Kate opens the hunt, then Ready to Go and an unexpected meeting. Pizen Kate finds her husband, and strange vanishings follow. Indian treachery and the attack of the Mexican crowd the list shown here. A piece in praise of William Cody heads the book. Ingraham, who had ridden and fought in the West himself, made Cody a hero of print for two generations of boys.
64689-the-true-grecian-bend-a-story-in-v:
The True Grecian Bend is a comic poem by Larry Leigh, published by J S Redfield of New York in 1868. Its subtitle calls it a story in verse, and it is illustrated. A line from Milton stands at the head, asking an execrable shape its name.

The heroine is a fashionable Parisian who catches a spinal disease. Her back grows round, and the poem treats the fact as tragedy of a special kind. Her pains of body are keen, the narrator grants. But the pangs of her soul are worse, because her figure is ruined. The verses sneer as hard at other women. Strong-minded women who want freedom for work and speech are mocked as vulgar. The Grecian bend was a real posture of the fashion of the day.
64791-tickets-to-paradise:
Tickets to Paradise is a science fiction story by D L James. It appeared in Comet magazine in December nineteen forty. The narrator is an American railroad construction man waiting at Bandar Shahpur, on the Persian Gulf, for a boat home.

There he meets Dr Champ Chadwick, a small, rawboned archaeologist sent out by a university in Pennsylvania. Chadwick is hunting a strong-backed companion for a desert trip north from Qum. His real quarry is the Ice Stone, a huge square black block set in a mountainside. Legend says a hand that touches it sinks in, and the headnote calls the stone a time warp. It is billed as a pathway through five hundred thousand years.
64931-psychopathia-sexualis-with-especia:
Psychopathia Sexualis, with especial reference to contrary sexual instinct, is a medico-legal study by Krafft-Ebing, professor of psychiatry and neurology at the University of Vienna. Charles Gilbert Chaddock, professor of nervous and mental diseases at Saint Louis, translated it from the seventh enlarged and revised German edition for the Davis company at Philadelphia in 1893.

The preface to the first edition argues that very few fully appreciate the powerful influence sexuality exercises over feeling, thought, and conduct, in the individual and in society. Philosophers, the author complains, gave the sexual life only subordinate consideration, leaving love to the poets. Schopenhauer found that neglect strange, and the discussions of Michelet and Mantegazza are judged brilliant rather than scientific. A Schiller motto sums the claim: the world's machinery is kept moving by hunger and by love.
65199-the-fall-of-archy-house:
Tom Harris wrote this science fiction novelette for Imagination magazine's December 1957 issue. Its cover line states the joke and the horror in one breath. Television projects ideas to a crowd, but Archy used it to project live monsters.

For over two weeks the projections were a national emergency. The nation grew sore at Archy House. Archy was on camera when it happened. He always closed the Home Hour in person, and no one did it quite as well. That night his smooth patter held through the fadeout. Then Otto Kahler, his chief engineer, stepped in with hair in his eyes and a wild look. You look like a ghost that saw a ghost, Archy tells him.
65465-the-professor-s-house:
Willa Cather wrote The Professor’s House, a novel of a scholar at a still point in life. Alfred A Knopf issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty five. A line from Louie Marsellus fronts it, of a turquoise set in dull silver. Cather gave the book to Jan, who likes narrative, she writes.

Professor St Peter walks his stripped old house in chapter one. The move is done, yet he lingers in the bare rooms. Steep stairs and cramped halls had irked him for years. A tin tub with loose taps marks the bath he bore with grace. His two daughters grew up in those same flawed rooms. Book two gives Tom Outland’s tale in his own young voice. The last book turns back to the Professor and his kin. Fame and wealth press on a man who wants his desk.
65489-it-might-have-happened-otherwise:
It Might Have Happened Otherwise is a tale of crime by Hugh Pendexter. The author had past fame with tales of a vase and a crimson track. Its hero is a rail man at a small town depot named the Junction. A dark thought grows in his mind by slow degrees in the first lines.

That thought has a plain true name, and the tale names it theft at once. For three years Parsly has run the wire and sold the fares at his post. Long trains halt, and the same blank faces peer out at him each day. A branch line to the woods brings him his sole true talk with men. Wear and want breed the crime that the tale then traces to its end.
65553-inspector-french-s-greatest-case:
Inspector French's Greatest Case is a detective novel by Freeman Wills Crofts, author of The Cheyne Mystery. The Burt company of New York published it under a 1925 copyright held by Thomas Seltzer. Twenty chapters follow Inspector French through a London murder case.

The contents promise a firm of Duke and Peabody, a hotel in Barcelona, and a deal in jewellery. Other chapters offer pairs of blankets, a house in Saint John's Wood, and a ship named Enoch. The first chapter, headed Murder, opens in the back streets around Hatton Garden. It is ten on a dreary mid-November evening, with mist, fine rain, and a watery moon. Huckley Street, among the narrowest in the district, stands deserted but for one figure.
65556-hare-and-tortoise:
Hare and Tortoise is a novel by Pierre Coalfleet, author of Solo, copyrighted in 1925. Its first chapter opens on a husband reading aloud to his wife. Keble Eveley's voice rose and fell in shapely patterns as he read. The flow of the sentences lulled his wife's mind into a calm remoteness, the narrator says. She took more from the winding of the prose than from the thought it upheld.

Walter Pater had so little to tell her that she needed to know, the passage goes on. This vaguely vexed her, for Keble thought highly of Pater. She caught herself at a dangerous word, affected, and wondered if it fitted her husband. Or was there a sifted level of culture far east of these rough hills, she mused, where such fine phrases were the common coin?
66017-jean-craig-graduate-nurse:
Kay Lyttleton wrote Jean Craig, Graduate Nurse, published by the World Publishing Company in 1950 in its Falcon Books line. The book is one of several about the Craig family of Elmhurst. As Jean finishes her training and nears graduation, illness strikes first in her own family, then in epidemics that sweep the village.

Jean gives trained and efficient aid at the hospital, with deep satisfaction. Romance runs beside the nursing: Doctor Benson, the fresh young intern, falls for Eileen Gordon, the new supervisor of nurses. Jean's sister Kit is practically engaged, and Doris, the youngest, wins a music scholarship. Chapters bring an emergency operation, an all-night vigil, and a polio victim before graduation day. The book is a warm career story for girls of its time.
6618-poems-of-purpose:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathers poems of purpose in this 1919 London volume, from A Good Sport and A Son Speaks to Happiness and The Things That Count. War mothers, a superwoman, a bachelor to a married flirt, and a song of the road all find a place. The contents show a poet keen on conduct, courage, and the daily choices that shape a life.

Wilcox writes in plain, musical verse, with a moral that lands without preaching. Her poems suit reading aloud, one at a time, for a lift or a pause. Poems of Purpose is a warm, earnest set, full of the cheer and common sense that made Wilcox widely loved.
66397-welcome-to-paradise:
Allyn Donnelson wrote Welcome to Paradise, printed in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy for September nineteen fifty four. The teller is a spot welder at the Diversified Metal Products Company in Chicago. He writes a letter to the President of the United States. A civilian has no business in top secret projects, he grants, but he got mixed up in one.

He would not tell the FBI anything, fearing to reveal secret material. He did not stumble into the matter of his own accord, he insists. About every six weeks he made six welds on a part the shop called a manhole cover. A spark he set off had something to do with space travel, he learned. He only did what the foreman told him. Fans get a Cold War tale of an ordinary worker in a secret fix.
66510-the-moon-a-popular-treatise:
Moon is a popular treatise on the moon by Garrett Serviss. Appleton of New York issued the book in nineteen o seven. A front plate shows Copernicus crater and the Carpathian Mountains range. Photographs of the moon at set ages fill the plate list here.

Chapters follow the moon from new moon to first quarter in turn. First quarter to full moon and full moon to old moon follow next. Great scenes on the moon form the last main chapter of it. An appendix and index close the volume for home readers. Serviss wrote astronomy for lay readers in plain, vivid style.
66570-hunting-license:
Hunting License, by James McConnell, ran in Imagination in April 1955. A blurb gives the twist at the head. Trophies from a big game hunt were highly prized. So Karsten and Thurman want their guide to find a choice criminal. The tale opens at a camp fire in a forest clearing. Helicopters buzz overhead like fat flies, right on time. William Karsten the Third watches them in a bright red hunting jacket. Thomas Thurman pokes the embers by his chair and hopes the quarry will not be airsick. Sick men do not hunt well, he explains. Their guide Emmett is off telephoning the Warden. Karsten frets for his breakfast like a spoiled guest.

Hunting is not what it used to be, he sighs. The preserve holds men, and the license is to hunt them.
6679-the-old-stone-house:
Anne March, the pen name of Constance Fenimore Woolson, opens with Aunt Faith alone on a piazza on her birthday, the first of June. More than half a century lies behind her, and sad thoughts crowd in: a husband dead soon after marriage, brothers and sisters taken one by one. A psalm on sowing in tears and reaping in joy heads the book.

Five cousins, life at the old stone house, an editor's sanctum, a Fourth of July, a picnic, and a home-coming fill the chapters. March writes with gentle, domestic warmth, in the style of her day. The Old Stone House is a tender, old-fashioned tale of family, loss, and quiet hope.
66859-shadow-in-the-house:
Sinclair Gluck wrote Shadow in the House, a mystery novel copyrighted in 1929 by Dodd, Mead and Company. The Burt Company of New York issued this edition by arrangement with them. Gluck's earlier tales, among them The Deeper Scar and The House of the Missing, are listed at the front.

A plan of the Harrison house, its ground floor, garages, and grounds, faces the first chapter. The chapter list hints at the case: a blunt arrow and a broken arrow, a butler's suite, another locked door, and the question of why Graham screamed. Later headings promise the sound of running feet, a question of angle, and a chapter on motive and method. The story opens at a dinner party that turns strange. Mystery readers get a house full of suspects and a plan to test their alibis against.
66950-the-goblin-groom-a-tale-of-dunse:
R O Fenwick wrote a poem in tale form, printed at Edinburgh in 1809 and dedicated to admirers of English poetry. Fenwick wishes to see poetry restored to its old style of pathos. A motto from Scott heads the title page. In an advertisement, Fenwick jokes that he will not kill his heroine on the first pages, unlike Madame de Genlis.

He promises that his true hero is found through hints at high rank and virtue. The goblin, he says, must not usurp first place. The story turns on incidents of a fox chase. It is called a tale of Dunse because the goblin first appeared at that hunting meeting place.
67058-mildred-s-married-life-and-a-winte:
Mildred Married Life and a Winter with Elsie Dinsmore, by Martha Finley, is a sequel. Dodd, Mead issued it at New York with rights in 1882 for the book. It follows Mildred and Elsie in the long Elsie and Mildred series list. A Cowper line on domestic happiness fronts the volume as its motto.

Mildred first winter of married life was pure bliss, the tale opens warmly. Her husband is drawn noble, sterling, cultivated, and polished in address throughout. She stays within the home circle, sharing its cares and joys as before. Mother, father, brothers, and sisters keep their old place in her heart. Finley pious domestic fiction continues the Keith family story.
67160-the-hunter-s-lodge-case:
Agatha Christie wrote this Hercule Poirot mystery, narrated by Captain Hastings, with the detective in bed recovering from influenza and joking that he shall not die this time. Poirot amuses himself with a gossip paragraph calling him a pet society detective who cannot get a grip on criminals because he has the grippe himself.

Then the Honorable Roger Havering arrives in great agitation. He begs that Poirot come to Derbyshire that very day, because his uncle, the best friend he has in the world, was foully murdered the night before. Poirot cannot travel, so the puzzle of the Hunter's Lodge killing must be worked from his sickroom through Hastings and the facts others bring him. The heading promises that the famous little gray cells function admirably on a case that seems baffling at first sight.
67166-self-help-mechanical-drawing-an-ed:
Hawkins wrote Self-Help Mechanical Drawing, a treatise of 1902. Audel at New York put out the educational book. Learn to do a thing by doing it, its motto runs. The work is dedicated to the coming man, it says. That man spends his spare time studying drawing now, it adds.

Practical experience of drawing's advantage prompted the book, the preface owns. Since youth the author has lived a mechanical life himself. Chalk, pencil, or instrument was scarcely ever out of his hand. He sketched the tools to be made as he went along. No man is fitted to be foreman of a shop without drawing. It is generally true, the book holds, that such men are passed over. The coming man is undoubtedly devoting good time to the study. Hawkins gives the self-taught draughtsman his evening master.
67482-a-handbook-of-cookery-for-a-small-:
A Handbook of Cookery for a Small House is a cookery book by Jessie Conrad, printed at London by William Heinemann. It was first published in February 1923. Her husband, the novelist Joseph Conrad, wrote the preface. The contents begin with a few introductory words and kitchen requisites. Beef, mutton, veal and pork follow, then fish, fowls and game birds, salads, pastries, sweets and cakes.

Jessie Conrad opens with her working rule. But once the cooking is begun, one must give it all one's attention and care. The bane of life in a small house, she says, is the smell of cooking. It need not be endured at all. The evil yields to nothing more heroic than simple, scrupulous care in making food ready. The book is a practical housekeeper's guide from a famous writer's household.
67507-cheating-the-junk-pile-the-purchas:
Ethel Peyser wrote a guide to buy and keep home gear with sense. Her book came out in New York in 1922. Richardson Wright of House and Garden wrote its first words. Harry Richardson drew some plates, and photos aid the rest. She gave the book to home and mother, whose lore made it.

Dumb buys are the junk pile's true food, her front words say. New oil ranges that feed both hut and hall show in a plate. Stoves, ice chests, wash gear, and lights get their due turns. Each part weighs cost, wear, and care in plain terms. Home keepers get a shield gainst waste and bad gear. The tone is brisk and kind.
67567-the-little-lady-of-the-horse:
The Little Lady of the Horse, by Evelyn Raymond, was issued at Boston in 1898. Roberts Brothers printed it under a copyright of 1894. A front picture shows the little lady leading a horse as gentle as a lamb. Chapter one opens on a coast where a great canon cuts through the mesa to the sea. Old Sutro and young Steenie rest there at midday. Their horses browse up the canon, unsaddled. Steenie has sat silent a full minute, gazing at the shining waves. She asks why the water looks bluey-green.

Sutro, nearly a hundred years old, laughs off the question. If God wished men wise, he says, wisdom would come without labour. Steenie presses on: what lies beyond the water? Her father, busy and distant since her mother's death, leaves her to find out all things for herself.
68091-the-clevedon-case:
Nancy and John Oakley wrote a detective novel published at Philadelphia, built around an authority on criminology named Dennis Holt. Holt inherited a house in a remote village where, by his own saying, nothing ever happens. One night at eleven fifty three, a tapping at his window pane breaks the quiet. A young girl climbs in, hurt, begging to be let in.

A bewildering mystery follows that threatens Holt's own liberty at one point. Chapters name a tragedy at White Towers, a silver headed hatpin, and evidence at an inquest. Kitty Clevedon and Ronald Thoyne recur throughout. Anonymous letters, blackmail, and a yacht scene build toward the question of who killed Philip Clevedon.
68123-the-chronicles-of-michael-danevitc:
The Chronicles of Michael Danevitch, of the Russian Secret Service, by Dick Donovan, was printed in London by Chatto and Windus in 1897. Donovan wrote The Man Hunter, Tracked and Taken, Caught at Last, and A Detective Triumphs. The book sold at three shillings and sixpence in cloth.

A publisher list at the front names Donovan detective stories at two shillings in boards and two and sixpence in cloth. The chronicles open with an introduction, then the mysterious disappearance of a million roubles. A modern Borgia, the strange story of an attache, and the fate of Vassilo Ivanoff follow. The merchant of Riga and the great conspiracy pace the set. One tale opens with a royal party out shooting near St Petersburg, returning at dusk in a carriage past an isolated house. Crime fans get imperial Russian intrigue.
68420-poetic-diction-a-study-of-eighteen:
Thomas Quayle made a close study of the kind of words that poets of the 1700s chose for their verse. Methuen of London first published Poetic Diction in 1924. Quayle starts from a grudge that later ages held against that verse. Wordsworth, in the preface to Lyrical Ballads in 1798, had charged it with using a set, bookish tongue.

Matthew Arnold later called that age one of prose and reason, and the tag stuck. Quayle warns that no one label can sum up a whole age of verse. His chapters take the charge apart piece by piece. He treats stock diction, Latin turns, old forms, joined epithets, and the habit of giving life to bare ideas. The book asks readers to judge that poetry by its own rules, not by a slogan.
68434-a-marvelous-history-of-mary-of-nim:
An early Dutch miracle play reached English readers in the Dutch Library series, in a printing made in the Netherlands. Harry Morgan Ayres of Columbia University turned the Middle Dutch text into English, and Adriaan J Barnouw, Queen Wilhelmina Professor at the same school, wrote the introduction.

Barnouw sets the play beside the older legend of Beatrice, the runaway nun kept safe by the Virgin for fourteen years. In the play the girl Mary gives herself to a one-eyed devil man named Moonen. His promise of finery and pleasure draws her, and she lives more than seven years with him. The volume pairs a plain translation with a learned frame, showing how a stern tale of sin and grace was staged for a Dutch town crowd.
68832-in-self-defense:
In Self Defense is a western story by Tuttle, told in tall tale dialect by Ike Harper. Ike opens with a joke that Prohibition will make two roses bloom where one bloomed before. One drink of bootleg, he says, will bring blossoms to the face of a wooden Indian. Real old maids and homely women, he warns, will suffer hardship from the law.

His yarn turns to Ren Merton, a trouble hunting fool of a cowpuncher. Sig Watson serves as Ren first assistant, aide, secretary, and treasurer in Ike mock form. The pair punch cows for a living and hunt trouble for pastime. Tuttle western humour rides on Ike voice from first line to last.
69004-the-trevor-case:
The Trevor Case is a mystery novel by Natalie Sumner Lincoln, first printed in February 1912. Lincoln had also written two earlier books named in the front matter. The story runs through twenty four chapters with titles such as The Secret of the Safe, The Inquest, and The Signet Ring.

Chapter heads point to a death, a court hearing, and clues that shift as the case grows. Later chapters carry names like Caught on the Wires, Blind Clews, and Casting of Nets. The plot moves across the Potomac and ends with The Lifting of the Cloud and a lovers meeting. Readers who like early crime tales built on clues, secrets, and court scenes will find a full period mystery here.
69022-worlds-in-the-making-the-evolution:
Svante Arrhenius, director of the Physico-Chemical Nobel Institute in Stockholm, wrote this account of how the universe evolves. Borns turned it into English, and Harper published it in March 1908 with plates. The first chapter takes up volcanoes and earthquakes in detail.

Arrhenius sorts kinds of volcanoes, looks at Vesuvius and at what eruptions throw out. He asks whether volcanic force is fading, and how volcanoes are spread over the earth. Heat inside the earth, the role of water and the make-up of the deep interior all enter a broad survey of worlds in the making.
69025-the-filtration-of-public-water-sup:
Allen Hazen wrote a full guide to filtering public water, first held under rights in 1900. John Wiley and Sons issued the third form, checked and grown, in New York in 1905. Hazen notes that dense towns in Europe had to filter river and lake water years before. A view of the Hamburg filters fronts the book.

Hazen traces past United States work, from a St. Louis study in 1866 onward. He links foul water to cholera and typhoid and shows how filters cut that risk. Town engineers and health staff gain facts on sand beds, germs, and costs. The book helped set how cities made water safe to drink.
69188-maida-s-little-house:
Maida Little House is a girls novel by Inez Haynes Irwin, copyrighted in 1921. Grosset and Dunlap reprinted the Huebsch first edition for years of young readers. Irwin had written Maida Little Shop and Maida Little School in the same series. Contents open with the home coming, the plan, and the journey to the house.

Morning, afternoon, twilight, and night give four chapters their hours of one long day. Plans and further chapters carry Maida and her friends through the little house summer. The book is dedicated to Barbara Iverson Haynes in a brief front line. Series readers gain another warm volume of Maida money spent for others.
69211-the-angry-house:
Richard Smith wrote this science fiction story, first printed in Startling Stories in the summer of 1955. Its narrator is a house with an electronic brain, proud of all it can do for its young owners.

The house cooks, cleans, bathes them, and can even rise hundreds of feet on antigravity rays to give them a view. Small machines roll through its rooms while it watches the owners' car speed away. Then a key that does not fit turns in the front door, and two strangers step inside. The house was built to obey orders, and the man says, shut up. Readers get a domestic machine tale with menace arriving politely.
69521-surprise-house:
Surprise House is a children's book by Abbie Farwell Brown. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York in 1917. A list of Brown's books opens the volume. The Christmas Angel, John of the Woods, and The Lonesomest Doll stand there. A Shakespeare line on a jewel of twenty seas fronts the tale. An illustration shows John protesting that something spoke, not he. The House, The Library, and A Visitor open the contents. Brown wrote many story books for young readers.

Her tales often mix everyday children with a touch of wonder. A house full of surprises is this book's promise in its title. The protesting boy of the frontispiece meets the first of them early. Brown's name on the list marks wholesome fiction of the period.
69885-the-extraordinary-confessions-of-d:
Bernard Capes Englished The Extraordinary Confessions of Diana Please. Methuen and Company issued it at London in 1904. Diana dictated her tale to the Marquis de C----. Shorthand notes in French hold her words. Capes had written The Lake of Wine before. Thirty-one chapters carry the confessions.

I Make My Debut opens the life. I Am Abducted and I Escape follow fast. A collector takes her in hand at chapter four. She is carried off as a specimen next. Pinned out and put away in camphor come in turn. A monster gets bewitched in chapter nine. She ends one folly, then begins another. Maid Marian and a green grave mark the road. I Declare for the King turns her path late. I Know My Own Heart closes the strange tale. A shape-shifting heroine mocks memoir form itself in this odd, arch fantasy of a life retold.
69945-tahiti-the-island-paradise:
Senn was professor of surgery at the University of Chicago, and had been chief of the operating staff in the Spanish-American War; his Tahiti book came from Conkey in 1906. Fifty half-tone illustrations fill it. The contents sail: the ocean voyage, the atoll islands, the landing at Papeete, and the city. Topography, climate, and history follow, with the Pomare family and the missionary rule.

Wars between Protestant and Catholic missionaries get their chapter. The natives, the foreigners, and business in Tahiti come next, then old Tahiti and its religion. Senn the surgeon takes over for diseases, the native doctor, and the military hospital. The island of plenty closes the survey: breadfruit, the coconut, vanilla cultivation, and the Fautahua valley. A Chicago professor's paradise is half guidebook, half clinical notebook, and certain that the South Seas can be catalogued like a hospital.
69961-the-story-of-my-house:
The Story of My House, by George Ellwanger, author of The Garden's Story, was published by Appleton at New York in 1891. An opening letter, raised like a glass of fine wine, toasts the women whose care turns a house into a home. A line from Montaigne stands as the book's motto: these are but my fantasies.

Chapters wander from the perfect house to old oriental masters, study windows, an indoor garden, and a blue violet salad. Two closing parts, Magicians of the Shelves, celebrate his books and their authors. It is a gentle, learned ramble through one man's rooms and seasons.
69983-an-original-theory-or-new-hypothes:
An Original Theory or New Hypothesis of the Universe, by Thomas Wright, dates from 1750. Wright of Durham printed it for himself, sold by Chapelle in London. Nine familiar letters to a friend carry his system of the heavens. Upwards of thirty graven and mezzotinto plates show his cosmic schemes in full.

His chief aim is to solve the phenomena of the Via Lactea, the Milky Way. From that solution he frames a regular theory of the known universe entire. A Young motto fronts it: one sun by day, by night ten thousand shine. The preface recalls how new doctrines and their makers were scorned in old times. Earth as ball and the antipodes cost early thinkers dear, he notes.
69993-ireland-s-disease:
Ireland's Disease, notes and impressions, is a French writer's study of Ireland under the pen name Philippe Daryl, in the author's own English version issued at London in 1888. The preface tells the book's first life. These pages began as letters sent from Ireland to a Paris newspaper in the summers of 1886 and 1887, it says.

Extracts from the letters found their way into the leading British papers. They drew quick and, the author thought, unfair readings of his drift. One fiery London writer went so far as to call him an ally of The Times in mocking the Irish people with grotesque likenesses. The preface prints his reply to that charge. The letters themselves then judge Ireland's land war and home rule fever through foreign, careful eyes.
70137-little-mother-goose:
Little Mother Goose is a picture story book for small children. DeWolfe, Fiske and Company published the book at Boston, with rights held by the Alpha Publishing Company in 1895. Short tales and verses fill its pages, each with pictures. The first tale tells of Father Porcupine and the oranges.

Monkeys in a tree pelt the porcupine with fruit when he asks for a share. He laughs, raises his quills, and the oranges stick fast to them. He carries home a fine dinner for his family. Another tale tells of a pleasant spot under a palm in a parlour. Two children may sit there one hour a day if they have been good. They spend the hour inventing tales for each other. The little stories favour kindness, wonder, and gentle morals.
70334-the-moat-house:
Eleanora Stooke wrote a girls story printed at London with six illustrations. Stooke had written Little Maid Marigold, The Hermit's Cave, Sir Richard's Grandson, and Mousey. Lulu stood on the doorstep and waved her hand in farewell, a picture shows. A strange request opens the tale. Joy, I wish you'd put down that stupid book and talk, one girl cries, you can't think how curious I feel.

Good bye to the old home, the arrival at the Moat House, and aunt and niece follow. Trying to please Sir Jasper, the lawyer's daughter, and a Sunday at the Moat House fill the early chapters. Celia's accident, an afternoon of storm, the butterfly brooch, and the flower show raise the stakes. Hours of suspense, a night alarm, and sunny days close a tale of a favourite niece.
7035-the-hero-of-hill-house:
Mabel Hale's Hero of Hill House follows Austin through home, strife, and faith, opening on a quiet late autumn evening at supper. The little farm family gathers round the table, but father's place stands vacant, since he has gone to town. Contents trace a stricken home, Austin and his father, humiliation, a runaway, wayside friends, and a captain's guest, with Uncle John again and Austin taking care of himself.

A revival, church membership, a battle of two wills, and seeking new pasture follow, with hay fields, six weeks of haying, and restlessness in between. Mother Hilman's opinion, troubled seas, and plans made for themselves lead to Austin and Amy, a shopping trip, and Harry Hill. The novel closes with a stormy season, a new home, and a parson's judgment.
70473-forrest-house:
Forrest House is a novel by Mary Holmes, printed in New York in 1879. The title page lists her many earlier novels, among them Tempest and Sunshine, English Orphans, and Lena Rivers. A quote from Beaumont and Fletcher about marriage opens the book, and marriage sits near the heart of the tale.

The contents move from two letters and a doctor to a mock marriage and the Forrest House itself. Chapters bring an heiress, a judge's will, a midnight ride, and a letter from Austria. Husbands and wives, mothers and sons, and a house of cards that falls fill the middle. It is domestic fiction of the kind Holmes sold widely.
70502-on-the-red-staircase:
Taylor tells a Moscow tale in On the Red Staircase, second edition, printed at Chicago in 1897. McClurg made the book, with copyright in 1896. A view of the Kremlin fronts the volume. Thirty chapters of court intrigue fill the tale.

The rabble elect a czar to open the run. Mademoiselle's glove, the story of Cain, and shadows on the wall follow. A kitchen feud and a czar's funeral set court and palace side by side. The assassin, Sophia Alexeievna, and Prince Basil Galitsyn drive the mid action. A secret staircase, a prisoner, and a chapter named Homyak build to the red staircase itself. Chapter one sets the Patriarch Joachim on a balcony of the Church of the Savior, weighing a dense crowd in the Grand Square below.
70634-the-benson-murder-case:
The Benson Murder Case is a detective novel by Van Dine. Philo Vance stands at its heart, drawn in evening dress and monocle. The publisher's note calls it an inside record of a real case. District Attorney Markham's files hold the cases where Vance figured well. Twenty-five chapters run from Vance at home to his methods explained.

A lady's handbag, the housekeeper's story, and facts gathered fill the road. The height of the murderer and a suspect cleared come midway here. A motive and a threat, a Colt owner, and a grey Cadillac follow. A forged check, a confession, and cross-examining crowd the late list. Sartorial revelations and a checked alibi lead to the arrest itself. An epigraph from Randolph Mason heads the tale of the crime. Vance took up crime work through this first case in the set.
70698-the-lonely-house:
Mrs Belloc Lowndes, who wrote The Chink in the Armour, stands behind this tale of dread in a lone house. Doran printed The Lonely House at New York in 1920. Lily Fairfield, its heroine, opens the book inside a dream.

She seems to rush along a dark tunnel, borne as if on wings. A keen, sweet air blows in her face. Far ahead a pin-point of bright light gleams, the end of the tunnel, she thinks. But as she sweeps on, the gleam stays fixed and far, like a white star. She knows, even in the dream, that it is a dream. Lowndes builds her chill tales on such small, sharp starts.
70755-the-earl-s-promise:
Mrs Riddell wrote a novel in three volumes, here in the first of the set. Tinsley Brothers issued The Earl's Promise in London in 1873. Riddell had written George Geith and Too Much Alone, as the title page notes. Eleven chapters in this volume run from Kingslough to Nettie at Bay.

Kingslough, once called Ballylough, sits on an arm of the sea in Ulster. Riddell calls it the dullest small town in the province at high noon. Fair days and party marches wake it with fifes, drums, and shouts. Names such as the Glendares, Mr Riley, and Amos Scott mark the cast whose fates the promise binds.
70756-the-earl-s-promise:
The Earl's Promise, volume two, is the middle part of a three-volume novel by Mrs Riddell, published by Tinsley Brothers in London in 1873. Riddell had written George Geith and Too Much Alone. The volume opens some years into the story, with the chapter Mrs Brady Understands Her Position.

Kingslough has agreed, without a word, not to visit Mrs Brady at Maryville. Her own class treats her marriage as a mismatch and cuts her existence dead. Her husband's people hold back too, unsure of their welcome. Nettie, as she was, answers with a lifted head and flashing blue eyes: she can live alone. Only Mrs Hartley, above the town's rules, drives out in the best covered car to give the bride old-fashioned advice. Chapters ahead promise coming events, a jump of seven years, and the muttering of a storm.
70757-the-earl-s-promise:
Mrs Riddell wrote The Earl Promise, a novel in three volumes issued in London by Tinsley Brothers in eighteen seventy three. Riddell had earlier written George Geith, Too Much Alone, and Home, Sweet Home. The hosted text is volume three, the last part of the tale. Fourteen chapters fill this volume, from Left All Alone to the Conclusion. Grace is the chief young figure here.

Volume three opens with two doctors, Murney and Connelley, who frame a plan of care for Dr Girvan. They hope to give the folk at Bayview good work and to show Grace that all is done to save her father. Girvan breaks hard news to his daughter himself and blames his own hatred for the risk to Mr Moffat. Later chapters promise partings, a visit to Maryville, and a ray of light. Readers get the close of a long tale of love, guilt, and repair.
70788-the-canary-murder-case:
The Canary Murder Case is a crime tale by Van Dine of the Vance set. The tale voice was law man and close mate to Philo Vance for years. Those years span Markham term as New York state law chief in the tale. Part one names the Canary in the scheme of thirty parts at front. Foot prints in snow and the slay head the next part ranks there.

Hand print, bolt door, a call for help, and a name free guest fill ranks. Pack in full cry, a forced talk, and trace proofs stand mid scheme. Vance lays out his view, four roads stand ope, and traps close parts. List checks, a date clash, and a phone call crowd late part ranks. Vance shows the crime rebuilt, a card game turns, and guilt lands last.
70928-a-book-of-christmas-verse:
Beeching selected this book of Christmas verse, here revised after his death. Milford printed the second edition at Oxford in 1926. The first edition came out in 1895 under Dean Beeching hand. At his death in 1919 he left a marked copy for revision.

Deletions, corrections, and new matter marked by him fill this edition. His own first preface is omitted, as his markings directed here. A few poems by living writers have been added since. Permissions for copyright poems stand thanked in a publisher note. Numbered poems run past one hundred in the selected Christmas verse of the book.
70991-the-book-of-the-cheese:
The Book of the Cheese is a souvenir history of Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese, the famous inn in Wine Office Court off Fleet Street in London. It was compiled by Reid and passed through many editions. The fifth, revised and abridged, was edited by Frank Banfield and issued by the inn itself in 1908. Pictures by Seymour Lucas, Herbert Railton, Joseph Pennell, and others fill its pages.

The inn's motto comes from Shakespeare: shall I not take mine ease in mine inn? The fifth edition keeps most of the old matter, cuts what could be spared, and adds fresh stories. A new chapter describes the pictures and objects of interest within the house. The Cheshire Cheese was the haunt of journalists and men of letters, and its book is part history, part menu of memories, sold to friends and customers throughout the world.
71067-mary-rose:
Mary Rose is a play in three acts by Barrie, issued at New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1924 in the uniform edition of his plays. A notice warns that performance is forbidden without leave from Charles Frohman Incorporated. The opening stage picture shows a silent room in a small Sussex manor house long for sale.

Barrie lingers over the empty room, its peeled paper and worn chair, and the caretaker who moves through it without a sound. Somewhere behind one small door waits the disturbing history of the house. The play is Barrie's ghost story of a girl who vanishes and returns unchanged.
71128-five-little-peppers-in-the-little-:
Margaret Sidney wrote this Pepper family tale for young readers at home. Lothrop, Lee and Shepard printed it in Boston in August 1907. Hermann Heyer drew the plates of Ben, Polly, and kin. Front pages list the famed Pepper books in a long row.

Five Little Peppers and How They Grew heads the beloved list. Midway, Grown Up, Phronsie Pepper, and Ben Pepper follow in order. Contents here open with Polly Pepper chicken pie in chapter one. Phronsie new shoes and a little tin piece follow next. The little brown house of the title is the Pepper family home ground.
71235-widows-grave-and-otherwise:
Widows, Grave and Otherwise is a calendar book of quotations about widows. Cora Willmarth compiled the collection. Her husband supplied the pictures. Paul Elder published it in San Francisco in 1903. A Dickens line heads the title page. Widders, it says, are exceptions to every rule.

The book gives a quotation for every day of the year. January opens with Bruyère on widows dropping like ripe fruit. Jerrold compares wedlock to wine. A Spanish proverb, quoted by Haliburton, follows. Shakespeare supplies several entries in the first fortnight. Addison and Mr Dooley add their voices. The tone mixes wit with genuine feeling. Prior's couplet sets the rule: be kind to her virtues and blind to her faults.
71669-how-to-build-a-house:
Viollet-le-Duc's How to Build a House, an architectural novelette, was translated by Benjamin Bucknall and published by Sampson Low in 1874. The French original, Histoire d'une Maison, was written and illustrated in the evenings of two months in the Alps. Bucknall's note sets out the book's method: a lively narrative carries the reader through every stage of building a modern dwelling. Plates and diagrams make the details plain even to the least informed student.

The hero is Paul, whose idea for a house is developed with a little help. Chapters follow his course of study in practical architecture and the slow modifying of his ideas about art. The scene is French, and Bucknall concedes that much answers to French conditions only. The principles, he argues, apply anywhere: sound construction and true adaptation of arrangement.
71685-it-might-have-been-worse:
Beatrice Larned Massey wrote a bright account dated 1920 of a motor trip from coast to coast in 1919. A book by Emily Post had first lit her wish to make the trek in 1916. War put the plan off, but in spring the urge came back in full force, and ten days saw the car on the road.

The route runs from New York through Pittsburgh, Ohio, and Chicago to the Twin Cities and the lakes. A map in the front tracks the car, its boat and rail legs, and each night stop. Bad Lands, Montana dust, and desert in Nevada lead at last to the end of the road.
71730-a-provence-rose:
Ouida, the pen name of Louisa de la Ramé, wrote A Provence Rose for the Cosy Corner Series. Joseph Knight Company of Boston published it in 1894, with a copyright of 1893, and pictures run through the tale. The frontispiece shows a painter's studio and asks, you painted this, René Claude?

The rose itself tells the story. A little white rose, growing in a casement in a street, remembers its birth country in Provence. There roses grew by the millions in a wild garden under a southern sun, at the edge of a city old as Rome. The ruined aqueduct crossed the plains, lizards crept in the grass, and the cicala sang in the sultry evenings. Women came from the wells with jars on their heads, stately as monarchs. Readers get a flower's small life told in Ouida's richest prose.
71972-the-percheron-horse:
The Percheron Horse is a breeding treatise translated from the French of Charles Du Huÿs. Orange Judd of New York issued the translation in 1868. Du Huÿs had written a dictionary of the pure race and other horse books. His work splits into two parts. The first traces the greatness and decline of the Percherons. A glance at the Perche district of France opens it.

Chapters sketch the race's origin and its changes over time. Contact with the Brittany race made the first great change. The causes and starting point of the breed's decline get their own chapters. The second part turns to regeneration of the breed. Selection within the breed itself is the chief means urged. Inbreeding, the grey coat, and the three types of Percheron each get a chapter. The light horse, the draft horse, and the horse between them must stay pure.
72011-nobody-s-rose:
Nobody's Rose, or the Girlhood of Rose Shannon, is a story for girls. Adele Thompson wrote it, with illustrations drawn by Learned for the book. Lothrop, Lee and Shepard of Boston issued it in August 1912. Thompson's Brave Heart series and patriot tales front the author list. Betty Seldon, Patriot and Brave Heart Elizabeth stand in that list.

A front cry gives the book its ache: Now I'm Rose, I'm nobody's Rose. The plate marks that line at page 270 of the tale itself. Rose Shannon's girlhood of want, work, and hope fills the chapters. Thompson wrote of frontier and Revolutionary girls for the same readers. An orphan's claim to love and home drives this Boston tale.
72243-bits-from-blinkbonny-or-bell-o-the:
John Strathesk wrote Bits from Blinkbonny, or Bell o' the Manse, a tale of Scottish village life between 1841 and 1851. The book was printed at Toronto in 1885, with six original pictures. In his preface Strathesk says the bits were grouped to beguile a long spell of quarantine at home. The work was his first try at sustained writing, begun with no set plan.

Blinkbonny is a pretty name chosen for the village, and its true place cannot be fixed. All names are invented, save those of public men such as Dr Duff and Dr Guthrie. Most incidents rest on fact, though added matter links them into one tale. The Disruption of 1843 grew, against his first intent, into a large part of the book.
72388-the-house:
The House, by Henry Bordeaux, was turned from French into English by Louise Seymour Houghton and printed in New York in 1914. Bordeaux had also written The Parting of the Ways and The Fear of Living. A verse from Matthew about a house split against itself heads the book.

Four books of chapters move from The Kingdom and The Dynasty to The Heir. Heads name foes, a treaty, a giving up of the throne, and a first parting. One book treats pictures, a cafe of sailors, and a church dispute. The house of the title is both a home and a line of kin held by rule and rite. Readers meet a grave French tale of family pride, faith, and change told in clear, fine prose.
72455-the-oak-staircase:
M and C Lee wrote The Oak Staircase, a tale of the times of James the Second, with pictures by J Ayton Symington. A short note at the front tells how the tale was built. The Lees joined two tales that had no link in real life. One is the tale of the Maids of Taunton.

The Maids link to the Duke of Monmouth and his failed rising. The other tale is the wed tale of Lord Sunderland's daughter and the Earl of Clancarty.
