In the book the pair become young Lord Desmond and Frances Dalrymple. Seven chapters tell the tale through tales told by hosts of folk. The schoolroom at Horsemandown opens the first chapter.
72489-nightmare-on-the-nose:
Nightmare on the Nose is a comic fantasy story by Evelyn Smith, printed in the magazine Fantastic Universe in the autumn of 1953. Its headnote introduces Incubus, who won every race but one. In that she matched Man o' War, yet she was not actually a horse at all.

Phil Watson loses money at the track, and every loss brings a nightmare. The night after he dropped two hundred dollars at Jamaica, the nightmare sits on his chest with red eyes glowing. She asks him not to turn over so much, since it makes her uncomfortable. When he protests, she kicks him with a sharp hoof and proposes a couple of games of Canasta. The editor's note jokes that talking horses go back at least to the siege of Troy, where the Greek warriors inside the wooden horse must have talked among themselves. Smith's filly, he promises, has something special.
72573-the-mother-s-recompense:
The Mother's Recompense is a novel by Edith Wharton, published by Appleton in 1925. Copyright entries reach back into 1924, when it ran in a magazine. Wharton's name on the title page carries The Age of Innocence behind it. 

The novel opens on the French Riviera with its heroine waking late. Kate Clephane lies in a shabby room in a third-rate hotel there. Morning sun through the window is the one thing she loves about it. No more early sunrises for her, the narration observes at once. Sunrises belong to lost joys in her crowded past. She remembers coming home from balls danced to tatters in younger years. The book builds its portrait of a mother from that guarded, backward-looking start.
72707-sea-curse:
Sea Curse is a weird tale by Robert Howard, set in the sea-coast village of Faring. A Kipling verse stands at its head, about the heels of dripping ghosts on the roofbeam. The narrator is a man remembering his boyhood. They were the brawlers and braggarts of Faring town, the loud boasters and hard drinkers.

The two rovers were feared and admired together. They were not content to ply their trade along the coasts among the shark teeth shoals. When a man was beaten or a woman insulted, the villagers muttered and did nothing. Moll had never married, and lived alone with the girl in a hut close to the beach. Howard's tale builds from that shame toward the curse its title promises.
72719-the-greene-murder-case:
S S Van Dine wrote The Greene Murder Case, a Philo Vance detective novel set in New York. A front plate shows the Greene mansion at the time of the notorious case, from a woodcut by Lowell L Balcom. Twenty six chapters fill the book. A Hamlet line heads the tale, on murder most foul, strange and unnatural. A cast list names the household.

Philo Vance and District Attorney John F X Markham lead the inquiry. Mrs Tobias Greene is mistress of the mansion. Julia, Sibella, and Ada Greene are the daughters, and Chester and Rex the sons. Chapters run from A Double Tragedy and The Missing Revolver through The Second Tragedy. The Third and Fourth Tragedies, The Two Wills, and In the Locked Library deepen the peril. Mystery fans get Vance at his most classic.
73121-little-miss-mouse:
Little Miss Mouse is a girls' tale by Amy Blanchard, printed in 1906. Hurst and Company of New York put this copy out that August. Jacobs and Company held the rights to the tale from the start. Blanchard had writ Little Maid Marian and Little Miss Oddity before it. Twelve chapters run from buttonholes to a journey at the story's end.

Ruth asks her Aunt Hester why she makes buttonholes she hates so much. Grown folk can do just what they like, the child had thought. Hester laughs and owns she once thought the same as a small girl. Now she sews near all day, though she swore off the needle then. Henrietta's red coat, a pocket, and Billy with a doll fill the road. A surprise party, a strange visitor, and Uncle Sidney come midway. Homesick hearts and a signed note close out the small tale.
73132-a-spring-time-case:
Jun-ichiro Tanizaki wrote A Spring-Time Case, or Otsuya Koroshi. Zenchi Iwado turned the tale into English. The Japan Times issued it in its fiction line. The book joins masterpieces of modern Japanese fiction. Tanizaki had just turned forty, the note says. He burst into fame some eighteen years before.

His fame has held with rare staying power, Iwado writes. Japan's public mind runs fickle, he notes. New stage pets flash and vanish in a season. Tanizaki climbed to the peak and stayed there. His glory stands unchallenged, the note claims. A translator's warm brief fronts the tale itself. A murder tale from Japan's modern master reached English readers early here, framed as proof of a new literature's strength.
7319-good-sense:
Baron d'Holbach's Good Sense, without God, or Freethoughts Opposed to Supernatural Ideas, comes here in an undated English translation of Le Bon Sens, its translator not stated. Its epigraph, borrowed from Bacon, argues that atheism leaves men to sense, philosophy, laws, and reputation as guides to virtue. Superstition, by contrast, dismounts them all and sets up an absolute monarchy in men's minds.

D'Holbach builds that case in short, plain arguments against priests, miracles, and fear, favouring reason and nature over revealed command. The Freethinker's Library edition keeps the tone bold and accessible, meant for readers, not scholars alone. The book remains a classic statement of Enlightenment unbelief.
73249-the-mating-impulse:
The Mating Impulse, by Edwin Balmer, is a story about the fight for votes for women. Balmer frames it as a tale of the Cause that came close to grief. An American girl turns into a fierce fighter for the vote and near misses a hunger strike in an English jail.

The tale opens in autumn on a train from London packed with sportsmen bound for grouse shoots in Scotland. Calm fields, woods, and old homes roll past the train. Against that calm scene, the girl and her cause bring clash and risk. Balmer mixes love, protest, and peril in a short, sharp plot. Readers get a period view of how the suffrage fight looked to American eyes.
73350-the-modern-packing-house:
The Modern Packing House is a complete treatise on the design, construction, equipment, and operation of meat packing houses. Nickerson and Collins published it in Chicago, with copyrights of 1905 and 1921. Wilder, for many years a general superintendent at Swift, wrote the first edition. Davis revised, amplified, and enlarged this new one. The preface calls it the first complete treatise on the business ever published.

The book follows the animals through the works. Operations run from the unloading at the pens to the finished product and its sale, in the order the work is done. A second great subject is by-products: converting everything once wasted into commercial articles. Tables, formulas, and practical suggestions fill the text, all indexed for instant reference. The treatise served the packing industry of Chicago and the Midwest as a working manual.
73393-jack-carstairs-of-the-power-house:
Jack Carstairs of the Power House, by Sydney Sandys, is an engineering tale. Methuen issued it at London, first in October 1909, second edition November. Stanley Wood drew four plates for this tale of very young men. Its subtitle calls electric power a very young industry of that day.

The book is dedicated to the memory of George Stephenson, locomotive pioneer. Jack, a young engineer, watches June sunset at a Scots power house gate. Salmon leap in the river; a battery carries the small town summer load. A highlander eats his piece inside while no machinery runs at all. Youth, machinery, and Highland scenery launch the story of the plant.
73472-the-bishop-s-purse:
The Bishop's Purse is a novel by Cleveland Moffett and Oliver Herford, published by Appleton with copyright in 1912. It was written at Lakewood, New Jersey, and dedicated to friends there. The frontispiece shows a girl doing the one thing that could save her.

The tale opens on a boat train in England. An English bishop rides in a first-class carriage with a bright American girl. She gives her name as Jenny Regan, though her true name is Hester Storm. A golf bag matters early. A face in the glass and a flash of memory follow. The Reverend Horatio Merle turns detective in the later chapters. A missing page, a locked door, and a storm bring the plot to its close.
73670-the-re-se:
François Mauriac wrote Thérèse, here in English translated by Eric Sutton, issued in New York by Boni and Liveright in nineteen twenty eight. A Baudelai epigraph opens it: Lord have pity on those who know not what they do. I shall be told, Thérèse, that you do not exist, but I know you do, he writes.

When I was young, I remember seeing your little white thin lipped face, as you stood in a stifling Assize Court, he recalls. You were at the mercy of lawyers not half so pitiless as the fine ladies, he says. Later he found her in a country house drawing room, drawn and pale. She prowls like a wild animal behind the living bars of her family, he says. Novel readers get the famed French tale of a woman tried for poisoning her husband.
7378-chantry-house:
Charlotte M. Yonge builds this Victorian family chronicle around a house and the brothers who belong to it. The narrator, pressed by the younger generation, sets down the story of Chantry House and his two elder brothers, working from diaries and letters. Memory reaches back to childhood, to a mother reading aloud, and to the family past that still shapes the present.

The tale unfolds through wills, discoveries, midnight chases, and reckonings, with a ghost of Lady Margaret haunting the margins. Yonge, a moral storyteller of the old school, ties the family's fortunes to duty, repentance, and restitution. The result is a long, leisurely novel of kinship and conscience, in which the house itself holds the family's history.
74020-outside-the-universe:
Outside the Universe is a science fiction novel by Edmond Hamilton. It ran in Weird Tales across four months of 1929. The story opens aboard a ship of the Interstellar Patrol. An uncharted ether current spins the ship in mid-space. The narrator rushes to the pilot room.

His two lieutenants stand at the controls. Korus Kan of Antares has a body of gleaming metal. Jhul Din of Spica is a crustacean being in black shell. Crews of the Patrol come from every peopled star. The squadron patrols the edge of the galaxy. Currents keep throwing the ships off course. The narrator orders his men to hold their path all the same.
74200-little-why-because:
Little Why-Because is Agnes Giberne's story of a questioning child, printed by the Religious Tract Society at London. Giberne had written Sun, Moon and Stars. Dudley Tennant drew the pictures. The heroine, Hecla, was born in Iceland under the shadow of Mount Hecla, which gave her the curious name. She lives with her aunt, Miss Storey, a small, still lady who knits by the fire.

Hecla can neither sit upright nor sit still. Hemming a handkerchief for Chris, she fires off questions without pause. What does ruthless mean? Why does Chris learn Latin? Why do blackbirds eat worms instead of crumbs? Chapters promise a vicarage dog, little Ivy, a temptation and a great danger. Consequences and a delightful toy-shop close the tale.
74217-the-bobbsey-twins-keeping-house:
The Bobbsey Twins Keeping House is a children's novel by Laura Lee Hope. Grosset and Dunlap published the book at New York in 1925. The title page notes that the book was made under wartime rules for saving paper, yet is complete. Bert, Nan, Flossie, and Freddie Bobbsey fill the story, as in the rest of the series.

The first chapter opens in the yard, where Nan runs a ball game for the small twins. Flossie begs for one more turn, jumping up and down in the cold. Freddie gives up his turn with good nature. Chapter titles promise a lost ring, bad news, and twins lost in turn. Later chapters bring snow, broken wires, a fire, and a rescue just in time. Aunt Sallie Pry comes and goes as a comic trial for the young housekeepers.
74519-the-uses-of-water-in-health-and-di:
Kellogg wrote The Uses of Water in Health and Disease, a plain guide to the bath and its uses, printed at Battle Creek in eighteen seventy-six. He says most past books on the water cure were ads for a man or a house, full of wild claims. Priessnitz had set off the craze some fifty years before. Kellogg aims to give a fair account instead.

The book sets out what water is, how it acts on the body, and how it can help in sickness. It shows that famed doctors of all ages used water as a cure. It also names the false and absurd uses that brought the cure into ill repute. Last, it serves as a handbook of ways to apply water, from baths to packs.
74554-sex-problems-of-man-in-health-and-:
Sex Problems of Man in Health and Disease is a book of heal lore for the crowd by Moses Scholtz. He was a chief of a cure house and a teach man in the lore of the skin and its ills at a great school. He was a fellow of more bands of heal men than one. The book was put out in nineteen sixteen at a river town. Its rights were held that year in his name.

Its own sub name calls it a work for the crowd on the lore of its theme. The list of parts gives its plan in full. A lead in on the weight of its theme in the life of a man heads the run. Then come two great heaps: its theme in health, and its theme in ill.
74619-a-book-of-women-s-verse:
A Book of Women's Verse was edited by Squire, with a prefatory essay, at the Clarendon Press in Oxford in 1921. Squire dedicates the anthology to Alice Meynell. The poems run in rough order of their makers' lives, and the first poet in the book is Anne Askew, martyred in 1546.

Askew's ballad, made and sung when she was in Newgate, opens the collection. Like an armed knight appointed to the field, she sings, she will fight with this world, and faith shall be her shield. A long footnote elsewhere preserves a scholarly woman's deathbed Latin, spoken to her husband: be not thou overmuch careful, or troubled. Drawing nearer and nearer, she told him the next day, and departed on the third without sigh or groan.
74635-the-minstrel-s-curse:
The Minstrel's Curse is a novel by Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller, author of The Bride of the Tomb. The story is told in four parts. It opens with a song of hopeless love for a queen. A singer's tenor voice dies away over the piano keys as the book begins.

The scene is a grand drawing room at Chilton Park in Somersetshire. Lady Edith Chilton asks her brother's tutor, Guy Winthrop, for one more verse. He refuses point blank, a liberty no one else dares with her. Winthrop says his low place frees him from the flattery of her lordly admirers. He can afford to speak his mind to her. Her blue eyes flash with anger at the slight. The exchange sets the proud lady and the poor musician on their course through the tale.
74949-helen-of-troy-and-rose:
Helen of Troy and Rose is a pair of stories by Phyllis Bottome, author of The Dark Tower, published by the Century Company in 1918 with illustrations by Norman Osborn. Helen of Troy fills the first 127 pages, and Rose follows. The frontispiece shows Miss Lestrange saying to a young woman: I want you to let my boy go. The first story opens on Horace Lestrange, throwing stones into a lake.

He makes each stone jump four times, but only his outer attention is on the game. Ten years ago he lost his wife, after one year's marriage. Perhaps, had she lived, he would have grown tired of her; but she was very beautiful, and she has kept her power. A passage preserved in the copy weighs those ten years.
75146-the-eames-erskine-case:
The Eames-Erskine Case is a detective novel by A Fielding. The A L Burt Company published it in New York, from a 1925 Knopf copyright. Fielding dedicates it to her mother, who first read and criticised the yarn. The first chapter brings the police to a hotel room. Four plain-clothes men enter noiselessly, one carrying a large box.

Chief Inspector Pointer of New Scotland Yard leads them. Detectives Watts, Miller, and Lester assist. Mr Beale, an American gentleman, took the room for one night and reported something wrong about the wardrobe. A large knot-hole pierces its back. Pointer runs a finger round it, gently as a mother feeling a baby's tooth. His face shows nothing. Flashlight photographs are taken before any touching. Then the men lift the wardrobe's top off and lay it on its side. A cry from the watchers greets what the opening reveals.
75147-the-collected-stories-of-elisabeth:
The Collected Stories of Elisabeth Sanxay Holding gathers the fiction she placed in Munsey's Magazine between 1920 and 1928. The first story shown, The Married Man, ran in the December 1921 number and bills itself as a modern comedy of enlightened thought. Holding was by then the author of Angelica.

Marian, the married man's wife, has grown used to Andrew's forgetting every anniversary, and rather likes it: each lapse gives her something to forgive. She is handsome, thrifty, never irritable, never gloomy, an excellent mother and a correct hostess. Andrew, clever and explosive, wants to struggle and rebel, and keeps trying to provoke a quarrel she will never join. On their tenth anniversary she waits with her sewing, certain he has forgotten, and will not admit the little wound even to herself. The comedy is all in what neither will say.
75180-children-of-the-lighthouse:
Children of the Lighthouse is a children's story by Nora Archibald Smith, printed at Boston in 1924. Smith also wrote The Christmas Child and verse for children, and worked with her sister Kate Douglas Wiggin on The Story Hour. A plate shows the children with Jenny Lind and Jim Crow.

The story opens on the shore. Lesley jumps up from the sand, crying a rhymed yes, and tucks her book into a cleft of the rocks. She scrambles up the cliff like a sturdy little mountain goat. The children of the title live by a lighthouse, and their days mix sea air, small duties, and play. Smith wrote from the Froebel kindergarten faith she shared with her sister. The book is gentle, salt-aired fiction for young readers of its time.
75213-account-of-the-skerryvore-lighthou:
An engineering account by Alan Stevenson, published at Edinburgh in 1848. Stevenson was engineer to the Northern Lighthouse Board. The commissioners ordered the book by their own direction. Its subject is the Skerryvore Lighthouse, off Scotland's west coast. Notes on the illumination of lighthouses complete the volume. A Greek inscription from the ancient Pharos of Alexandria graces the title page.

Stevenson's preface apologises for defects with candour. Official duties kept interrupting the writing for months. He thanks his father, architect of twenty-five lighthouses. The Bell Rock light was among the father's works. He also thanks Leonor Fresnel for the dioptric system. That lens system, invented by Fresnel's brother, transformed lighthouse light. The account remains a classic of lighthouse engineering.
75232-the-unseen-universe:
The Unseen Universe opens with two mottoes on its first page. A Greek line from the Corinthian letters treats things unseen as eternal. Hadrian's Latin verse to his little soul stands beside it. A long quotation sorts the faculties of man by objects. We discover sensible things by our senses, it says.

Rational things we find by reason, intellectual ones by understanding. Divine and celestial things are reserved for the exercise of faith. Faith is a kind of divine and superior sense in the soul, it holds. Reason may snatch a glimpse but cannot take a steady prospect. By natural reason I may know a God exists, it owns. He is the first cause and original of all things, it adds. His essence and will lie hid in inaccessible light. The book argues from nature toward the unseen order.
75240-suspense:
Suspense is a mystery novel by Isabel Ostrander, published in New York in nineteen eighteen by Robert M McBride and Company. Ostrander had already written The Clue in the Air and The Primal Law, and this tale opens with a newspaper advertisement.

A young woman, well bred and educated, a stranger in the city without relatives, offers herself as companion or social secretary to a lady of standing, with salary optional. The chapter titles promise a girl with a scar, a silent intruder, a message from Pharaoh, ten thousand sheep, an orchid lady, and a portrait of Beethoven. That odd advertisement is the hook: a heroine who asks almost nothing is exactly the person a secretive house would hire.
75246-it-pays-to-advertise:
Roi Cooper Megrue and Walter Hackett wrote this farce in three acts, copyrighted in 1914 and first produced at the George M Cohan Theatre in New York that September. Grant Mitchell played the young hero.

The cast lists Mary Grayson, a comtesse, Rodney Martin, and his father Cyrus Martin, a soap maker. Act two moves to the office of the 13 Soap Company, between two acts in the Martins' library. The title states the play's whole argument: advertising works wonders, even for a soap nobody has heard of. The printed text carries the publisher's stern warnings about amateur and professional rights. Theater readers get the hit Broadway farce that made a slogan into a plot.
75391-ocellus-lucanus-on-the-nature-of-t:
Thomas Taylor turned Ocellus Lucanus On the Nature of the Universe into English prose. The book was printed for Taylor in London in eighteen hundred thirty one. John Bohn and Thomas Rodd sold the small volume there. Three more old tracts on time’s long span stand with it.

Taurus, a Platonist, writes on the world’s endless age next. Julius Firmicus Maternus maps the stars at each age’s birth. Proclus adds theorems on time that never ends at all. True science treats things that last and must be, Taylor holds. Passing things are shadows on shadows, in Plotinus’ phrase. Ocellus lived near five hundred years before Christ, men guess. Archytas told Plato he had the man’s books from his kin. Laws, rule, piety, and the world’s birth were Ocellus’ themes.
75476-the-poisoned-chocolates-case:
The Poisoned Chocolates Case, by Anthony Berkeley, published by Collins in 1929, is a detective novel built around a club of crime lovers. Roger Sheringham, who founded and runs the Crimes Circle, dines with members who must prove real skill in detection and criminal psychology to join. Chief Inspector Moresby of Scotland Yard sits as guest of honor.

The club takes up a real poisoning puzzle, and the members compete to solve it. Berkeley, a master of the fair play mystery, lets each sleuth build a different answer from the same facts. The dedication teases a friend who, for once, did not guess it.
75511-a-lyttel-booke-of-nonsense:
A Lyttel Booke of Nonsense holds limericks by a writer who signs as R D, printed in London by Macmillan in 1912. Old woodcuts fill the pages. The writer says few of the cuts are less than four hundred years old.

In a note to the reader, R D says new rhymes on old cuts should be no slur on their worth or beauty. He thanks book men for help and owns a debt to Edward Lear, the master of the form. One verse tells of a young fellow of Sark who feared the dark. One tells of an old man of Sheerness who lent his chess set to a niece and lost her address. One tells of a fellow of Trent who sold scent boxes. Nonsense fans get Lear style fun with antique art.
75576-the-old-stanfield-house:
The Old Stanfield House, or The Sin of Covetousness, is a moral tale by Guernsey, author of past tales for the young on girls and school life. It was put out by a Sunday school guild with shops in three great cities of America. Its rights were set in law in the early eighteen eighties.

A front plate shows a dusk meet at the old house, with a short hail between two men. A line from Scripture heads the book: love not the world, nor the things that are in the world. The tale then works that text in a plot of greed and its fruits in a home and a town, made for young readers of the Sunday school shelf.
75669-the-templeton-case:
The Templeton Case is a tale of crime by Victor Whitechurch. It was put out at New York by a house of that town. Its list of parts runs to one and twenty. A church man of rank stands in its folk, with a sleuth of the force in a chief place. The parts start with the come of the hero to a small port town.

The call on the far shore and a dire find come next. What that church man found on a small boat of the port stands past them. The sleuth finds clues, and the sleuth is beat, in the next two parts. The court of death, a call by a maid of the tale, and a band of a smoke stick fill the first run.
757-fifty-bab-ballads-much-sound-and-lit:
W. S. Gilbert gathered fifty of his Bab Ballads, comic verses written for the magazine Fun under the pen name Bab. The ballads tell absurd tales in brisk rhyme: policemen, sailors, ghosts, and lovers caught in topsy-turvy plots, all resolved with a wink. The subtitle, Much Sound and Little Sense, gives the game away.

Gilbert's humour is dry and precise, with a love of logic pushed to folly. These verses were the seedbed of his later operas with Sullivan, and many of their jokes and types reappear on stage. The book delights readers who enjoy nonsense verse with a sharp edge, where sense and sound swap places for fun.
75938-a-new-selection-of-miscellaneous-p:
Christian Gray wrote A New Selection of Miscellaneous Pieces in Verse, printed at Perth in eighteen hundred twenty one. Gray had been blind since infancy. She lived at Milton in the parish of Aberdalgie in Perthshire. Lines from Milton on lost sight face her title page.

She gave the book to the ladies who had backed her first set. That first set, twelve years past, had sold past her hopes. Most new verses came from her young years, she says. Some came late, in a long sick spell that kept her indoors. She hopes sales will cheer the lone last years of her life. Faith, place, and thanks run through the short, plain rhymes.
76767-the-story-of-john-smeaton-and-the-:
The Story of John Smeaton and the Eddystone Lighthouse is a short life of the great engineer and his famous tower. T Nelson and Sons of London, Edinburgh, and New York published it in 1900. A frontispiece shows Smeaton's lighthouse on the Eddystone Rock, and verses from Longfellow stand at the head of the book. The pages rest on Samuel Smiles's Lives of the Engineers and on Smeaton's own account of the Eddystone Lighthouse.

Four chapters divide the tale. Ancient and Modern Lighthouses and The Eddystone Lighthouse come first, then How John Smeaton Rose in Life, and Smeaton in Private Life, his last years and character. The opening chapter argues that men needed lights as soon as they went down to the deep in ships, and that the Greeks credited Hercules with the invention.
76977-little-button-rose:
Louisa Alcott wrote a short tale for girls about a child named Rosamond. The book came out in Boston in 1887. Alcott is the author of Little Women and Little Men. Rosamond is known in the tale as little Button Rose. A front plate shows her as she looks round a room.

Rosamond walks in on three aunts at their work with calm trust. She bears a letter for Cousin Penelope in her hand. The thin aunt, the stout aunt, and the fair young aunt greet her each in turn. Love and small trials shape the days that ensue. Young readers get Alcott's warm hand in brief form.
77282-neufcha-tel-and-cream-cheese:
Neufchâtel and Cream Cheese: Farm Manufacture and Use is Farmers' Bulletin 960. K J Matheson and F R Cammack of the Dairy Division wrote it. The Department of Agriculture issued it at Washington in July 1918. John R Mohler headed the Bureau of Animal Industry. Copies were free from the Division of Publications. The bulletin teaches farm households to make soft cheese.

Neufchâtel takes its name from a town in northwestern France. Cream cheese is made from milk of about 6 per cent fat. Neufchâtel uses ordinary 4 per cent milk. A pimiento form of cream cheese was already popular. The contents walk through manufacture step by step. Milk quality, clean utensils, ripening, and starters come first. Standardising and pasteurisation precede the making itself. Cost tables follow for each cheese. Returns from 100 pounds of milk are computed. Equipment, keeping qualities, and dietary uses close the bulletin.
77477-correction-of-underweight-and-over:
Benson wrote this health guide as Little Blue Book number 1479, copyrighted at Girard, Kansas in 1929. Reducing drugs and how to reduce sanely open the contents at page nine. Exercises fill the middle of the book, from page twelve onward in the list.

About one-fifth of the American people are burdened with overweight, Benson writes. Excess weight blocks an active, vigorous and normal life and cuts the chance of long life, he argues. Prevention beats cure, he warns young adults, and a second part treats underweight and malnutrition, with causes and special exercises to build the body up.
77527-keepers-of-the-house:
Lester del Rey wrote a tale of a dog who keeps a house of men. A front note calls this one of his best tales yet. Del Rey was known for a host of tales of science and dream. King, the dog, stands on a rock shelf by a river. His great gaunt frame shifts as he scents the wind.

No mark sets that morn apart from a host of past ones. Yet King's hackles rise and his ears probe each sound. He can call back how grand the house once seemed to men. What science did to his friends lies at the tale's heart. The dog's view gives the loss its sharp edge.
77602-the-hidden-staircase:
The Hidden Staircase, by Carolyn Keene, was published in 1930. Grosset and Dunlap issued the Nancy Drew mystery at New York. Tandy drew the illustrations. Twenty five chapters make the story. A rude visitor opens it, and a warning of trouble follows. The ghost calls twice in the early contents. An anonymous message and a cry in the night raise the stakes. Carson Drew himself is a chapter's worry midway. A prisoner, a new clue, and an underground passage come late. Captured ends the list. Chapter one finds Nancy alone and restless. Her father is out of the city on a law case. Hannah Gruen, the housekeeper, has her day off.

Nancy tosses her book aside, aching for another adventure. The doorbell rings twice, sharp and startling. A tall, thin stranger stands at the door.
77672-the-giant-and-other-nonsense-verse:
Albert W Smith wrote The Giant and Other Nonsense Verse, issued by Andrus and Church at Ithaca, New York, in nineteen ten. The Giant, the Arctic Ball, and Funnyland first appeared in the Ladies Home Journal. Smith gave the book to Ruby, Alpheus, Dorothy, and Ruth. The title poem opens the fun. There is a Giant in the world whose head is up so high, it begins.

He has to get down on his knees to look up in the sky, the verse says. When he needs food, he wades out in the sea and fishes out a whale or two to fricassee. Near Hindustan he gathers young elephants for oriental stew. When he tires of earthly food, he eats planets roasted well and hung outside to cool. His wife skims the Milky Way for cream for the planet sauce. Children get tall nonsense in bouncing rhyme.
77746-the-oxford-book-of-portuguese-vers:
The Oxford Book of Portuguese Verse gathers poems from eight centuries of song. Aubrey Bell chose the poems for the Clarendon Press at Oxford. The book came out in the year nineteen twenty five. Its span runs from the twelfth century to the twentieth century.

Early love songs of kings and troubadours open the long run of verse. Most poets in the book are dead, since the pick shuns the living by rule. Thanks in the front note name four poets who let new work in print. A gift page honours a great scholar of the tongue and its books. The poems stand in their own tongue, in the forms their makers used.
77750-doubly-false:
Doubly False is a novel by Ann Stephens, one of America's first best selling women writers. Peterson published it at Philadelphia, entering it in 1898, though Stephens dedicated it to her son's wife in 1868. Her other tales are listed at the front: Fashion and Famine, The Soldier's Orphans, The Heiress, and The Old Homestead among them. Verses on honour and truth stand as its motto.

There is no pathway leading to the light, save that which honour treads, the verses say. The false, even to themselves, are traitors all, and deceit must end in weary strife. The tale opens on a splendidly bright day in early spring. The ocean lies unusually calm, its greenish blue broken by sunshine into ripples of quicksilver over crystal. This one joins sea scenery to a plot of double dealing, in her high coloured style.
77798-secrets-of-crewe-house:
Campbell Stuart wrote Secrets of Crewe House, the story of a famous campaign, for Hodder and Stoughton. The book first came out in September 1920 and ran to a fourth edition by March 1921. A photo shows Viscount Northcliffe, director of propaganda in enemy countries. Stuart gives the book to Northcliffe in grateful appreciation. His foreword owns that some courage is needed to add to the swollen list of war books.

The plea for this one is that it records British propaganda in enemy lands in 1918. Some of that work was pioneer work, Stuart holds, and of historic weight. Issue had to wait till the main lines of peace were set, lest Allied governments be embarrassed. Much that was dramatic can never be told, for fear of reprisals on brave helpers.
78230-accepting-the-universe:
Accepting the Universe is a book of essays in naturalism by John Burroughs, the American nature writer. Houghton Mifflin published it in Boston and New York in 1920, the year before Burroughs died. A verse from the Rubaiyat heads the book: men argue about the universe, and come out by the same door wherein they went.

The contents lay out his creed. An opening essay asks whether we shall accept the universe. Then come essays on manifold nature, on each thing for its own sake, and on the universal beneficence. The good devils and the natural providence follow. Later essays treat the faith of a naturalist, tooth and claw, men and trees, and the problem of evil. A closing set of horizon lines asks about the origin of life and whether there is design in nature. Burroughs spent a long life watching birds and woods; these essays gather his philosophy.
78495-collected-works-of-padraic-h-pears:
The Collected Works of Padraic Pearse gathers the Irish leader's plays, stories, and poems. The Phoenix Publishing Company issued it at Dublin. This copy is the sixth edition, from 1924. The copyright dates to 1917. A photograph of Pearse fronts the volume. The contents divide into three clear parts.

Four plays open the book. The Singer and The Master lead them. Twelve stories follow, many turned from the Irish by a translator. The poems close the volume. Titles like I Am Ireland and The Rebel mark their temper. A publisher's note tells a wartime story. Final manuscripts of two plays burned in an office fire at Easter 1916. Other copies, happily, survived with the author's corrections.
78632-a-bull-movement-in-yellow-horse:
Tuttle wrote a western tale of two cowpunchers and a strange track. Cobalt Williams and Slim Hawkins crawl on hands and knees in the road and gaze frowning at the dust. Pears to me she's tracks of some kind, Cobalt says. Slim agrees, brushes off his trousers, and says it looks like a stump had crow hopped down the road.

The marks show no remarkable difference at either end, and they head for Yellow Horse, the men's own destination. Slim twirls his forty five Colt and muses that the critter may be so enormous a six gun is no use. Come on, Cobalt urges, let us find out what she is anyway. Humor and mystery ride together.
78655-the-scarab-murder-case:
The Scarab Murder Case is a Philo Vance story by Van Dine, published by Scribner of New York in 1930. The book is dedicated to three men of the Egyptian Department of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

A frontispiece by Raymond Sisley shows Vance lifting Salveter to his feet. The scene is the Bliss Museum of Egyptian Antiquities, run by Bliss. District Attorney Markham and Sergeant Heath work the official side. Chapter titles promise tracks in the blood, finger-prints, and a hieroglyphic letter. A golden dagger, a tin of opium, and a granite sarcophagus follow. The narrator notes that chance, not Markham, drew Vance into the case.
78960-for-the-parson-of-paradise:
W C Tuttle wrote this western story of the town of Paradise, told by Ike, who rides in with Magpie Simpkins and ties his burro to a rack. They find Old Testament Tilton, the parson, sitting before the Ace Full saloon.

Tilton's tale is hard luck. He almost saved Sad Semple, who hugged him in public and made a date for church. Then Sad stopped at a saloon, lost a dollar on the wheel, and accused the dealer of rigging it. His well-chosen words were spoken over Sad instead of to him. Now the church pays no dividends and the pantry is empty. Tuttle's Hashknife style of comic western talk carries the tale.
79022-collected-works-of-padraic-h-pears:
The Collected Works of Padraic H Pearse opens with his political writings and speeches. Maunsel and Roberts published the volume at Dublin and London in 1922. The contents run by date. The Murder Machine of 1912 stands first. Orations on Wolfe Tone in 1913 and on Robert Emmet in 1914 follow. The Coming Revolution dates to November 1913, and The Psychology of a Volunteer to January 1914.

To the Boys of Ireland, from February 1914, and Why We Want Recruits, from May 1915, come next. A character sketch of O'Donovan Rossa and his graveside oration date to August 1915. From a Hermitage, Peace and the Gael, and Ghosts carry the run into 1916. The Separatist Idea, The Spiritual Nation, and The Sovereign People close the book, the last dated March 31, 1916.
79141-replace-the-horse:
Larry Harris wrote Replace the Horse, a tale told by a horse trainer. A headnote states its theme: lots of people think they can beat the races, and Willy Dunstan knew he could, but no wild inventor's trick will replace the horse. The only trouble with Willy Dunstan, the teller opens, was that he was a scientist. Had he been a middling or even a poor one, things would not have been so bad. Willy had to be a good scientist.

That ruined him, and ruined the teller too. Arthur Holly tells it, a trainer by trade. He got the chance to buy a plug, a worn-out horse of no use. Greg called the animal a business chance. Holly saw through the sprucing-up at once: a swaybacked, empty-bellied, cross-eyed old plug. The horse went at auction for one hundred and thirty-five dollars.
79226-a-three-fold-promise:
Hurrell also wrote Cecily Mordaunt. The book has eight chapters, with names such as In Disgrace, The Missing Child, Discovery and Reunion. The story opens in a poor London home. A widowed mother must part from her young son Gerald Weston for the first time in his life.

The boy's father is dead and the family is very poor. An uncle has agreed to provide for Gerald if the mother gives him up for two years. At the parting she asks the boy to promise three things while she is away. He must never forget his prayers. He must speak the truth always. And he must hold in mind that God loves him and watches over him. The eight year old makes the promise as a new life starts for him.
79668-the-neurotic-rose:
The Neurotic Rose is a science fiction story by Nearing. An editor's headnote frames the joke. A food-and-sex complex in the vegetable kingdom may lack the dark meaning it carries in humans, but who can be sure plants cannot go haywire too?

Professor Ransom, a botanical genius of the mathematics faculty, has grown a plant that is half dog. The rose on his windowsill has shaggy reddish hair like a hound's ears. Its centre protrudes like a snout, slit by two rows of white teeth, and it smells doggy. Offered a grasshopper, the creature twists its stem and turns coldly away, like a child on a hunger strike. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
805-this-side-of-paradise:
F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote this first novel about Amory Blaine, a handsome youth who grows from a romantic boy into a Princeton man and then into a disillusioned young adult. Book One, The Romantic Egotist, follows Amory's school and college days, his friendships, and his first loves, in prose that mixes narrative, verse, and drama.

Fitzgerald captures the restless mood of a generation after the Great War, with its hunger for beauty, wealth, and meaning. Amory's search ends not in triumph but in self-knowledge, hard won. The novel made Fitzgerald famous at twenty-three, and it remains the classic portrait of American youth on the edge of the Jazz Age.
8182-the-ghost-of-guir-house:
Charles Willing Beale published The Ghost of Guir House in 1897, opening with Mr Henley returning to his dingy little house in Twentieth Street. New York, where a servant hands him a letter the postman struggled to deliver. The letter bears several erased addresses and a note in the corner: Dead. Try Paul. Unfamiliar with the handwriting, Henley carries it upstairs, lights the gas, and begins to read, setting the mystery in motion.

The novel that follows links a New York present to a haunted house and a past that will not stay buried. Beale writes a Victorian ghost story of letters, identities, and old wrongs. For lovers of supernatural fiction, it is an atmospheric period piece, with a New York opening that leads into genuinely eerie territory.
835-the-grey-brethren-and-other-fragment:
Michael Fairless, author of The Roadmender, gathered these fragments in prose and verse in 1911. The Grey Brethren, the title piece, leads a set of short meditations, tales, and poems in the same gentle, devout spirit. Duckworth issued the volume, which reached a third impression in its first year.

Fairless writes of faith, nature, and the quiet duties of life, in prose that is simple and musical. The fragments are brief, meant to be read slowly and pondered. The book suits readers who loved The Roadmender, offering more of its author's calm wisdom in small, polished pieces.
8448-honor-edgeworth-or-ottawa-s-present:
Honor Edgeworth, or Ottawa's Present Tense, by Vera, was entered for copyright in Canada in 1882 by A. S. Woodburn of Ottawa. The preface promises an honest tale, plainly told, in Shakespeare's phrase, and the novel follows Honor Edgeworth through Ottawa society, in the capital's present tense, as the subtitle says.

Vera's novel belongs to early Canadian fiction, written when Ottawa was a young capital finding its social life. Readers get a period romance of manners, with Canadian settings and characters, from a writer using a pen name. The book interests students of Canadian literature, and readers who like Victorian domestic novels in a colonial setting.
8572-cord-and-creese:
James De Mille opens this adventure novel in Sydney, New South Wales, on the morning the ship Rival brings the English mail in July 1840. Crowds gather at the post office, street corners buzz with news from home, and a letter from beyond the sea sets the plot moving. Warehouses, offices, and the harbour give the opening a busy colonial port for a backdrop.

From that arrival, the story widens into the tangled fortunes, secrets, and sea-going ventures that the title hints at. De Mille, already known for The Dodge Club, writes at a brisk pace, letting letters, chance meetings, and sudden turns carry the reader forward. It is a good pick for anyone who likes old-fashioned adventure built on mystery, travel, and the long reach of a single piece of news.
8575-the-happy-days-of-the-empress-marie:
Imbert de Saint-Amand wrote The Happy Days of the Empress Marie Louise, translated by Thomas Sergeant Perry and illustrated. It follows the young empress from early years through 1809, the preliminaries of her wedding, and the betrothal. A religious difficulty, an ambassador extraordinary, the wedding at Vienna, the departure, the transfer, and the journey to France follow.

Marie Louise, Napoleon's second wife, lived her happy days before exile and loss, and Saint-Amand, a historian of Napoleon's women, tells them with court detail. Readers get a biography of a young empress at the height of empire, before its fall. The book suits readers of Napoleonic history, and of royal lives told through ceremony and anecdote.
8933-popular-tales-from-the-norse:
Sir George Webbe Dasent collects Popular Tales from the Norse, with an introductory essay on the origin and diffusion of popular tales. His introduction moves through origin, diffusion, Norse mythology, Norse popular tales, and conclusion, arguing that stories travel and change across peoples while keeping their bones. Notices to the first and second editions frame a book that helped create the study of folklore in English.

The tales themselves include True and Untrue, Why the Sea is Salt, the old dame and her hen, East o' the Sun and West o' the Moon. Boots who ate a match with the troll, Hacon Grizzlebeard, Boots who made the princess say that's a story, the twelve wild ducks. The giant who had no heart in his body. The fox as herdsman, the mastermaid, the cat on the Dovrefell, and the princess on the glass hill follow.
9221-the-old-manse-from-mosses-from-an-o:
Between two tall gate-posts of rough stone, Hawthorne first beheld the gray front of the old parsonage at Concord. The gate had fallen from its hinges at some unknown time. A year had passed since the last clergyman's funeral train left for the burying-ground. Grass overgrew the drive, grazed by vagrant cows and an old white horse.

Hawthorne, the new tenant, makes the reader acquainted with his abode, its avenue of black-ash trees, and its half-asleep shadows. The house seems barely of the material world. This preface remains a beloved opening to Mosses from an Old Manse, full of quiet wonder.
9224-buds-and-bird-voices-from-mosses-fr:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this spring sketch for Mosses from an Old Manse, as winter loosens its grip. Balmy Spring comes late, yet at last revives the moss on roof and walls of the old house. She peeps into his study window, and he throws it open to mix her genial breath with the stove's black cheer.

Thoughts and fancies of winter fly out into infinite space as the casement rises. Visions gay, grotesque, and sad give way to a fresh existence made of sunshine. The sketch is a joyful ode to spring, and to the mind waking with the year.
9225-monsieur-du-miroir-from-mosses-from:
No one in Hawthorne's circle has he studied more, yet known less, than the gentleman called Monsieur du Miroir. The narrator, a student of human nature, seeks who this figure really is, how he connects to himself, and what their joint interest may bring. He lays a few remarkable points before the public, hoping for a clue.

Readers soon guess the jest: Monsieur du Miroir is the man in the mirror, the self seen in glass. Hawthorne turns a fancy into grave reflection on identity. The sketch remains a witty, uncanny piece on the double every person carries.
9226-the-hall-of-fantasy-from-mosses-fro:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this sketch for Mosses from an Old Manse, on a hall he claims to visit at times. Its interior is a spacious hall with white marble floors, a lofty dome, and pillars like Moorish work from the Alhambra. Stained windows fill it with many-colored light, painting the floor with grotesque designs.

Inmates breathe a visionary air, as in a Gothic cathedral of the mind. Hawthorne uses the hall as an image of fancy itself, where famous shades meet. The sketch is a playful allegory of imagination, and a favorite among his shorter pieces.
9227-the-new-adam-and-eve-from-mosses-fr:
Suppose Father Miller's reading of prophecy came true, and the Day of Doom swept away all mankind. Hawthorne, in Mosses from an Old Manse, imagines a new Adam and Eve waking in a world emptied of artifice. We who live in an artificial system, he says, can hardly know how little in us is natural, and how much is man's perverted craft.

Art has become a stepmother, teaching us to scorn nature's wholesome gifts. Only fancy can loosen the fetters we call truth. The tale follows the pair through cities and fields, learning life anew. It remains a bold, strange fable on nature versus custom.
9228-the-christmas-banquet-from-mosses-f:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this tale for Mosses from an Old Manse, drawn from his unpublished Allegories of the Heart. Roderick, sitting with Rosina and a sculptor in a summer-house, unfolds a manuscript. He seeks to grasp a man who glides past him in life, a puzzle his sad experience cannot solve.

The sculptor urges him to propound the man, whom Roderick likens to marble carved with a mockery of intellect, yet lacking a heart. Hawthorne's allegory probes cold genius and feeling. The tale is dark, strange, and deeply characteristic of its author.
9229-the-intelligence-office-from-mosses:
A grave figure in mysterious spectacles sits at a desk in a city intelligence office, a pen behind his ear. Around the walls stick notices of things lost, wanted, or for sale, covering nearly all that human fancy has contrived. Tall buildings and blue and crimson show-bills shadow the room, while street noise beats outside.

Hawthorne, in Mosses from an Old Manse, uses the office as an emblem of human wanting itself. Seekers come and go, each with a loss or a wish. The sketch is a sly, humane satire on desire, and on the trade that promises to meet it.
9230-p-s-correspondence-from-mosses-from:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this tale for Mosses from an Old Manse, around his friend P., whose mind mixes past and present. P. has lost the thread of his life through long spells of disordered reason. Yet from a small whitewashed, iron-grated room he travels far in fancy, meeting persons long dead to all eyes but his.

Hawthorne calls this sport of imagination, half wilful and half forced by disease, vivid as a play on stage. The letters that follow show P.'s spectral meetings. The tale is tender and eerie, a study of madness as a kind of second sight.
9231-earth-s-holocaust-from-mosses-from-:
Once upon a time, whether past or to come matters little, the world grew overburdened with worn-out trumpery. Its people chose to rid themselves of it by a general bonfire on a broad western prairie, where no house stood in danger. Hawthorne journeys there, hoping the flames may reveal some moral truth hidden in mist.

The heap grows as old books, weapons, and vanities feed the fire, yet the heart's rubbish proves harder to burn. Hawthorne's fable asks what reform can truly purge. It remains a brilliant satire on progress, showing how little fire alone can change mankind.
9233-sketches-from-memory-from-mosses-fr:
Hawthorne's sketches from memory open in mid-September, on the road to the White Mountains. Since sunrise the party has climbed from Bartlett up the Saco valley, between mountain walls, toward old crystal hills whose brilliancy gleamed from afar. Height after height towers up, till clouds hang below the peaks.

Red pathways of slides scar the slopes, where avalanches of earth and trees left tracks ages cannot efface. Mountains stand behind, beside, and ahead. Hawthorne's prose turns travel into poetry. The sketches remain a classic of American mountain writing, observant and grand.
9235-a-virtuoso-s-collection-from-mosses:
With a leisure hour to spare, Hawthorne steps into a new museum, drawn by a small sign: To be seen here, a virtuoso's collection. Up a sombre stair he pays half a dollar to a doorkeeper in a faded great-coat, whose marked face promises something out of the ordinary way. Inside waits a cabinet of wonders.

The collection holds relics of history and fable, each with a tale attached, from famous folk and fabled beasts. Hawthorne turns the museum into a meditation on fame and curiosity. The sketch is a delightful cabinet piece, witty and quietly melancholy.
9410-helen-of-the-old-house:
Harold Bell Wright, a best-selling American novelist, published Helen of the Old House in 1921. The novel sets a mill town's labor strife beside two women both named Helen, and an old house that binds their fates. A figure called the Interpreter speaks for a moral view of work and wealth. The book moves from a hut on a cliff to the mill, the strike, and the town's reckoning.

As the strike builds, managers, workers, and town folk clash over wages, power, and fair dealing. Wright pleads for a middle path: honest work, fair pay, and care for the common good. The prose is earnest and plain, aimed at a wide crowd. A reader gets a popular 1920s take on capital and labor, told as a human story, not a tract.
9606-a-little-book-of-western-verse:
Eugene Field wrote A Little Book of Western Verse in 1889, poems of the American West and of home. Field dedicated the book to Mary Field French, who fostered him as a child after his mother's death. His dedication thanks her patient heart and asks her kind eye for his faults. The poems that follow mix memory, humor, and tenderness.

Verses recall loved ones passed away, western scenes, and small home joys, in Field's easy, musical style. A Memory opens the run, on loss and the ache of absence. A reader gets a fond, old-style book of verse, where the West meets the hearth, and a poet's gratitude runs through every line.
982-the-book-of-nonsense:
Edward Lear wrote this Book of Nonsense, a set of drawings and verses for children, dedicated to the great-grandchildren, grand-nephews, and grand-nieces of Edward, thirteenth Earl of Derby. The opening limerick tells of an Old Derry down Derry, who loved to see little folks merry and made them a book at which they shook with laughter.

Lear's limericks, with their odd folk and places, and his drawings to match, invented a whole genre of nonsense verse. The book, made for the Derby children, has delighted generations since. It remains a classic of children's literature, where silliness is an art and every page invites a laugh.
9889-songs-and-other-verse:
This ninth volume of Eugene Field's collected writings gathers his songs and shorter poems. Field, a Chicago journalist and poet, wrote verses meant to be read aloud, full of children, home, and everyday feeling.

Among the pieces are a dream-ship ballad, a song for a mother's grave, love songs after Heine, and light tales of tailors and journalists. The tone shifts from tender to playful without losing its musical ease. Readers who like poetry that sings rather than puzzles will find Field at his most charming here, in short pieces that reward reading aloud.
9979-de-libris-prose-and-verse:
Austin Dobson's 1908 book of prose and verse takes books and their associations as its subject, as its title, De Libris, promises. Dobson addresses the reader as lector benevole, the kindly reader of old, and admits he cannot make anyone read the pages that follow.

Inside are essays and poems on books, authors, and the pleasures of collecting, in Dobson's polished, eighteenth-century manner. Published by Macmillan in London, the book suits lovers of old volumes and quiet libraries. Readers who enjoy bibliophily will find wit, learning, and affection on every page.
9989-bees-in-amber-a-little-book-of-thou:
John Oxenham's 1913 little book of thoughtful verse opens with a credo and moves through the year's days, a philosopher's garden, and flowers of the dust. Oxenham, a popular devotional poet, writes short poems meant to be pondered, not merely admired.

Later pieces follow the pilgrim way, the potter and the pruner at their work, whirring wheels, the bells of Ys, and a little poem of life. The tone is earnest, hopeful, and plain. Readers looking for brief, reflective poetry for quiet moments will find these verses easy to carry and return to.
a-book-of-nonsense: Edward Lear offers his classic book of nonsense drawings and verses. The volume opens with an old man of Derry who made a book to set little folks laughing. Its limericks and pictures pair odd figures with absurd fates in short rhymed lines. Lear dedicated the collection to the young kin of the Earl of Derby, for whom many of the pieces were first made.
a-catechism-of-christian-doctrine-no-3-f: Januarius De Concilio presents the third Baltimore catechism for post confirmation classes. Designed for a two year course, it adds prayers such as the Lord's Prayer, the Creed, and acts of faith, hope, love, and contrition. The volume was supplemented by Thomas Kinkead and published with ecclesiastical approval. It gives older pupils a fuller course in Catholic doctrine and prayer.
a-doll-s-house: Henrik Ibsen writes a doll's house drama of Nora and Torvald Helmer. The action takes place in their comfortable home, with Doctor Rank, Mrs. Linde, and Nils Krogstad among the visitors. Nora's secret debt and her husband's view of marriage drive the play. Ibsen's famous ending breaks the doll's house open and changed modern drama.
a-general-sketch-of-the-european-war-the: Hilaire Belloc sketches the European War in its first phase. The book first treats the general causes of the war, including the German object and the contrast with the wills of other nations. Prussia, Austria, particular causes, and the immediate occasion follow. Belloc then sets out the forces opposed and their geographical position.
a-legend-of-montrose:
Walter Scott set his novel during the Scottish civil wars of the 1640s, when the Marquis of Montrose raised the Highlands for the King. Scott's introduction says the tale centers on the sad fate of young Lord Kilpont and on James Stewart of Ardvoirlich, the man whose hand struck him down. Feuds between great families open the story.

The main text follows soldiers and Highlanders through camps and marches, with the talkative soldier Dugald Dalgetty among its best-loved figures. Appendices add Clan Alpin's Vow and The Children of the Mist, with Scott's notes. Battles, loyalty, and clan hatred drive a compact, stirring piece of Scottish history in fiction.
a-little-book-of-western-verse: Eugene Field gathers a little book of western verse and lullabies. Its pieces include Casey's table d'hote, Our Lady of the Mine, and lullabies English, Cornish, Norse, Sicilian, and Japanese. Field dedicates the book to a patient heart who fostered the author's child. The verses mix western humor with tender song.
a-set-of-rogues-namely-christopher-sutto: Frank Barrett tells the wicked conspiracy of a set of rogues: Christopher Sutton, John Dawson, Don Sanchez del Castillo de Castelaña, and Moll Dawson. The faithful confession of Sutton recounts stocks at Tottenham Cross, robbery at Edmonton, and Moll's marriage by sinful means to a worthy gentleman. Her fall and remorse lead to her sale to Algerine pirates into Barbary slavery. Through strange places and great sorrow, the rogues atone to Richard Godwin.
a-short-history-of-the-united-states-for: Edward Channing writes this short school history of the United States, with maps and illustrations, published in 1908. The contents run from discovery and exploration between 1000 and 1600 through colonization, a century of colonial history, and colonial union toward the war of independence. French colonists, Virginia and Maryland, New England, and New Netherland appear in turn, giving pupils a clear road from first landings to revolution.
a-virtuoso-s-collection-from-mosses-from: Nathaniel Hawthorne imagines a virtuoso's collection in this sketch from Mosses from an Old Manse, opening with a leisure hour and a small sign. Stepping into a new museum from the sunny sidewalk, the narrator mounts a sombre staircase. He meets a doorkeeper in an old-fashioned great-coat, wind-flushed and sunburnt. Three shillings Massachusetts tenor, or half a dollar as reckoned in these days, buys admittance to curiosities not quite in the ordinary way.
an-anthology-of-australian-verse:
Bertram Stevens edited this gathering of Australian poets, writing the introduction himself. The contents begin with William Charles Wentworth and Charles Harpur, early voices of the colony. They run through Sir Henry Parkes and Rolf Boldrewood. They end with Adam Lindsay Gordon, whose Sick Stock-rider became a bush classic. Henry Kendall's Leaves from Australian Forests and Songs from the Mountains appear in force.

The poems sing of drought, floods, horses, shearing sheds, and the strange light of the bush, beside love lyrics and city verse. Stevens aimed to show that a young country had already made a literature. The anthology served for years as the standard doorway into Australian poetry.
as-a-matter-of-course:
Annie Payson Call published As a Matter of Course in 1894 as a handbook for calming the nerves. Call, already known for Power Through Repose, aims to remove nervous irritants from daily life. Her preface says such irritants cause disease and spoil usefulness and pleasure. The governing image is a stone in the traveller's path.

Call argues that small obstacles should be stepped over as a matter of course, without fretting. Chapters treat physical care, amusements, brain impressions, and the triviality of trivialities. Others handle moods, tolerance, sympathy, children, and illness. She distinguishes sentiment from sentimentality near the close. The book belongs to the New Thought movement, which taught mental habits as a path to health, and it still reads as gentle, practical psychology.
at-the-villa-rose:
A. E. W. Mason's At the Villa Rose is a detective novel of the French Riviera and Geneva. Mr. Ricardo, a rich widower approaching fifty, takes his annual cure at Aix-les-Bains. He pretends to take the waters and plays baccarat at the Villa des Fleurs. Inspector Hanaud of the Paris Sûreté is holidaying nearby.

A cry for help draws Ricardo into the murder of Madame Dauvray at her villa. Her companion Celia disappears, and her maid Hélène Vauquier gives evidence. Chapters pursue an unopened letter, an aluminium flask, and a séance. Hanaud explains at the close, gathering the threads in Geneva and Aix. Mason writes polished fair-play detection, with Ricardo as the bewildered amateur beside the great detective. The novel helped define the country-house mystery between the wars of crime fiction.
autumn-leaves-original-pieces-in-prose-a:
Anne Wales Abbot edited this gift book of original prose and verse, published at Cambridge by John Bartlett in 1853. A note explains that the pieces, with two exceptions, were written for a private circle's entertainment, not for print. Shakespeare supplies the motto: our wits are so diversely coloured. The volume came from the press of Metcalf and Company, printers to the university.

Stories, poems, and sketches mix edification with humour. One tale replays a parish fight over church stoves. The fathers worshipped in the cold and scorned the enervating luxury. Then rheumatism disabled the bigots, and the degenerate descendants carried the day with shorter services. The humour is gentle and churchly throughout. Gift-book annuals like this one show how literary families entertained themselves, and each other, in print.
bees-in-amber-a-little-book-of-thoughtfu:
John Oxenham published this little book of thoughtful verse in 1913, dedicating it to those he held dearest as this of his best. Credo opens the contents, and the titles map a cheerful faith: Philosopher's Garden, The Potter, The Pruner, The Inn of Life, Life's Chequer-Board, and Don't Worry. Poems on Stephen and Paul, Gadara, and the Bells of Ys mix scripture scenes with daily counsel.

A sample stanza sorts mankind by purse and finds the poorest rich in happiness. The Prince of Life hymns Christ's tenderness running through life's remotest vein, tuning common rounds to loftier grace. Oxenham sold such verse by the hundred thousand to readers who wanted doctrine in singable form. Bees in Amber — small poems preserved like insects in resin — was his best-known collection.
boris-godunov-a-drama-in-verse:
Alexander Pushkin's Boris Godunov, rendered into English verse by Alfred Hayes, dramatizes Russia's time of troubles. The cast list names Boris, afterwards Tsar, with Princes Shuisky and Vorotinsky at his court. Father Pimen, an old monk and chronicler, keeps the record. Gregory Otrepiev, a young monk, will become the Pretender.

The play opens in the Kremlin palace in February 1598, as Boris hesitates to accept the crown. Pimen's cell reveals the murder of the Tsarevich Dimitry, the secret on which Boris's reign is built. Gregory flees to Poland, takes Dimitry's name, and wins Marina Mnishek's ambition. Armies, taverns, and battlefields carry the short scenes onward. Pushkin wrote in Shakespeare's chronicle manner, letting the people themselves judge their tsar. It remains Russia's great historical drama.
brentano-die-drei-nusse:
Three nuts, each holding a wonder and a test, drive Brentano's fairy tale Die drei Nuesse, given here in German. The hero's fortune turns on what the nuts conceal and when he dares to open them. Folk tradition supplies the bones; Brentano's Romantic richness supplies the flesh.

Small as the tale is, it shows a master working magic in the briefest compass. Wishes, dangers, and rewards arrive in classic fairy-tale rhythm. The German text lets readers savor his musical prose directly. Brentano could fill a paragraph with more enchantment than others manage in a chapter. The story makes a perfect short sample of his art for new readers.
britannica-1911-abruzzi-e-molise:
Abruzzi e Molise receives a regional entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The compartimento joins four provinces, Teramo, Aquila, Chieti, and Campobasso, along Italy's Adriatic side. Apennine heights fill the interior, crowned by the Gran Sasso, while a thin coastal strip fronts the sea.

Snow holds the high peaks much of the year, and north-east valleys run fertile under rivers like the Pescara and Sangro. Flood and landslip follow rain and reckless timber felling, though oak, beech, and pine woods still shelter wolves and boars. Flocks once ruled the economy, driven seasonally to the Roman Campagna; farming now grows, helped by the drained Fucino bed. Campobasso arms, Castelli majolica, and Pescara water power mark its industries. Some 1.44 million folk lived there in 1901.
britannica-1911-acerose: Acerose is a botanical term meaning needle-shaped, used since Linnaeus to describe leaves such as those of pines. This entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the word two possible Latin roots, one meaning a needle and another meaning sharp. It also warns of a trap: a separate word from a Latin term for chaff carries the distinct meaning mixed with chaff. Readers meeting acerose in plant descriptions should picture the pine needle, a leaf drawn out long, narrow, and pointed.
britannica-1911-addison-s-disease:
Addison's disease is the subject of a medical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The illness shows in darkened skin, deep weakness, an upset stomach and bowel, and a weak and uneven action of the heart. The cause is loss of work by the suprarenal glands, two small glands that sit above the kidneys. The article notes that the disease can occur with no change in skin colour.

Dr Thomas Addison of Guy's Hospital first set out the illness in a work of 1855. Sir Samuel Wilks pushed for its acceptance in England, and Brown-Sequard in France took up study of the glands. Later work on the ductless glands revived interest. Schafer and Oliver then showed that the glands make an inner secretion the body needs.
britannica-1911-almshouse: Two houses show what an almshouse is. The Hospital of St Cross, near Winchester, dates from 1136, and Coningsby Hospital at Hereford from 1614; both still stand. Each is a home built and funded by private charity, where poor people, usually old, could live. Most such houses went up after the Reformation, and these two stand as proof of England's long habit of endowed housing for the poor.
britannica-1911-anise:
Anise is an umbelliferous plant, Pimpinella Anisum. Egypt and the Levant are its home. European growers cultivate it for medicine. The fruit is the officinal part. Two united carpels form that fruit. Dried, it is sold as aniseed. Aniseed tastes strongly aromatic. Its odour is powerful too. Distillation yields a volatile oil from it.

That oil treats flatulence and colic. Children especially receive it as medicine. Water and spirit preparations carry different doses. Anethol forms up to ninety per cent of the oil. Most commercial oil actually comes from elsewhere, though. Star-anise, Illicium verum, supplies the bulk. That plant is native to north-east China. Liqueur makers prize its star-shaped fruit. The Bible's anise is actually dill. Matthew's verse uses the word for that herb.
britannica-1911-applause:
Applause is treated in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as praise shown first by the clap of hands. The word comes from a Latin verb for to strike on or clap. In wide use it means any sign of praise at all. The rite is as old and as broad as man kind, the entry holds.

Forms of praise noise are as wide as men can devise. Set rules still bound the rite in more than one age. The Romans had a set scale of praise for public shows. They snapped finger and thumb, or clapped with flat or cupped palm. They waved the flap of the gown as well. One emperor swapped that wave for a cloth given to all town folk. At the end of a play the lead called out a set plea. The crowd then sang praise led by a guide in the house.
britannica-1911-apse:
Apse is the subject of a building article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An apse is a half round recess covered with a half dome vault. The term also names the end of a choir, transept, or aisle of a church. Such an end may be half round or many sided in plan. A church that ends in an apse is called apsidal.

The article gives the earliest known apse to a temple at Rome from two years before Christ. The form became the favoured end for the rear of a temple. In law court halls the apse was screened off by columns and held the court of justice. In the first Christian churches at Rome the apse stood at the west end. In the eastern church it was built at the east end instead.
britannica-1911-bandelier-adolph-francis:
Adolph Francis Alphonse Bandelier (born 1840) was an American archaeologist, born at Bern, Switzerland, on 6 August 1840. He came to the United States as a youth. After 1880 he gave himself to archaeological and ethnological work among the Indians of the south-western United States, Mexico, and South America.

Starting in Sonora, Arizona, and New Mexico, Bandelier became the leading authority on that region's history and, with F. H. Cushing, on its early civilization. In 1892 he moved to Ecuador, Bolivia, and Peru. The 1911 Britannica entry praises his exposure of false historical myths, above all on the Inca civilization, and lists his studies of ancient Mexican warfare and of land holding and inheritance customs.
britannica-1911-base:
Base is a word with two separate roots, untangled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. One base, from a Latin word for low, is an adjective meaning low or mean, worthless or wicked. The other comes from a Greek word for stepping, and so a foundation. It names a starting point in many fields. Examples include a line on which a figure stands in geometry, a measured base line in surveying, and bases in hockey and baseball.

Chemistry and building get fuller treatment. In chemistry a base is a substance that combines with an acid to form a salt, turning red litmus blue and cancelling the acid's action. In architecture the base is the lowest member of a column. Its history runs from the raised slab that kept a wooden Greek or Egyptian column dry, through Assyrian moulded forms, to the high, richly carved bases of Persian building.
britannica-1911-benlliure-y-gil-jose:
José Benlliure y Gil (born 1858) was a Spanish painter born at Valencia. He studied under Domingo and showed such marked talent from the first that the state sent him to the Spanish school in Rome. There he joined the select circle of artists pensioned by the Spanish government for residence in Italy.

Benlliure carried out state orders for decorating public buildings in Spain. His chief fame, though, rests on large historical paintings, above all the “Vision in the Coliseum.” He became the leader of the Spanish art colony in Rome, working there as both painter and sculptor. The entry is a compact note on a state-backed career spent mostly in Italy.
britannica-1911-berceuse: Berceuse is the French word for a lullaby, drawn from berceau, a cradle. It names a cradle-song, the same thing German calls a Wiegenlied. As a musical term it covers a composed piece in that spirit, not just a song sung over a child. Its mark is the quiet rocking accompaniment beneath the tune, the gentle swing that imitates a cradle being rocked. The whole entry is that brief definition: the word’s root, its German twin, and the rocking motion that defines the form.
britannica-1911-bird-louse:
Bird-louse names a family of small parasitic insects found on birds and mammals. The 1911 Britannica entry calls them flat, degenerate, and wingless. They belong to the group Mallophaga among the nerve-winged insects. They feed on skin excretions and the softer parts of hair and feathers. The name biting-lice is also given to them at times. That name points to their chewing mouth-parts, which bite rather than suck.

Those jaws set them apart at once from the true lice. True lice, of the order Rhynchota, have sucking mouth-parts instead, the entry explains. The bird-louse note is a short glossary entry of a few lines. It gives the group's form, food, hosts, and the jaw test. No species or life habits are named in the text. The mouth-part distinction is its one firm teaching point.
britannica-1911-birds-of-paradise:
Birds of paradise are a group of perching birds from New Guinea and nearby islands. Dutch voyagers named them for their brilliant plumage. Old belief held that the birds had neither wings nor feet. They were said to live in the air on their plumes, sipping dew and flower nectar. Skins sold to traders lacked feet and wings, which fed the tale. Linnaeus named the chief species apoda, footless, as late as 1760.

The birds belong to the family Paradiseidae, close kin to the crows. The great emerald bird, about a jay's size, opens the survey. The 1911 Britannica article walks through species after species in detail. Velvet-like head feathers, ribbon tail plumes, and wire-like bristles all get described. The twelve-wired bird of Waigiu's red species closes the catalogue. Alfred Newton signs the long, richly illustrated piece.
britannica-1911-blank-verse:
Blank verse is unrhymed verse in lines of ten syllables and five beats, the standard measure of English epic and drama. Its name marks the missing rhyme the ear expects at each line end. The entry traces the line back to a Provençal poem of the 10th century and to Chaucer's use of it about 1370.

Rhyme was the rule everywhere until Italian poets dropped it in the early 1500s. Trissino's tragedy Sophonisba (1515) is named as the first finished work of the kind, and Rucellai's poem The Bees (1525) gave the form its Italian name, versi sciolti. Comedies by Ariosto and plays by Tasso and Guarini took it up before it passed into English, where its career proved longer and greater.
britannica-1911-blockhouse:
Blockhouse is a term of fort building explained in a short note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A blockhouse is a small roofed work that serves as a strong post for a small garrison. The word has been in use since about 1500, though its root is not sure. It once named a lone fort that blocks the way to a landing, a channel, a pass, or a bridge.

The modern form is a building of one or two floors, loopholed on all sides for fire. Some two-floor forms have a gallery at the top. They are built of wood, brick, stone, or iron sheet. In the South African War many were sent from England in ready-made parts.
britannica-1911-blouse: Blouse, a word taken from the French, is defined in a very short 1911 Britannica note. It names any loose fitting top garment belted at the waist. In France it first meant the loose upper dress of linen or cotton, most often blue, worn by French workmen to guard their own clothes. By a shift of sense, the word came to name the workman himself as well as his dress.
britannica-1911-boise:
Boisé, now Boise, is the capital of Idaho and the county seat of Ada county, standing on the north side of the Boisé river at about 2700 feet. Its growth was rapid: 2311 people in 1890, 5957 in 1900, and 17,358 in 1910. The Oregon Short Line and electric lines tied it to Nampa and Caldwell.

Chief buildings named are the state capitol, the federal building, a Carnegie library, and a swimming hall fed by hot artesian water at 175 degrees, which also heated many homes. The valley grew fine apples and prunes, and the city traded with a wide fruit, farm, and mining country. Settled in 1863 and chartered in 1864, it boomed after 1900 on great irrigation works.
britannica-1911-bonald-louis-gabriel-amb:
Louis Gabriel Ambroise de Bonald (1754–1840) was a French thinker and politician of the far conservative school. Born at Le Monna near Millau, he hated the Revolution's principles, emigrated in 1791, and joined the prince of Condé's army. Settled at Heidelberg, he wrote his Théorie du pouvoir politique et religieux (1796).

That book, highly conservative, was condemned by the Directory, and back in France he had to live quietly under suspicion. Later he helped run the Mercure de France with Chateaubriand and served the Imperial University he had often attacked. After the Restoration he sat as a deputy from 1815 to 1822, spoke for the extreme right, and even backed a censorship of literature. Made a peer, he lost the title in 1830 for refusing the oath.
britannica-1911-bonded-warehouse:
A bonded warehouse is a store, set up by the state or by private firms, where goods owing customs duty sit until the duty is paid. The entry first shows why the older way hurt trade. Before bonding, importers paid at once on landing or found sureties for later payment.

Sureties were hard to find, and men were forced into quick sales at bad prices just to raise the duty. Paying in a lump also raised prices by the interest on the capital, and only rich houses could import heavily taxed goods at all. Walpole's excise scheme of 1733 proposed warehousing for tobacco and wine to cure these ills and check fraud. The history of the system in Britain and its rules fill the pages that follow.
britannica-1911-borghese:
Borghese is a noble Italian family from Siena, first mentioned in 1238, that rose to the top of Roman society. Marcantonio Borghese settled in Rome and fathered Camillo Borghese, who became Pope Paul V in 1605. The pope made his nephew prince of Vivaro in 1609, and Spain added the title of prince of Sulmona in 1610.

The family's place among the great Roman houses was sealed in 1614 when the prince's son Paolo married Olimpia Aldobrandini, heiress of her house. In 1803 Camillo Filippo Ludovico Borghese married Pauline, Napoleon's sister and General Leclerc's widow, and was made duke of Guastalla in 1806. The Borghese palace in Rome is praised as one of the city's grandest buildings, and its picture gallery was largely moved to the Villa Borghese.
britannica-1911-brighouse:
Brighouse is a borough in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, 5 and a half miles north of Huddersfield by the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway, set on the river Calder.
