It held 21,735 people in 1901 and covers 2231 acres. Rule rests with a mayor, 8 aldermen and 24 councillors, and the town was incorporated only in 1893.

Work is the town's story: it sits in the heart of the West Riding factory district. Large woollen and worsted mills lead its trades, with carpets, machinery and soap also made in quantity. The short notice gives place, growth and industry in compact form. Its late borough charter, big population and cluster of heavy trades mark how fast such Calder valley mill towns grew in the 19th century.
britannica-1911-bright-s-disease:
Bright's disease is a medical label for a class of kidney diseases, acute and chronic nephritis, whose clearest sign is albumen in the urine, often with dropsy beside it. The pairing of those signs with kidney trouble was first described in 1827 by Dr Richard Bright (1789–1858), whose name the term keeps in his honour.

Later study showed the signs spring not from one kidney disease but from many, so the name must be read in a broad, generic sense. Attacks are often severe: pain in the back, vomiting and fever open the illness. Dropsy can range from slight puffiness of the face to fluid swelling that burdens the whole body and hinders breathing. The urine falls in amount, turns dark, smoky or bloody, and under test and microscope shows much albumen, blood cells and casts.
britannica-1911-cadamosto-alvise:
Alvise Cadamosto is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1432, he was a Venetian explorer, sea captain, and writer. He is famed for his voyages to West Africa in the service of Portugal.

The article tells how chance put him on that path. In 1454 he sailed from Venice for Flanders but was held by bad winds off Cape Saint Vincent. There Prince Henry the Navigator took him into his band of explorers. In March 1455 he sailed south in command of a ship. He viewed the Madeira and Canary isles and coasted the West Sahara. At the Senegal and the Gambia he wrote of lands, tribes, and trade in rich detail. A second voyage in 1456 found the Cape Verde isles by chance.
britannica-1911-caisson-disease:
Caisson disease is the illness that can strike men who work under squeezed air. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ties it to bridge and tunnel work under water. Air inside a work chamber must push back the water above it. At a depth of one hundred feet, that push reaches four times the push of open air. Men who come out of such air too fast can fall ill.

The signs range wide, the entry says. They include pains in the joints known as the bends. Loss of hearing, hard breath, and fits of palsy also occur. In bad cases men faint or even die. At the St Louis bridge works, 119 of 600 men fell ill and 14 died. The cause, by the view then held, was gas freed in the blood. Nitrogen soaks into body fluids under high push. It bubbles out when the push drops fast.
britannica-1911-case:
Case is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word with several senses in grammar and law. All of them trace to the Latin casus, that which falls or happens. In grammar, the cases are the forms a noun takes in declension. The Latin word renders the Greek ptosis, falling. Aristotle applied it to variations from a word's simple form. Later grammarians narrowed the term to nouns and counted the nominative among the cases.

In law, a case is a cause or suit before a court. The entry sets out the special uses one by one. An action on the case seeks damages for an indirect injury. A case stated sends facts from one court to another for an opinion on the law. A special case does the same by agreement of the parties. A leading case settles a point of importance.
britannica-1911-chasse: Chasse is a very short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, a single sentence long. The word is French for “chased.” It names a gliding step in dancing. The step takes its name from its motion, since one foot is brought up behind the other, as if chasing it. The entry adds one variety: the chassé croisé, which it calls a double variety of the step.
britannica-1911-cheese:
Cheese is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a solidified preparation from milk, from the Latin caseus. Its essential constituent is casein, the protein substance of milk. All cheese also holds some fatty matter or butter. In the finer varieties the butter often outweighs the casein. Since cheese has no fixed composition, it comes in many varieties and qualities. These are generally known by the names of the places where they are made.

The main differences come from the milk itself, from the method of making and curing, and from the animal used. Goat's and ewe's milk cheeses are made on a commercial scale, beside cow's milk. The entry sends readers to the article on Dairy for the kinds and the making. It ends with slang: “the cheese,” meaning the perfect thing, from the Urdu chiz, “thing,” by Anglo Indian usage. A cited American bulletin of 1908 sums up the varieties.
britannica-1911-choriambic-verse:
Choriambic verse, a Greek song measure, is scanned in a verse entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its beat rests on the choriambus, a foot of four beats. That foot joins a trochee first and an iambus after it. Choriambs never stand alone as a full line of verse. A spondee goes before them and an iambus after in the line.

The line so built is called an asclepiad by custom. Tales credit Asclepiades of Samos with the making of that line. Poets of the Greek isles first took the measure up in song. Sappho drew grand effects from it in her lyric verse. Mixed with other measures it served the chorus well in plays. Men held it gave song a wild and strange air.
britannica-1911-chose:
Chose is a French word for thing, used as a term in English law in more than one sense. A chose local is a thing fixed to a place, as a mill is. A chose transitory is a thing that can be moved from place to place. Those two uses are now in effect dead. The word lives on in two phrases: chose in action and chose in possession.

A chose in action, in its strict sense, is the right to enforce a claim by suit at law. The claim may be for the pay of a debt or for money for a breach of contract. In loose speech the money itself, or the paper that proves the right, is at times called by the same name. In strict terms only the right can bear it.
britannica-1911-chrysoprase:
Chrysoprase is an apple green kind of chalcedony used as a jewel stone. Its stone entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its Greek name joins words for gold and for leek, a green plant. The green hue comes from nickel held in a water borne form.

Heat or strong light can fade the stone to pale or clear tones. Damp air can bring the green hue back to the stone again. Most supply comes from near Frankenstein in Silesia, with serpentine rock. Small amounts occur in the Urals, in India, and in North America. The entry warns that the old stone of Pliny was not the same gem.
britannica-1911-clavijo-y-fajardo-jose:
Jose Clavijo y Fajardo lived from 1730 to 1806 and was a Spanish publicist. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Lanzarote in the Canary Islands. He settled in Madrid and took the helm of El Pensador there. His drive against the public playing of autos sacramentales bore fruit at last. Those old sacred plays were banned from the stage in 1765.

In 1770 he took charge of the royal theatres of the realm. He left that post to edit the Mercurio historico y politico of Madrid. At his death he was secretary to the Cabinet of Natural History. The entry praises his courage, his grit, and his sharp gift of phrase. His love affair with a sister of Beaumarchais fed Goethe's first print work.
britannica-1911-clearing-house:
Clearing-house is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term names a central office used by large linked trades to make the settling of accounts easy. The entry takes banking as its case. The London Clearing-House was set up between 1750 and 1770. There the clerks of the city bankers could meet each day to swap the cheques and bills drawn on each other's houses.

The article shows what a waste the old way was. Before it, each banker had to send a clerk to every other bank in London to collect what was owed. That ate time, used more cash than the work needed, and put money at risk on the road. In 1775 a room was fixed as the common centre of exchange. At first only the private bankers of the city took part.
britannica-1911-clonmacnoise:
Clonmacnoise is one of the most noteworthy early religious settlements in Ireland, on the river Shannon in King's County, nine miles south of Athlone. Saint Kieran founded an abbey here in 541, which as a seat of learning gained European fame. Offerings came, for example, from Charles the Great, whose companion Alcuin was partly educated by the teacher Colcu here. Several books of annals were compiled at the foundation, which became the seat of a bishopric.

The English plundered and wasted it in 1552, and in 1568 the diocese was united with that of Meath. Its most remarkable literary monument is the Book of the Dun Cow, written about 1100 and preserved by the Royal Irish Academy. That book holds a large number of romances, copied from an original on the skin of Saint Kieran's favourite cow. Remains of all seven churches stand, with two round towers.
britannica-1911-close:
Close, from the Latin clausum, shut, is a closed place or enclosure, and the entry sets out its senses in law, building and common speech. In English law the term applies to a portion of land, enclosed or not, held as private property. It also covers any exclusive interest in land sufficient to maintain an action for trespass, quare clausum fregit. In Scotland the word names the entry or passage, with the common staircase, of tenement houses.

In architecture a close means the precincts of a cathedral or an abbey, a shut precinct around a great church. The adjective close, meaning closed, appears in phrases such as close time or close season in the game laws. Close borough, close rolls and close writs name other shut or limited things. From closed up and confined comes the common meaning of near, the entry concludes.
britannica-1911-colet-louise:
Louise Colet, a French poet and novelist who lived from 1810 to 1876, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Aix in September 1810, she came from a Provençal family named Revoil. In 1835 she moved to Paris with her husband Hippolyte Colet. He was a composer and a teacher of harmony at the conservatoire. Her first book, a volume of verse, came out in 1836.

More verse, a one-act comedy, novels, and poems followed in quick order. Her works won prizes from the Institute five or six times. The article says she owed that honour more to Victor Cousin's influence than to the worth of her work. Criticism of the prizes stung her into public quarrels. She also faced a suit over letters she had published. She is best known now for her close ties to famous men of her time, among them Flaubert.
britannica-1911-common-lodging-house:
A common lodging house, in English law, is a house where poorer persons are taken in for gain. Its inmates share one or more rooms in common, for eating or for sleeping. They are not members of one family in such a house. No statute defines the class of houses covered by the term. A judge made definition from a case of eighteen seventy seven is widely taken as sound.

Such houses must be registered and inspected under the Public Health Acts. Each district council must keep registers of keepers and houses in its area. The lists show where each house stands and how many lodgers it may take. Councils may require a notice on the outside of the house. They may make rules on numbers, on split sleeping by sex, and on cleanliness. Rules also cover fresh air and steps to take in sickness.
britannica-1911-contat-louise-francoise:
Louise Francoise Contat, a French actress who lived from 1760 to 1813, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. She made her first appearance at the Comedie Francaise in 1766, as Atalide in a tragedy by Racine. It was in comedy, though, that she won her first success. That came as Suzanne in the Marriage of Figaro by Beaumarchais.

The entry says she raised several small character parts to the first rank. As the soubrette in the plays of Moliere and Marivaux she found roles exactly fitted to her gifts. A soubrette is a lively maid part in comedy, played with wit and charm. She retired from the stage in 1809 and married a nephew of the poet Parny. Her sister was also an actress of note.
britannica-1911-corpse:
Corpse is a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It states the rules of English law for a dead human body. A corpse is not goods in law, and it cannot hold goods of its own. For that cause the theft of a corpse is not theft in the strict sense.

The entry lists crimes tied to the dead that do count in law. It is wrong to block a burial, to dig up a body with no right, or to show it bare in public. Kin and friends must see to a due burial if they can. If none can act, the parish must take up the duty. A corpse cannot be seized or held for a debt.
britannica-1911-cremieux-isaac-moise:
Isaac Moise Cremieux, known as Adolphe, was a French statesman in this 1911 Britannica life. Born at Nimes in seventeen ninety six, he came of a rich Jewish house. He began as a court speaker in his home town in the south. After the revolt of eighteen thirty he moved to Paris for work. There he won fame as a bright voice for free thought.

He won a diet seat in eighteen forty two and led the fight on a weak rule team. In eighteen forty eight he took the post of law chief in a short rule. Death for state crimes fell by his hand in that post. Jail in eighteen fifty one cut his path for near two years. He came back late in life and won votes for Jews in Algeria.
britannica-1911-crevasse: Crevasse, a French word, is defined in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, with two senses. In French Switzerland, and from there in all high mountain lands, it names a crack in a glacier. Such cracks can run very deep, and climbers often fall in through a light bridge of snow that hides the gap. In its second sense, taken from the French of Louisiana, it names a breach in the bank of a canal or river, above all in the levee of the Mississippi.
britannica-1911-custom-house:
Custom-house names the house or office set by a state for duties on goods, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. There taxes on imports and exports are gathered. Duties, bounties, and drawbacks due on trade in or out are paid or received at the same place. Ships are also entered and cleared there.

In the United Kingdom a custom-house stands at each port or harbour with much shipping. The officer in charge bears the title collector of customs. In the minor ports the officer goes by other names. He may be called superintendent of customs or principal coast officer. The short entry gives a clear base for how trade was taxed and checked at the ports.
britannica-1911-daudet-alphonse:
Alphonse Daudet was a French novelist who lived from eighteen forty to eighteen ninety seven. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Nimes, of a middle class family on both sides in France. His father Vincent was a silk maker dogged by failure all life.

Daudet boyhood was grim, with much truancy from school at Lyons. In eighteen fifty six he left school and worked as an usher at Alais. That post proved so harsh he fled it in eighteen fifty seven. He joined his brother Ernest in Paris and took to the pen. Poems, plays, and Figaro work soon marked him as a voice of promise.
britannica-1911-demise:
Demise is an Anglo-French legal term, from words meaning to send away, for the transfer of an estate, above all by lease. In a lease the word carries force of its own, implying a covenant for quiet enjoyment. The entry points to the landlord and tenant article for that working of the term, and treats demise as a word of transfer rather than of ending.

The phrase demise of the crown names the instant passing of sovereignty to the successor, with no gap between reigns, under the maxim that the king never dies. At common law the sovereign's death dissolved parliament and ended crown offices. The Representation of the People Act 1867 and the Demise of the Crown Act 1901 removed both effects. The word is now often used loosely for death itself.
britannica-1911-esquiros-henri-francois-:
Henri Francois Alphonse Esquiros is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Esquiros was a French writer, born in Paris in 1812. After minor works he published The Gospel of the People in 1840. That book presented Jesus as a social reformer.

The work was judged an offence against religion and decency. Esquiros was fined and sent to prison for it. In 1850 voters sent him, as a social democrat, to the Legislative Assembly. The next year his stand against the Empire drove him into exile. He returned in 1869 and sat in the Assembly again, then entered the senate in 1876. His years in England bore fruit in a five-volume study of English life. The entry lists his many works on social questions, from a history of the Montagnards onward.
britannica-1911-euclase:
Euclase is a very rare mineral, now and then cut as a cabinet gem-stone. It is a silicate of beryllium and aluminium that also holds hydrogen. The analyses give the formula HBeAlSiO5. It crystallizes in the monoclinic system, usually as prismatic crystals striped lengthwise. Its cleavage is perfect along one plane. Haüy coined the name from Greek words for easily and fracture.

That easy cleavage makes the stone fragile and prone to chip, which spoils it for wear. Its colour is generally pale blue or green, sometimes none at all. Cut, it resembles aquamarine or topaz, but its specific gravity of 3.1 sets it apart. Its hardness, 7.5, falls a little below topaz. It occurs with topaz at Boa Vista near Ouro Preto in Brazil. It also turns up in the gold gravels of the Sanarka river in the South Urals, and rarely in Austrian mica-schist.
britannica-1911-excise:
Excise is a duty charged on home goods, either during manufacture or before sale to home buyers. Such a tax needs a commonwealth with manufactures and markets already grown. It presses so directly on industry and liberty that states seldom levy it except in dire financial need. Rome had a mild forerunner, the toll on goods sold at auction or market. Augustus imposed it at 1 per cent, Tiberius halved it, and Caligula abolished it in A.D. 38.

Britain's excise dates from the civil wars, when the republican government copied Holland. The restored royalists kept the duties despite their origin and unpopularity. The first goods taxed were malt liquors, cider, perry and spruce beer. Later the surviving duties shrank mostly to licences: game, guns, plate sellers, auctioneers, pawnbrokers. The railway passenger duty, made excise in 1847, takes 2 per cent on town fares and 5 per cent elsewhere.
britannica-1911-falaise:
Falaise is a town in north western France, in Calvados, on the Ante river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it south of Caen by road. Its people passed six thousand in 1906 by the count given. A castle on a high crag above the town draws most interest there.

That castle was the seat of the dukes of Normandy in old times. William the Conqueror was born within its walls, the entry notes. A bronze horse statue in town honors him for its growth. Churches mix Gothic and later styles, with older work in one. Tanning and hosiery making form its chief trades in that day.
britannica-1911-farnese:
Farnese is the name of a great Italian family that ruled the duchy of Parma for two centuries. They appear first as lords of Farneto or Farnese, a castle near the lake of Bolsena. As consuls and signori of Orvieto they stood with the Guelph Monaldeschi against the Ghibelline Filippeschi. One Pietro Farnese led the papal armies under Paschal II. Another Pietro beat the Pisans for Florence in 1363.

The family's rise dates from Alexander VI, lover of Giulia Farnese, called Giulia Bella. He made her brother Alessandro a cardinal in 1493. Alessandro became Pope Paul III in 1534 and showered fiefs on his natural children. Pierluigi, the most famous, took the duchy of Castro, then Parma and Piacenza in 1545. His cruel, tyrannical rule stripped the nobles of privilege. The entry follows the house through its later dukes to the Palazzo Farnese in Rome.
britannica-1911-felo-de-se:
Felo de se, the old legal name for self-murder, gets a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term means one who is a felon against himself. The rules of murder set the bounds of the charge. A man who dies by his own unlawful act counts, the entry says. So does one who shoots at a foe and is killed when the gun bursts.

Old law gave such a corpse a shameful burial by the highway. A stake was driven through the body at the grave. An act of 1823 ended that rite and set a night burial instead. An act of 1882 let the body rest in a parish burial ground. Goods could once be seized by the crown, but that loss ended in 1870.
britannica-1911-foot-and-mouth-disease:
Foot-and-mouth disease, also called aphthous fever or epizootic aphtha, is a virulent contagious malady of animals that can be passed by inoculation. It is marked by a first fever, then by vesicles or blisters. They form on the tongue, palate and lips of cattle, sometimes in the nostrils and the gut. They also appear where the skin is thin: on the udder, between the claws, and on the heels and pastern.

The disease begins suddenly and spreads very fast. Fever comes before the blisters, with heavy salivation and a peculiar smacking of the lips. The blisters grow and break, leaving red raw patches that are very sore. The animal cannot feed well, loses condition, gives less milk, or may abort if pregnant. Lameness is a constant sign. The article goes on to the course of outbreaks, their spread between herds, and the measures used against them.
britannica-1911-freire-francisco-jose:
Francisco José Freire (1719-1773), Portuguese historian and scholar of language, was born at Lisbon on 3 January 1719. He belonged to the monastic society of St Philip Neri and to the Academy of Arcadians, where he wrote under the name Candido Lusitano. He did much to improve the style of Portuguese prose, though his bid to reform national poetry through a rendering of Horace Ars poëtica fared less well.

His Maximas sobre a Arte Oratoria of 1745 attacked the poor taste of current prose and opened with a table that forms almost a social history of Portugal. His best-known work, the Vida do Infante D. Henrique of 1758, placed him in the first rank of Portuguese historians and was translated into French. He also made a poetical dictionary, translated Racine Athalie, and left reflections on the Portuguese tongue printed long after his death at Mafra in 1773.
britannica-1911-glucose:
Glucose takes its name from a Greek word for sweet, and it is a sugar with a known makeup. In trade the name covers a mixed set of sugars made by boiling starch with weak acids. In chemistry it names one clear compound, in right turning, left turning, and inactive forms. The right turning form is by far the most common in nature. Its other names are dextrose, grape sugar, and diabetic sugar.

Those names point to its twist of light, its wealth in grapes, and its place in diabetic urine. In the plant world glucose occurs with fructose in many fruits. Grapes, cherries, and bananas are named in the entry. Joined with other groups it forms a large class called glucosides. Plants seem to build it from carbon dioxide and water. In the plant it turns freely into more complex sugars.
britannica-1911-golden-rose:
Golden Rose is the name of a gold ornament blessed by the pope, as set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is wrought in gold and set with gems, most often sapphires. The pope blesses it on the fourth Sunday of Lent. It is then sent as a mark of high favour to a person, a church, or a town.

At first it was one plain rose in red gold, but in time it took the form of a thorny branch. Leaves, blooms, and one chief rose crown the stem, all decked with gems. The custom may go back to the 11th century, though its start is not clear. Popes sent roses to kings of England and Scotland and to towns such as Lucca, and from the 1500s a letter went with each gift to state why it was sent.
britannica-1911-grains-of-paradise:
Grains of Paradise is a plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes the hot seeds of a reed like plant from west Africa. The plant bears large pale blooms and a red fruit when fresh. Its seeds sit in sour pulp inside that fruit pod.

The entry gives the size, shape, and shell of the ripe seeds in detail. Tests found a small share of scented oil and a strong hot resin in them. The seeds saw use in old drug books of Britain in past ages. From the thirteenth century on they served as a spice and a drug. The plant grows wild on isles in the gulf and is raised in other hot lands.
britannica-1911-hearse:
Hearse now names a vehicle for carrying a dead body. The usual shape is a four-wheeled car. Its body is roofed, enclosed and sometimes glass-panelled. The coffin rides inside that body. The word adapts the French herse, a harrow. Latin hirpex, a rake or harrow, lies behind it. Earlier English herse meant simply a harrow. Resemblance carried the name to other objects.

A portcullis took the name, and heraldry followed. Funeral objects, though, gave the word its main history. A hearse was first a frame over a bier. It held lighted tapers and decorations. Royal funerals raised it into an elaborate pagoda of woodwork. Banners, candles and armorial bearings crowded it. Inigo Jones designed one for James I. Permanent iron hearses still stand over some tombs. The Beauchamp Chapel at Warwick holds a brass one.
britannica-1911-heroic-verse:
Heroic Verse, in the 1911 Britannica, is a study of a verse form whose meaning shifts by tongue. In old Greek and Latin works the term meant the dactylic hexameter, the line of the Iliad and the Aeneid. In English it means the rhymed iambic line joined as a heroic couplet. One line of ten syllables is not enough, since that would wrongly class blank verse with it.

The entry faults Dryden for a loose line on the form and sets it right. In French the alexandrine holds the same place. Chaucer is named as the first English user, in his Legend of Good Women and the Canterbury Tales. His heirs let the form lapse, but Blind Harry kept it alive in Scotland. Gavin Douglas used it for his Aeneid version of 1513 with great skill. The couplet is the true unit.
britannica-1911-jebb-sir-richard-claverh:
Richard Claverhouse Jebb, an English classical scholar who lived from 1841 to 1905, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Dundee, he was the son of a noted barrister and grandson of a judge. He was educated at Charterhouse and at Trinity College, Cambridge. There he won famed scholarships and placed first in classics in 1862.

He became fellow and tutor of his college in 1863, the entry says. He served as public orator of the university for six years. Then he held the Greek chair at Glasgow from 1875 and at Cambridge from 1889 until his death. In 1891 he was elected to Parliament for the university, and he was knighted in 1900. The article calls him one of the most brilliant classical scholars of his time.
britannica-1911-kermesse:
A kermesse, also spelled kermis and kirmess, was at first the mass said on the anniversary of a church's founding and in honour of its patron. The word is the same as Kirkmass. Such feasts were held as a rule in the Low Countries and in northern France, and they came with feasting, dancing, and sports of all kinds.

They still survive, but now they are little more than country fairs, and the old symbolic shows are rare. The Brussels kermesse is still marked by a procession in which the figures of the Mannikin and of medieval heroes are carried. At Mons the feast falls each year on Trinity Sunday and is called the procession of Lumeçon. Its hero is Gilles de Chin, who slays a dreadful monster, the captor of a princess, in the Grand Place. The tale is that of George and the Dragon in local dress.
britannica-1911-lighthouse:
Lighthouse, a tower built to carry a guiding light, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its work is to warn or guide, above all at sea. The article opens with the early history of such towers. The first on record stood in Lower Egypt, raised by Libyans and Cushites.

Priests kept beacon fires burning in some of those early towers. A Greek poet names a lighthouse at Sigeum in the Troad. That light seems the first kept burning steadily for sailors. The famous Pharos of Alexandria followed, built under Ptolemy the Second. Men counted it among the wonders of the world. Its island home gave all later lighthouses their common name of pharos. An earthquake destroyed it in time. Roman towers at Ostia, Ravenna, and Dover carry the story westward. The tower of Cordouan, on a sea rock off France, is the oldest wave-swept light still standing.
britannica-1911-manganese:
The 1911 Britannica article on manganese treats a metallic element, symbol Mn. Its dioxide, pyrolusite, was known from early times. It was long mistaken for an iron ore. Pott showed in 1740 that the mineral held no iron. Scheele proved in 1774 that it was the oxide of a distinct metal.

The article covers where manganese occurs in nature. It appears in ores such as braunite and hausmannite. It is found even in sea water. The article then gives the many ways the metal was prepared. Gahn first isolated it in 1774. Later workers used the electric furnace and the thermite method. The metal is used in special steels.
britannica-1911-manse: Manse is a short word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, from a medieval Latin term for a dwelling. At first it meant a house with land enough to feed one family. In church law it named the house and glebe that every church held by common right, free of all service. The word now serves chiefly for the home of a Church of Scotland minister, which the landed owners of a rural parish must build and keep up.
britannica-1911-marchena-ruiz-de-castro-:
José Marchena Ruiz de Castro, a Spanish author who lived from 1768 to about 1821, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Utrera in November 1768. He studied with distinction at the university of Seville. He took minor orders and taught for a time at the seminary of Vergara.

He became a convert to the doctrines of the French philosophes. He shocked his acquaintances with his professions of materialism. He also denounced celibacy in plain terms. His writings were brought before the Inquisition in 1792. Marchena escaped to Paris. There, it is said, he worked with Marat on a revolutionary paper. At a later date he raised a revolutionary movement at Bayonne. Back in Paris, he declared his sympathy with the Girondists. He refused the advances of Robespierre. The article shows a church-trained scholar turned rebel in two lands.
britannica-1911-marie-amelie-therese:
Marie Amelie Therese was queen of the French as wife of their king, and lived from seventeen eighty-two to eighteen sixty-six. She was born at Caserta, child of the king of Naples. A strict school fed her pious and just bent, which won her a home name that means the saint. War drove her folk to flight twice in her youth.

In exile at Palermo she met the duke she wed in eighteen nine. Back in France, fresh exile drove her to England with her young. As queen past the change of eighteen thirty she took no part in state craft. Her care was her large brood.
britannica-1911-marie-louise:
Marie Louise (1791-1847), second wife of Napoleon the First, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Francis the First, emperor of Austria, and was born in December 1791. The entry describes a fresh and natural temper, but one lacking the traits that make for greatness. Nothing in her youth promised high place.

Reasons of state changed that. Soon after Napoleon divorced Josephine, he sought the Austrian princess in marriage. The idea may first have come in secret from the Austrian chancellor Metternich. The plan was warmly taken up in Paris, and the hitches over the divorce were cleared to suit both sides. The wedding took place by proxy in a Vienna church in March 1810. The new empress was escorted into France by Queen Caroline Murat, whom she soon learned to distrust.
britannica-1911-marie-therese:
Marie Therese, queen wife of Louis the Fourteenth of France, gets a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at the Escurial in sixteen thirty eight, she was a child of Philip the Fourth of Spain. A peace pact of sixteen fifty nine set her marriage to the French king. She gave up all claim to the throne of Spain in that pact. Her dowry was due as the price of the deal.

She wed Louis in June of sixteen sixty at a meet on an isle. Her soft ways and true faith could not hold his heart, the text says. He turned to a string of mistresses at court in plain sight. She bore his scorn in still faith and gave him no fight. But one of her six children lived past her death in sixteen eighty three.
britannica-1911-markham-gervase:
Gervase Markham, an English poet and writer on many topics, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born probably in fifteen sixty eight, he was a son of Sir Robert Markham of Cotham. He served as a soldier of fortune in the Low Countries. Later he was a captain under the earl of Essex in Ireland.

He knew Latin and several modern tongues, the entry notes. He also had deep practical knowledge of forestry and farming. He was a noted breeder of horses and is said to have imported the first Arab horse. Very little is known of the events of his life, the entry admits.
britannica-1911-marti-juan-jose:
Juan José Martí, a Spanish tale thief, is caught in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Orihuela about 1570, he took law degrees at Valencia. By 1598 he held a post as examiner in church law there. Six years he kept that post, till his death in 1604. He joined a night club of letter men in that city.

Martí is best known by a false name on a false book. As Mateo Luján he put out a fake next part in 1602. It claimed to go on from Alemán's famed Guzmán tale of 1599. He had seen that man's draft and stole thoughts from its pages. Alemán's true next part mocked the theft with sly praise in print. Some have linked Martí to the fake Quixote tale of 1614.
britannica-1911-meniere-s-disease:
Ménière's disease is a form of giddiness tied to the ear. A French doctor, Emile Antoine Ménière, first set it out in 1861. It most often strikes men and women of middle age whose hearing was sound before. Politzer lists as its chief causes great heat and time in the sun. Other causes named are rheumatism, flu, and a lack of blood. The disease takes more than one form as it shows itself.

The most common form comes from a bleed into the labyrinth of the ear. It is followed by a loss of hearing in one or both ears, in full or in part. An attack starts with giddiness, noises in the ears, and a sick stomach. The gait staggers, and the man may fall down with a loss of sense. The fits come at odd gaps of days or weeks.
britannica-1911-michel-clemence-louise:
Clémence Louise Michel (died 1905) was a French anarchist called the Red Virgin of Montmartre, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells her story. She was born at the château of Vroncourt, the daughter of a serving-maid and the son of the house. Raised by her father's parents, she got a free and full education. She trained as a teacher but refused to own Napoleon the Third, which barred her from state schools.

In 1866 she found her way to a school in the Montmartre quarter of Paris. There she threw herself into works of charity and into revolutionary politics, turning fiercely against the Bonapartes. Under the Commune she joined the National Guard. She offered to shoot Thiers and made her last stand with the Communards in the Montmartre cemetery.
britannica-1911-mignot-claudine-francois:
Claudine Francoise Mignot was born about 1617 and died in 1711. The 1911 Britannica life calls her, in plain terms, a French adventuress. She was born at Meylan near Grenoble, of humble stock and place. At age sixteen her looks caught the eye of a treasurer's aide. That treasurer wed the girl himself in the end and took her home.

He left her his fortune, which his kin then fought in court. In 1653 she went to Paris to secure her rights by law. There she sought the shield of Marshal de l'Hopital, aged seventy five. He wed her within a week, and left her part of his estate. A third match with a former king of Poland brought a third fortune.
britannica-1911-mise: Mise is an Anglo-French term for the settling of accounts or disputes by deal or by an umpire, as the 1911 Britannica entry explains. In English law it named the point at stake in a writ of right. In history it named the payment made for set rights by the county palatine of Chester to each new earl. The Welsh made such payment to each new lord of the Marches. Two famed cases are the Mise of Amiens and the Mise of Lewes, both from 1264.
britannica-1911-monrose: Monrose (1783-1843), a French actor whose real name was Claude Louis Seraphin Barizain, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Besancon, he was playing children's parts at the time of the Revolution. He joined the national theatre of France in 1815 and became a full member two years later. Small and quick, with a mobile face, he was famed as the rascally servant in plays such as The Barber of Seville. His son was also an actor under the same name.
britannica-1911-mora-jose: José Mora was a Spanish sculptor who lived from 1638 to 1725. The short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls him a pupil of Alonso Cano. He died at Granada in 1725 and was buried in the Albaicín church there. His work can be studied in eight statues in a cardinal's chapel in Córdoba Cathedral. Two more figures, of Saint Bruno and Saint Joseph, stand in the Cartuja near Granada.
britannica-1911-mortise: Mortise is a term for a socket or hole cut in a piece of wood or other stuff, shaped to receive a matching peg end called a tenon. Its brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica notes the word came through French forms, while its first origin is unknown. When tenon and mortise are fitted together they form a mortise joint. That joint serves to fasten two beams or other pieces of timber firmly together in building and craft work.
britannica-1911-odense:
Odense, a city of Denmark, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the chief town of the county of its name, in the north of the island of Funen. The entry gives it 40,138 people in 1901. The city lies four miles from Odense Fjord, on the Odense Aa stream, most of it on the north side.

A canal gives the town access from the fjord, and a railway route links it toward Copenhagen and Jutland. Saint Canute's cathedral, once tied to a great Benedictine monastery, is one of the largest and finest buildings of its kind in Denmark. It is built of brick in a pure Gothic style and was rebuilt in the thirteenth century. Under its altar lies Canute, patron saint of Denmark, slain at Odense in 1086. Kings John and Christian the Second are also buried within its walls.
britannica-1911-parclose: Parclose is a term of architecture for a screen or railing in a church, as a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records. The word comes from an Old French verb meaning to close thoroughly. A parclose shuts off a chantry, a tomb, or a chapel from the rest of the church. The term also names the space thus shut in. Church builders used such screens to give a tomb or chapel a room of its own.
britannica-1911-pare-ambroise:
Ambroise Pare is the subject of a short life note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French surgeon who lived from 1510 to 1590. He was born at Laval, in the province of Maine, and died at Paris.

The note is brief because his career is told in full under the heading Surgery. What it gives here is the record of his books. A set of his works came out at Paris in 1575 and was reprinted many times. Versions in German and Dutch followed in due course. An English version by Thomas Johnson came out in 1665. The piece ends with a list of lives of Pare in French and English. One French set of his full works, printed in 1840, is named first.
britannica-1911-paul-veronese:
Paul Veronese, who lived from 1528 to 1588, was a painter of the Venetian school, born Paolo Caliari. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born in Verona, in 1528 by some accounts and in 1532 by others. His father was a sculptor who set him to learn that craft. The boy showed more gift for paint, so he went to his uncle, the painter Antonio Badile. In time he wed his uncle's daughter.

Young Paolo copied prints by Dürer and drew from the works of Parmigiano. Work in Verona was scarce, so he painted with a partner in the lands of Vicenza and Treviso. A cardinal took him to Mantua at about the age of twenty, where he beat rivals on a cathedral piece. He then moved to Venice. His church work there in 1555 won such praise that he ranked near Tintoretto.
britannica-1911-peltier-jean-charles-ath:
Jean Charles Athanase Peltier, a French physicist who lived from 1785 to 1845, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Ham, in the Somme, in February 1785. He was a watchmaker at first by trade. About the age of thirty he left business and gave himself to the study of nature by test and observation.

His many papers deal chiefly with air electricity, waterspouts, and the colour of the sky. He also worked on the heat of water in the spheroidal state and on boiling points at great heights. His name lives on in the Peltier effect, his great find. When a current passes through a circuit of two metals, it cools one junction and heats the other. The entry links that find to the wider study of thermoelectricity, treated in its own article.
britannica-1911-penthouse:
Penthouse is a 1911 Britannica article on a word with roots in building and in siege craft. A penthouse is a sloping roof fixed to a building. It can serve as a porch or as a cover for an arcade. If walls support it, it forms a shed, a lean-to.

In the history of siegecraft, the word has a special sense. It named the fixed or movable shelters that guarded men at siege work. Such shelters shielded miners and crews of battering-rams and catapults. The word thus translates Latin terms for those engines' covers. A Roman shelter of locked shields bore the same sense. The Middle English form was pentis. It came from an Old French word for a small structure that hangs on a larger one. The modern form grew from a supposed link with the word house.
britannica-1911-philip-landgrave-of-hess:
Philip, landgrave of Hesse, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Marburg in fifteen hundred four, he was the son of Landgrave William the Second. He became landgrave on his father's death when he was still a child. Declared of age in fifteen eighteen, he wed a Saxon duke's daughter.

In his early years he helped quell risings in Germany. He took a leading part in crushing the peasants' revolt in the north. His force was chiefly to blame for their defeat at Frankenhausen. About that same time he adopted the reformed faith. He became afterwards one of its chief princely backers.
britannica-1911-plagioclase:
Plagioclase is the subject of a mineral entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name covers a key group of rock forming minerals. Those minerals form a chain between two end kinds. One end is albite, or soda felspar, in the chain. The other end is anorthite, or lime felspar. Kinds in between mix soda and lime in grade. Their traits shift by slow steps with that mix.

Set names mark the bands of that long chain. Six names from albite to anorthite are listed in order. All kinds split in one slanted crystal system. They split cleanly on two faces at a slant angle. That slant gave the group its Greek based name. A rival felspar splits at a right angle instead. Crystals are most often flat like thin boards in form. Notes on their shapes and marks fill the rest.
britannica-1911-pontoise:
Pontoise is a town of north France, chief town of a district north west of Paris on the rail line to Dieppe. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count in the early years of the age. It stands in a fine site on the right bank of a river, where a small stream joins it.

Trade on the main river is large, and the small stream drives a host of mills. Of the many churches the town once had, two stand. One is a work of the middle ages, reshaped in later years by a famed church builder, with a fine tomb shrine. The other holds the tomb of a saint abbot. Grain and flour lead its trade, and a famed fair is held each fall.
britannica-1911-prose:
Prose is held to come from a Latin word that means direct or straight. It names the plain speech of mankind, in writing or in set speech, with no heed to the rules of verse. Men have been used to split prose off from poetry in a sharp way. Ronsard said his training as a poet had taught him that the two were mortal foes. The article warns that poetry is too cloudy a term to serve as a clean mark of split.

A dull work in rhyme is not poetry, yet it is most sure not prose; it is verse. On the other hand, a work of high-wrought plain writing is often called a prose-poem. That phrase shows the blur in the line between the two. The article works through the terms with care before it settles what prose is.
britannica-1911-pulse: Pulse is a word with two chief senses, both set out in the 1911 Britannica entry. In botany it is a shared name for beans, peas, and kin plants of the legume order, marked by a pod as their fruit. In the study of the body it names the rhythmic beat in the arteries. That beat comes from shifts in blood pressure as the walls of the arteries stretch and spring back with each stroke of the heart.
britannica-1911-raynaud-s-disease:
Raynaud's Disease is a malady first described by P. Edouard Raynaud in 1862, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a medical entry. His paper treated local asphyxia and symmetrical gangrene of the extremities. The condition is said to arise from the central nervous system, with cold, fright and emotional upset among the causes that dispose to it.

The disease strikes in childhood or in early adult life, and women are affected more often than men. Raynaud laid the symptoms to a halt in the flow of blood to the parts, caused by a spasm of the small arteries. If that spasm lasts long enough to close the channels in full, gangrene of the part may follow. The entry divides the local signs into three marked stages. The first is local syncope, in which the parts turn bloodless, white, cold and without feeling, as in a common dead finger.
britannica-1911-rivoli-veronese:
Rivoli Veronese is a village in Venetia, Italy, and a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains why its name is known. The village stands on a hill on the right bank of the Adige, thirteen miles north west of Verona. It sits 617 feet above the sea and held 1,340 people in 1901.

Rivoli is famed as the scene of a great battle of the French Revolutionary Wars. On the fifteenth of January 1797, Napoleon there won a decisive victory over the Austrians. Their commander was Josef Alvintzi, Baron von Barberek. A noted street in Paris, the Rue de Rivoli, marks the win. Marshal Masséna later took the title duke of Rivoli. The strong ground around the village guards the routes from Tirol into the Italian plain.
britannica-1911-sea-horse:
Sea-horse is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a small sea fish. Sea-horses form the group named Hippocampina in the text. With the pipe-fishes, they make up one branch of fishes. Their gills are not laid out in thin leaf-like rows. The gills form a round mass of small lobes on the gill arches. A figure shows this mass with the gill cover pushed aside.

Sea-horses stand apart from pipe-fishes in one clear way. They have a tail that can grip, and the tail bears no fin. The tail is long, thin, and four sided in cross cut. The whole body sits in a shell of horny rings. That shell still lets the fish bend, most of all at the belly side.
britannica-1911-skinner-s-case:
Skinner's Case is the name of a famed clash between the two houses of parliament. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica centres it on the Lords' right to hear civil suits first. In 1668 a London merchant, Thomas Skinner, petitioned the king. He claimed the East India Company had harmed his property and that no court would aid him. The case went to the House of Lords. Skinner won a verdict of 5,000 pounds there.

The company then complained to the House of Commons. That house declared the Lords' acts illegal. Each house jailed the other's man in the quarrel. The Commons seized Skinner; the Lords fined and jailed the company's chairman. After a year of deadlock, Charles the Second stepped in. He urged both houses to drop the case and erase its record. That was done, and the Lords quietly gave up the claim for good.
britannica-1911-spinola-ambrose:
Ambrose Spinola, Spain's great captain in Flanders, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Genoa in 1569, he was the eldest son of a marquis. His house was old, rich, and strong in that trading city. Genoa then stood under the shield of the Spanish crown. Its bankers held the purse strings of the Spanish monarchy itself.

Spinola wed in 1592 and lost a law fight to the Dorias. That rival house ruled the roost in Genoa at the time. Stung, he chose to seek his house's rise in Spanish service. In 1602 he struck a bold bargain with the Spanish crown. He pledged his whole great wealth on the venture in Flanders. He would raise nine thousand men for war on land.
britannica-1911-staircase:
Staircase names the stairs that lead to the upper floors of a building, along with the walls around them, in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A plain house may have just one staircase, while a large house adds a service stair. Grand homes place a fine main staircase up to the chief rooms.

The entry traces stairs back through time, starting with early work in Egypt built inside thick temple walls. It cites a stone staircase found at Cnossus in Crete, six feet wide and rising through two floors. Greek temples, the Tabularium at Rome, and round stone stairs in church towers all get a mention.
britannica-1911-steeplechase:
Steeplechase is a kind of horse racing that is not run on the flat. It is run across country, or on a made course with false fences and water jumps. Its start and its name come from matches run by the owners of hunters. The goal of those matches was a clear mark on the land, such as the steeple of a church nearby. An early case on record is a match in Ireland in 1732. The course ran four and a half miles, from one church to the spire of a second.

The name is at times used of a run across country by men, or of a race on a made course over hurdles. It is also the name of an English form of an old French board game. In that game, two dice are used on a board that shows a race course.
britannica-1911-syracuse:
Syracuse, the Sicilian city now called Siracusa, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry places it on the east coast of the island, south of Catania, and gives its town and commune counts for the late years before the book came out. It calls Syracuse the chief Greek city of ancient Sicily.

The history starts with the founding tale told by Strabo and Thucydides. Archias of Corinth is said to have led settlers there the year after Naxos was founded. He drove the Sicel people from the island site. From that start the entry builds a long city history. Readers get place, size, and past in one clear account that suits both quick checks and deeper study of Greek Sicily.
britannica-1911-tortoise:
Tortoise names the land members of an order of reptiles that also holds turtles and terrapins. A 1911 Britannica entry sorts the three names and their roots at the start. Tortoise comes from an old French word for twisted, from the bent forelegs. Turtle is thought a worn form of that same old French word.

Terrapin has been used since the 1500s for fresh water kinds of the tropics. Sea and fresh water kinds now take the turtle name in common speech. As an order they are toothless reptiles with strong, well formed limbs. Back and belly shells of many bony plates guard the soft body within.
britannica-1911-traverse: In the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, traverse names a mass of earth or other stuff set across a fort to shield troops from fire along the line. It stands at a right angle to the parapet held by the men who defend the work. Its length to the rear and its height shift with the need at hand. A traverse can also serve as a casemate. Short broken trenches gain the same guard from the solid earth left between each length.
britannica-1911-treatise: Treatise is a short word entry in the 1911 Britannica. It sets out what the word means in plain terms. A work of this kind deals in full with the rules of a grave topic, step by step. The word comes from old French forms that meant a tale or an account. Those forms link back to a Latin word for handling a thing. By its root sense the word means a thing well handled or well made.
britannica-1911-turquoise:
Turquoise, a mineral used as an ornamental stone for its blue or blue-green colour, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The name is held to mark the stone as coming from Turkey. The finest kinds reached Europe from Persia by way of Turkey. Venetian traders called it turchesa. Some writers link the word to the Persian name instead.

The mineral occurs in small rounded nodules, crusts, thin seams, and scattered grains. Its form suggests it was laid down from solution, and it is sometimes found in stalactitic masses. The typical colour is a delicate sky blue, shading by degrees into green. Colour can fade as the stone dries or faces sunlight, and old stones often turn green. Turquoise is opaque in mass but lets light through in thin splinters. It takes a fair polish, though its lustre is weak and waxy.
britannica-1911-verse:
Verse, from a Latin word for a furrow line, names words set for metre. Its form entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. A verse is a set of words placed to make a measured effect. The art of making and the science of scanning verse is versification.

In modern speech verse stands in direct contrast with prose writing forms. Verse rests on set rules of form in a way prose does not. Men speak of a verse for one case and verse for the art whole. A verse is a chain of timed syllables split by pauses in sound. In writing it is meant to fill a single line on the page.
buds-and-bird-voices-from-mosses-from-an:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote a spring sketch that stands inside Mosses from an Old Manse. Late spring comes to the old house at last, weeks past hope. Sun peeps in at the study pane and calls the writer out. Air from the fresh season mixes with the stove's black cheer.

Thought forms kept through the slow cold fly out as the sash lifts. Gay, odd, and sad visions leave with them. Dream scenes in rainbow hues fade as they go. Brooding Thought, owl-like, beats off from the noon cheer. New life is to be shaped from sun and air in their place. Frost panes, crackling fires, and snow-choked wood paths give way in one stroke. Season's turn, felt in one room, is the whole stock of the piece.
bulchevy-s-book-of-english-verse:
Arthur Quiller-Couch edited this great anthology of English verse, issued here under a generic title because the Oxford name was a trademark. Quiller-Couch arranged the poems by author in time order, beginning with anonymous songs from about 1250. Chaucer and Hoccleve appear early; the book runs on to poets born in the later nineteenth century.

His preface explains the choices: the best poems, whole where possible, in the order English poetry grew. Ballads, lyrics, odes, and dramatic verse stand side by side. Generations of readers met English poetry through this single shelf-sized volume. It works still as a map of the tradition, generous in range and firm in taste.
cap-and-gown-a-treasury-of-college-verse:
Frederic Lawrence Knowles picked a store of college verse, dated 1897. Frances James Child, great scholar and teacher, gets the book in warm words. A short verse at the front sets the bounds: no epic strain lives here. Youth, joy, and love — the boy's creed — form the stock, it says.

Gay verse of class life must not be weighed too deep, the front note warns. Such verse claims no high rank as art. Light, bright, and full of jest is its right key, with grave notes at times. Young men and maids at the edge of grown life have grave hearts in truth, the note grants. Knowles had form in the field, as his Golden Treasury of American Songs and Lyrics heads his name. Campus song from many schools fills the frame.
cape-cod-ballads-and-other-verse:
Joseph C. Lincoln wrote verse of Cape Cod life, dated 1902, with drawings by Edward W. Kemble. His wife gets the book. The Cod-Fisher opens the set. Song of the Sea and the Wind's Song come next. The Life-Saver gives the brave note, with a hero born and bred whose head stays plain, by one plate's line.

Evening hymn, meadow road, and a bullfrog serenade fill the soft run. Sunday rest, old photos in tin, and the best spare room paint home life. Old carryall, first fire-crackers, and Nathan at the choir mark youth's joys. Hezekiah's art and a Sunday school picnic crowd the heart. Aunt Mandy, the story-book boy, and the school board man fill the folk list. Tongue of the Cape, in rhyme and jest, is the book's whole stock.
captain-fracasse:
Theophile Gautier's Captain Fracasse follows the ruined young Baron de Sigognac, who leaves his decaying Castle Misery with a traveling theater troupe. The contents promise the Chariot of Thespis, brigands, a snowstorm, and the Blue Sun inn. Sigognac takes the stage name Captain Fracasse, a braggart soldier's part.

He falls for the actress Isabella while the Duke of Vallombreuse schemes to steal her, setting duels, abductions, and melees in motion. Gautier, who adored the theater, fills seventeenth-century France with players, swordsmen, and the gypsy girl Chiquita. The baron's first victory gives him confidence his enemy must now reckon with. Gautier's swashbuckler remains a French classic of romantic adventure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-and-sch:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Clonmacnoise describes the abbey and school on the Shannon, halfway between Athlone and Banagher, as the most remarkable of Erin's ancient schools. Its founder, St. Ciaran, called Son of the Carpenter, chose a bleak region as better suited to followers of the Cross than the rich plains nearby.

Born at Fuerty in 512 and schooled by St. Finnian at Clonard, Ciaran joined the saintly youths later known as the Twelve Apostles of Erin. Finnian trusted the young Ciaran to teach and give out prayers in his absence, and would gladly have resigned his chair to keep him. The entry follows Ciaran's foundation and the school's fame among Ireland's monastic centres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-melr:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Melrose describes an abbey in Roxburghshire, founded in 1136 by King David the First as Scotland's earliest Cistercian monastery. Its first community came from Rievaulx, and St. Mary's Abbey stood complete within ten years in a wide valley south of the Tweed.

English incursions ravaged Melrose repeatedly: Edward the Second's soldiers desecrated, pillaged and burned the church, and Richard the Second laid waste the country and fired the abbey in 1385. Through Robert the Bruce's generosity a statelier church began in 1326, cruciform and two hundred and fifty feet long, famed for the fairy lightness of its carvings and window tracery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-newh:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Newhouse describes the first Premonstratensian abbey in England, near Brockelsby in Lincolnshire, founded in 1143 by Peter de Gousel. Peter acted with his lord Hugh de Bayeux's consent and Bishop Alexander of Lincoln's approbation, bringing a colony from Liegues Abbey near Calais under Abbot Henry.

William, Earl of Lincoln, hospitably received the White Canons and confirmed the gifts to Gelro, Newhouse's first abbot. Raised for Our Lady and St. Martial of Limoges, Newhouse became parent house to eleven English Premonstratensian houses. Granted to Charles, Duke of Suffolk, in Henry the Eighth's thirtieth year, only parts of its old foundations remain, and twenty-six abbots' names are known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-fa:
The name Alessandro Farnese belongs to two cardinals, and this entry treats the younger. He was the son of Pier Luigi Farnese, first Duke of Parma, born in October 1520 and dead at Rome in February 1589. While a student at Bologna, he was made administrator of Parma in 1534. His uncle Paul III created him Cardinal-Deacon of Sant' Angelo that December and conferred offices and benefices on him.

Farnese was zealous for the poor and served the popes on legations and embassies, including a 1539 mission to Charles V and a 1545 embassy on the council. He accompanied papal troops against the Smalkald League in 1546 and stood as a candidate for the papacy in 1580. A promoter of the Tridentine reforms and a patron of literature, science, and art, he backed the architect Vignola for the Gesù in Rome and the palace at Caprarola. He was buried before the high altar of the Gesù.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-of-repo:
The altar of repose, sometimes called sepulchre or tomb, more often repository, holds the Sacred Host consecrated at Holy Thursday Mass until Good Friday's Mass of the Presanctified. It must stand in the church, other than the altar where Mass is celebrated. Two hosts are consecrated on Holy Thursday. After the first is consumed, the second rests in a chalice covered with pall and inverted paten, under a white veil tied with ribbon, on the corporal until Mass ends.

The host is then borne in solemn procession to that altar of repose. It is kept in the tabernacle or an urn above the altar. Churches vie to adorn these altars and chapels with rich hangings, flowers, and lights, and Holy Thursday becomes a day of exceptional devotion. No mention of altar and procession appears before the late fifteenth century, earlier reservation having served Communion distribution, not the next day's service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-vase:
The Caeremoniale Episcoporum sanctions flowers between the candlesticks as certainly appropriate altar ornaments. Altar vases hold flowers decorating the altar, natural or artificial blooms set between the candlesticks as fitting ornaments for worship. Cut flowers, leaves, and ferns are meant here, rather than soil-potted plants, though potted plants may adorn the sanctuary around the altar.

Artificial flowers must use superior material and copy nature's variations faithfully and with some accuracy. Paper, cheap muslin, calico, and other inferior stuffs, and old or soiled flowers, are never allowed on the altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Funen, Langeland, Taasinge, Laaland, Falster, Als, and Aero made up Odense. It was founded before 988, split off from Schleswig, and its first Odense church honoured Saint Mary. Othinkar Hvide the Elder preached in Funen. Reginbert, an Englishman, is the first bishop known with certainty. Canterbury's Archbishop Alnoth consecrated him in 1020 or 1022, and King Canute the Great sent him to Denmark.

After Eilbert of Bremen, Roskilde held the vacant see until Hubald, an English Benedictine, took it as bishop in 1086. In that year King Saint Canute was murdered in Odense's Saint Alban church. Miracles and poor harvests after the murder led to his canonization. Hubald moved his relics in 1101 to the new church of Our Lady and Saint Alban. Twelve Evesham monks, sent in 1100, served the new Saint Canute cathedral and formed its chapter. Odense later counted among Denmark's richest bishoprics. Its cathedral crypt holds Canute and his brother Benedict.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anise:
Since Wyclif, English versions have rendered anethon in Matthew 23:23 as anise, but that rendering is not accurate. Dill, anethum graveolens, is anethon's exact equivalent, while anise is pimpinella anisum. The mistake matters little, since both plants belong to the parsley family and share many properties. Dill grows as an annual, with striated stems one to one and a half feet high, pinnate leaves, and yellow flowers. Jews used it as a condiment.

Rabbinic literature mentions it several times, especially over tithes. Beside the articles named in the Mosaic Law, the Rabbis over time brought many other objects under tithe, extending it to every edible product that could be preserved. A single Gospel word thus opens a study of translation, botany, and Jewish tithe practice, showing how a familiar rendering can hide a different plant and a wider custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apocalypse:
Apocalypse, from a Greek verb meaning to reveal, is the name attached to the last book of the Bible, also called the Book of Revelation. Though Christian, it belongs to a class of writing on end times much in vogue among Jews of the first century before and following Christ. Its author calls himself John, writing to seven churches in Asia from the island of Patmos. Tradition identifies this seer as John the Apostle, son of Zebedee, the disciple Jesus loved.

By the end of the second century the principal churches accepted the work as genuinely John's. Melito of Sardis, one of the seven churches, wrote a commentary on it. Irenaeus in Gaul firmly held its divine and apostolic authority, and African witnesses agreed. The article then treats authenticity and interpretation, giving readers the Catholic case for a book of visions that closes the New Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-appeal-as-fro:
Appeal as from an abuse, in French appel comme d'abus, began as a recourse to the civil court against a church court seizing civil jurisdiction. Likewise it was a recourse to the church court against a civil court seizing church jurisdiction. So defined, it was in itself legitimate, since its object was to guard the rights of state and church alike. An abuse meant an act by either side, without due authority, beyond its own ordinary and natural bounds.

Church canons did not bar recourse to civil authority when a church judge invaded civil ground. That reciprocity let church authority repel a lay judge's invasion of church rights with the same weapons. Recourse to the supreme civil ruler was likewise not deemed wrong when a church court overstepped. The entry traces a device meant to keep two powers in their lanes, before it hardened into a tool of state control.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apse:
An apse, from Latin apsis and Greek apsis, an arch, is the semicircular or polygonal end given to a church's choir or aisles. Sometimes it is given to transepts and nave. In church architecture it generally marks the part where clergy sit or the altar stands, named for its usual dome or vault. The word also covers a canopy over an altar, a dome, or a semicircular recess vaulted with a half dome.

The apse is always solid below, though usually pierced by windows above. A chevet is an apse enclosed by a colonnade on the ground floor, opening into an aisle that in turn opens into three or more apse chapels. Sometimes a smaller semicircle sprouts from a simple one, as at Canterbury. The entry is a lexicon of one shape and its many church uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archdiocese: Archdiocese, from Greek archidioikesis, does not name an ecclesiastical province as a whole. It names only the province's diocese which is the archbishop's own, over which he holds direct and exclusive jurisdiction. The entry distinguishes the archbishop's home diocese from the wider province he presides over, and cites Ferraris, Wernz, Smith, Phillips, and other canon law authorities for the definition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-be:
Bernard of Besse, a Franciscan chronicler of Aquitaine, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth date is uncertain, and he served as secretary to St. Bonaventure, the order's great theologian. After Bonaventure's death he took up the pen, as he put it, to gather the ears dropped from his master's sheaf.

His Book in Praise of Blessed Francis, written about 1280, gathers early legends and gives precious notes on Francis's companions and the founding of the three Franciscan orders. It alone among thirteenth-century documents lists the first lives of Francis. The entry presents a modest secretary preserving a founder's memory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-everald-ha:
Blessed Everald Hanse, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Northamptonshire and educated at Cambridge, he held a good parish living until his brother William, ordained in 1579, pressed him toward conversion. A sharp illness turned him inward, and he went to Reims in 1580 for ordination.

His English ministry proved very short. Visiting Catholic prisoners in the Marshalsea in disguise in July 1581, his foreign-made shoes betrayed him to the keeper, and examination exposed his priesthood. With no law yet against priests as such, prosecutors stretched treason law to condemn him. He was executed on 31 July 1581.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-frances-d-:
Blessed Frances d'Amboise, Duchess of Brittany and later Carmelite nun, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1427, daughter of Louis d'Amboise, she was betrothed at four to Peter, second son of Duke John V, and married at fifteen. A morose husband ill-treated her at first, but her gentleness changed his heart.

After his succession in 1450, her influence widened into works of charity and good government across Brittany. Widowed, she entered the Carmelites and died at Nantes in 1485, having founded a Carmelite house there. The entry presents a duchess whose patience reformed a court and then a convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-woo: Blessed Thomas Woodhouse, a martyr, suffered at Tyburn on 19 June 1573. He took orders under Queen Mary, served briefly as a Lincolnshire rector, and tutored privately in Wales in 1560. Arrested while saying Mass in 1561, he spent the rest of his life in custody. He said Mass in secret daily and recited his Office. A letter to Lord Burghley in 1572, urging reconciliation, brought his execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boise:
Boise, the Idaho diocese created by Leo XIII in 1893, covers the whole state, 84,290 square miles. Catholic work began in 1842 with a Jesuit mission to the Coeur d'Alene Indians, whose first church used wooden pegs instead of nails. Secular priests reached the Boise Basin miners in 1863 and built Idaho's first churches for white settlers within six months.

Idaho became a vicariate apostolic in 1868 under Louis Lootens, consecrated at San Francisco. He reached Idaho in January 1869, and the first Boise church rose in 1870, only to burn soon after dedication. His successor Alphonsus Glorieux, consecrated in 1885, found about 2,500 Catholics and ten churches served by two secular and several Jesuit priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burse:
A burse is the flat case that carries the folded corporal, the linen cloth used at the altar, to and from Mass. In Roman form it is two pieces of stiff card, about ten inches square, joined on three sides and open on the fourth to take the cloth. Its outer side matches the vestments in use, while the inside is lined with linen or silk.

The burse is fairly recent. Once the corporal shrank to its present small size, it was carried in the missal or in a box or bag. That holder at last took this flat form. A Mainz chronicle of 1140 to 1251 mentions a precious corporal case, and Saint Charles Borromeo describes a small corporal bag apart from the storage case. Between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries the burse spread, and by 1692 Mass without one was everywhere unlawful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camaldolese:
The Camaldolese are hermits and cenobites in one order, founded by Saint Romuald early in the eleventh century. About 1012, after founding or reforming nearly a hundred houses, Romuald reached the diocese of Arezzo. There Count Maldolus, who had dreamed of white-clad monks climbing a ladder to heaven, gave him the field that became Camaldoli. A villa below became Fonte Buono, serving as infirmary, guest-house, and bursary so the hermits stayed free of worldly business.

For six centuries the order grew as one body under the Holy Hermitage. It then split into five congregations: the Holy Hermitage, San Michele di Murano, Monte Corona, Turin, and Notre-Dame de Consolation. By 1907 three congregations remained, with houses chiefly in Italy, plus Bielany in Poland and Nuova Camaldoli in Brazil. The hermits at Camaldoli and the cenobites at Fonte Buono still stand as models of austerity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cause:
Cause, from the Greek aitia and Latin causa, is understood as that which gives existence to a thing, produces a result, or accounts for its origin. The article warns that cause, being transcendental, admits no strict logical definition. It then surveys the idea across philosophy, science, and law. It opens with the Pre-Socratics, Plato, and Aristotle. Their thought shaped every later account.

The scholastic analysis follows, dividing causation into material, formal, efficient, and final causes. The survey continues through Bacon, Descartes, Hume, Reid, and Kant, then Hegel and Schopenhauer. Later sections treat cause in science, in common sense, and in law. In law, a cause of action means an enforceable claim that may lapse with time or await a legal condition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chapter-house:
A chapter house stands beside a monastery or cathedral and holds the chapter's meetings. In monasteries it served each day after Prime, and at times after Terce, for reading the Martyrology and Necrology, correcting faults, and assigning the day's tasks. It also hosted the superior's exhortation and the evening Collation before Complin. Secular canons used it for similar purposes and for the formal business of the body corporate.

The chapter house appears in neither St. Benedict, who died in 543, nor the ancient plan of St. Gall drawn up in 820; monks then probably met for chapter in a cloister walk near the church. A separate building soon proved necessary, and the chapter house is named in Aachen council statutes of 816. Its shape varied from rectangular to apsidal, circular, or polygonal, with the polygonal form, carefully designed and richly ornamented, a triumph of thirteenth-century England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-const:
Charles Constantine Pise was a priest, poet, and prose writer born at Annapolis in 1801 and dead at Brooklyn in 1866. Educated at Georgetown College and for a time a Jesuit, he taught rhetoric at Emmitsburg's Mount St. Mary's College, where his pupils included the future Archbishop of New York, John Hughes. Ordained in 1825, he served at Baltimore cathedral and at St. Patrick's in Washington. There he was elected Senate chaplain in 1832, the only Catholic priest yet appointed to that office.

He was a friend of President Tyler. He became pastor of St. Peter's in New York in 1848. From 1849 until his death he served St. Charles Borromeo's in Brooklyn. His books include a five-volume History of the Catholic Church, Father Rowland, Alethia, St. Ignatius and His First Companions, and Christianity and the Church. His poem Clara and his drama Montezuma were never published. He also composed Latin verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-de-la:
Charles de La Fosse was a painter born at Paris in 1636 and dead there in 1716, buried in the church of Saint Eustache. Seventh of sixteen children of a jeweller and Marguerite Langlois, he trained under François Chauveau and then in Lebrun's studio. He later decorated the Tuileries. On 23 June 1673 he joined the academy, and five months later he married Elizabeth Beguin at Saint Sulpice.

Lord Montagu, ambassador to Paris in 1688, admired his work so much that he called him to England to decorate Montagu House. William III begged him to stay and decorate Hampton Court, but the architect Mansart recalled him to Paris for the dome of the Invalides. The Louvre's Galerie d'Apollon ceiling is also his, and he did much work at Versailles, including the Salle de Diane and the chapel roof.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charterhouse:
An entry on the charterhouse, the English name for a Carthusian house, from Chartreux near Grenoble, where St. Bruno founded the first house. Just as such houses are called cartuja in Spain and certosa in Italy, so Chartreux was corrupted in England into charterhouse. Henry II founded the first English house at Witham in Somerset in 1181, and Henry V founded the last, Sheen in Surrey, in 1414.

Other houses stood at Hinton, Beauvale, Coventry, Hull, and Mountgrace, but the most famous was the London charterhouse, founded in 1371 by Sir Walter Manny. Its prior, Blessed John Houghton, was put to death in 1535, and Henry VIII broke up its community. The entry also lays out the common plan of Carthusian houses: two courtyards, cells for choir monks and lay brothers, and a chapter house and refectory. The church has no aisles, and a great cloister gives onto each monk's cell and garden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronicle-of-:
An entry on the Chronicle of Melrose, a monastic history opening in 735 and ending abruptly in 1270. It rests solely on the Cottonian manuscript Faustina B. the British Museum's nine, the only ancient copy, from which all others are transcripts. Its authors are unknown, but its language proves it was written in Melrose Abbey, and its shifting hands show monks of successive periods at work.

The first part, to about 1140, compiles the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and histories by Simeon of Durham and Hoveden, and must be used with caution. The second part, from about 1140 to 1270, ranks among the most credible sources of its age, since its entries are largely original and generally contemporary. The manuscript, likely carried off at the Reformation, was edited by Stevenson for the Bannatyne Club in 1835. Melrose also left hundreds of charters from David the First to Bruce, edited by Cosmo Innes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civita-castel:
Civita Castellana, a town on the Treia in Rome province, was built on the ruins of ancient Falerii, capital of the Falisci. That Latin tribe warred often with Rome until Camillus subdued it in 394 before Christ, though it rose again in 356 and during the Samnite War. Digging there has revealed much Faliscan civilisation. Alexander the Third died and was buried at Civita Castellana, and in 1798 the Austrians under Mack were beaten there by the French general Macdonald.
