The first known bishop, Crescentius, found the relics of Martianus and Johannes in 998. In 1437 the diocese united with Orte, the ancient Horta on a travertine hill north of Rome, near the newly found catacombs of Saint Eutychius. Gallese joined Civita Castellana in 1252, was restored in 1562, and was suppressed again in 1573. The diocese, directly subject to the Holy See, counts 40,200 people, twenty-nine parishes, and over two hundred churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
The Councils of Anse, several medieval synods in a French town near Lyons, open in 994 with a decree for Sunday's vigil: no servile labour after three o'clock on Saturday afternoon. The 1025 council settled a clash between Cluny's monks and the Bishop of Macon over ordinations. Ancient canons read at the meeting subjected abbots and monks to their own bishop.

Later meetings pursued Gregory VII's reforms in 1076, heard Lyons' archbishop seek a Jerusalem journey subsidy in 1100 before Anselm of Canterbury, and decreed on faith and investitures in 1112. The 1025 ruling forced Vienne's archbishop to apologise to Macon, a small scene of medieval jurisdiction in action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocese:
A diocese is the territory and churches subject to a bishop. The word began in Greek as the management of a household, then meant government in general. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry shows how Roman law used it for a district tied to a city. Since the Christian bishop usually lived in such a city, his territory took the same civil name.

Later sections treat the making, splitting, joining, and ending of dioceses, their different ranks, and how they are run. The bishop rules as a whole, yet must keep the general laws of the Church, and some sees stand free of any archbishop, answering straight to Rome. The entry closes with a survey of the diocesan system across the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dom-francois-:
Dom Francois Armand Gervaise was a Discalced Carmelite born at Paris in 1660. After brilliant studies he joined the order and served as prior of a convent. Bossuet noticed him there as a single man combining fervent religious life, learned writing, and eloquent speech. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how hunger for a stricter life took him to La Trappe in 1695. There he became the favored disciple of the Abbe de Rance.

On the death of Rance's first successor, the king, urged by Bossuet, named Gervaise as second successor. His rule brought strife, and he was at last banished by royal order to the monastery of the Reclus, where he died in 1761. To the end he kept the full rigor of the Trappist life he had embraced.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enemond-masse:
Enemond Masse was one of the first Jesuits sent to New France, born at Lyons in 1574 and dead at Sillery in 1646. He sailed to Acadia with Father Biard, and when no good could be done there, the two set up a new mission at what is now Bar Harbor in Maine. English attackers soon destroyed it, setting Masse adrift at sea in an open boat.

He reached a French ship and came home, only to sail again for Canada in 1625, staying until the fall of Quebec. A third voyage in 1632 brought him back for good, but age kept him from labouring among the native peoples. He lived mostly at Sillery, which he built as a reserve for converted Indians, and a monument now stands there on the site of the old Jesuit church above Quebec.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-d-ai:
Francois d'Aix de la Chaise, also called Chaize, was born at the Aix mansion in Forez on 25 August 1624 and died at Paris on 20 January 1709. He was confessor to Louis XIV for thirty-four years.

He is often blamed for conniving at the king's liaison with Madame de Montespan and advising the revocation of the Edict of Nantes with violent suppression of Protestants. The entry corrects the record. La Chaise used all his influence, with Madame de Maintenon, to end the Montespan liaison. After Queen Maria Theresa's death in 1683 he advised the king's marriage to Maintenon, which changed court life for the better. How far he backed the revocation is unknown, but the charge that he urged violence is baseless and clashes with his admitted mildness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-d-ambo:
George d'Amboise, a French cardinal, archbishop, and statesman born in 1460, ruled France beside Louis XII for a dozen years. Named Bishop of Montauban at fourteen, he took office at twenty-four and became Archbishop of Rouen in 1493. When his ally the Duke of Orléans took the throne as Louis XII in 1498, d'Amboise became prime minister and a cardinal the same year.

At home d'Amboise cut taxes a tenth, set finances in order, and reformed law and courts. Abroad he pushed Louis toward Milan. As a churchman he fared worse, chasing the papacy at Alexander VI's death and polling third with thirteen votes, then backing Pius III and flirting with schism against Julius II. Julius still made him legate for all France, an office he held until his death at Lyons in 1510.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-gervas:
George Gervase, a priest and martyr born in Suffolk in 1571, died at Tyburn for the priesthood alone. Orphaned young, he was kidnapped by pirates and held beyond the seas over twelve years, losing his religion in captivity. Back in England he found his brother Henry exiled in Flanders for the faith, followed him there, and was reconciled to the Church. He entered Douai's English College in 1595 and was ordained in 1603.

Gervase labored on the English mission over two years before arrest and banishment in June 1606. A Roman pilgrimage followed, then, refused by the Jesuits, he took the Benedictine habit at Douai. Against his brother's wish for a safe living near Lille, he returned to England, was arrested, and refused the new oath of allegiance. Convicted merely of being a priest, he was hanged, drawn, and quartered in April 1608.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-andr:
Giovanni Andrea Cortese, known in religion as Gregorio, was a cardinal and Benedictine reformer born at Modena in 1483, who died in 1548. Trained in humanities and law, he took his doctorate at seventeen and served Cardinal Giovanni de' Medici as legal auditor. In 1507 he left the Curia for the monastery of Polirone. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his drive for monastic and church reform.

He carried the Cassinese reform through Italy and, at Lérins from 1516, founded an academy that brought Italian humanism to French youth. Elected abbot there in 1524, he later held abbacies at Modena and Perugia. Paul III made him cardinal in 1542 and Bishop of Urbino, and set him on the committee preparing the Council of Trent. His elegant Latin letters, poems, and translation of the New Testament mark him as a leading humanist writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-golden-rose:
The Golden Rose is a precious and sacred ornament of pure gold, made by skilled artificers, which popes have blessed each year for centuries. They confer it occasionally on illustrious churches and sanctuaries, Catholic kings or queens, princes or princesses, renowned generals, governments, or cities conspicuous for Catholic spirit and loyalty. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces a gift of esteem and paternal affection.

It is blessed on Laetare Sunday, the fourth of Lent, often called Rose Sunday. Rose-colored vestments then replace penitential purple as signs of hope and joy. The golden flower shows forth Christ and his kingly majesty. Its fragrance is the sweet odor of Christ to be spread by the faithful, and its thorns and red tint tell of his Passion. Before Sixtus IV it was a simple single rose; later it grew into a branch with leaves and many roses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grasse:
François-Joseph, Count and Marquess de Grasse-Tilly, was lieutenant-general of the naval forces, born near Toulon in 1723, who died at Paris on 11 January 1788. At eleven he entered the naval service of the Knights of Malta, then joined the French navy in 1739 and was captured and held in England for two years in 1747. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the admiral whose fleet sealed Yorktown.

After service in the Seven Years War and the East Indies, he sailed from Brest in March 1781 with twenty-three ships of the line. He fought Hood off Martinique and took Tobago in June. At Cap Français he found dispatches from Washington and Rochambeau urging cooperation against the English in Virginia. He acted promptly, and his control of the sea left only one issue at Yorktown, where Cornwallis surrendered on 19 October 1781.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-duc-de-:
French duke Henri de Joyeuse, born in 1563, lived twice as a Capuchin friar and twice as a soldier and marshal, earning Voltaire's teasing title of warrior monk. Third son of Marshal Guillaume de Joyeuse, he married Catherine de la Valette, fought Huguenots in Languedoc, and on his wife's death took the Capuchin habit as Père Ange in September 1587.

Released from vows to command in Languedoc after his brother's drowning in 1592, he made peace and became marshal of France and governor of Languedoc under Henry IV. He then rejoined the Capuchins in February 1599, preached before king and court, and served as provincial of France. He died of fever at Rivoli in 1608 on his way from Rome's general chapter, where he had been made definitor-general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-marie-g:
French cardinal Henri-Marie-Gaston Boisnormand de Bonnechose, born at Paris in 1800, moved from the magistracy to Rouen's archbishopric and the Senate. Attorney-general at Besançon in 1830, he took orders at Strasbourg and taught sacred eloquence at Besançon's higher school. After a Roman trip to settle a clash over his Philosophy of Christianity, he became superior of St. Louis in 1844.

Bishop of Carcassonne in 1847, of Evreux in 1854. Archbishop of Rouen the same year, he was made cardinal in 1863 and senator by office, defending the pope's temporal power and protesting the French army's withdrawal from Rome. In 1870, old as he was, he trekked to Versailles in winter to beg King William to cut Rouen's war contribution. Under the republic he opposed anti-congregation laws while urging deference to civil authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hesse:
Hesse is both a German tribe and a district stretching along the Lahn, Eder, Fulda, Werra, and lower Main and Rhine. Today it spans Hesse-Darmstadt, a grand duchy, and Hesse-Nassau, a Prussian province, with Kassel as capital. Its people descend from the Chatti, who, alongside the Cherusci, ruled Germany before Rome arrived, and Frankish times split their land into several counties.

Christianity reached parts of the region about 350 through St. Lubentius, and St. Goar and St. Kilian preached there in later centuries. The chief missionary was St. Boniface, who baptized counts at Amöneburg, cut down Thor's sacred oak at Geismar, and founded the first Hessian bishopric at Büraberg in 741. From Fulda and Hersfeld, founded by his disciples, Christian houses spread across the land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-house-of-guis:
The House of Guise, an offshoot of Lorraine's ducal family, played a major part in France's religious troubles during the sixteenth century. Claiming descent from Charlemagne, the Guises briefly claimed the French throne. They upheld Catholic interests firmly in France and in Scotland, where Mary Stuart and her mother Marie de Lorraine were kin.

Their own violence and their partisans' often stained their religious zeal, and it masked political plans dangerous to monarchical centralization. Their thirty-five years of ties with Spain roused French patriotic suspicion. In their favour, the entry notes, Huguenots also committed violence and appealed to England, while the Calvinist nobility threatened French unity even more. The article treats those members most notable for religious history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-incense:
Sweet smoke from tree resin, burned in worship, is the subject of this entry, which moves from nature to rite. Two resin trees supplied the ancient world, one in Arabia and one in India, and their bark yielded the gum. Blenders mixed in other scents, sometimes four kinds and sometimes as many as thirteen, to thicken the smoke and deepen the scent.

Beyond the temple, incense also served daily life as a guard against heat and weariness, much as perfume does now. The entry then turns to its place in Jewish worship and in Catholic liturgy. It closes with the practical side. The vessel called the incense boat holds incense for use. The server who carries it is the thurifer. Swings of the censer mark the rank of person or thing honored.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste de la Brosse, a Jesuit missionary born in France in 1724 and dead in 1782, carried his work to Canada in 1754 after ordination the year before. He first served the Abenaki, held posts at Quebec College, and in 1765 took over the Montagnais mission at Chicoutimi, the twenty-first Jesuit to hold it.

From Tadousac at the Saguenay's mouth, his rounds reached along the Labrador coast, to Micmac country, and east to Prince Edward Island. Beyond doctrine he gave the Montagnais lessons in reading, writing, and chant, and had an alphabet, catechism, and prayer book printed at Quebec in 1767. That catechism ranks among the first books printed in Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-jacques-:
Jean-Jacques Bourassé, a French archaeologist and historian born in 1813 and dead at Tours in 1872. He trained for the priesthood in Paris and taught natural science at Tours's preparatory seminary in 1835. There he began a course in archaeology that drew notice in a field then still new in France.

Bourassé counts as a true pioneer of Christian archaeology in his country. After six years teaching dogma at the grand seminary, he quit teaching to write full time. His best-known books survey Christian archaeology, the cathedrals of France, the world's finest churches, and Romanesque churches of Touraine, grounding church art in history and place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-belasyse:
John Belasyse, Baron Belasyse, was a loyal Catholic nobleman who fought for Charles I and lived to serve James II. Born about 1614, second son of the first Lord Fauconberg, he sat for Thirsk in the Short and Long Parliaments until disabled as a Royalist. He then raised six regiments at his own expense and fought at Edgehill, Newbury, and Naseby, becoming lieutenant-general in the north and Governor of York.

After the Restoration he served as Lord-Lieutenant of the East Riding and Governor of Hull, and commanded the forces at Tangier. The Test Act of 1673 forced him as a Catholic to resign his posts. Denounced in the Oates Plot as commander of a supposed popish army, he endured long imprisonment in the Tower without trial. He was restored to favor under James II as First Lord Commissioner of the Treasury in 1687, and died in 1689.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-tasse:
Joseph Tassé was a French-Canadian writer, journalist, and senator. Born at Montreal in 1848, he studied at Bourget College in Rigaud and began editing Le Canada at Ottawa at nineteen. In 1869 he took over La Minerve, Montreal's leading Conservative paper, until 1872. He entered the House of Commons for Ottawa in 1878 and the Senate in 1891.

Tassé wrote over a hundred articles for La Revue canadienne and papers for the Royal Society of Canada. His books cover Philémon Wright and the timber trade, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Ottawa Valley, and, most importantly, Les Canadiens de l'Ouest of 1878. He lectured widely in Canada and the United States, praised for a clear and warm style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-crosse:
La Crosse is a Wisconsin diocese erected in 1868 from land north and west of the Wisconsin River. After Superior split off in 1900, it covered twenty-two counties and 17,299 square miles as a suffragan of Milwaukee.

At its founding, twenty-two priests served twenty-three churches and about fifty stations, with English, German, Polish, and Italian congregations and six parish schools. Its first bishop, Michael Heiss, born in Bavaria in 1818, came to America in 1842, built Milwaukee's first parish church in 1846, and headed St. Francis Seminary. In twelve years at La Crosse he raised churches, including the cathedral, and the bishop's house, before succeeding at Milwaukee in 1880.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-grande-cha:
La Grande Chartreuse, mother-house of the Carthusian Order, stands in a high Dauphine valley at 4,268 feet, fourteen miles from Grenoble to the north. Medieval writers marvelled at the spot's bleakness, while modern eyes praise its beauty or, like Ruskin, call its cliffs commonplace.

St. Bruno built the first house in 1084, an avalanche wrecked it in 1132, and new buildings rose on the grand cloister's site. Fire struck eight times between 1320 and 1676, and Prior Innocent Le Masson then rebuilt most of it in the solid, severe style that still shapes it. The church keeps Gothic parts from about 1320. Under the 1901 Association Laws, dragoons expelled the last monks on 19 April 1903.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-morse:
A morse, also called monille, firmula or pectorale, began as a rectangular ornamented cloth piece. It joined the two front edges of a cope near the breast so the vestment would not slip from the shoulders. Fitted with hook and eye, such pieces were often richly embroidered or set with precious stones.

The name passed to metal clasps used in their place, found in miniatures and inventories as early as the eleventh century. These clasps slowly lost practical use and turned into pure ornaments. They were sewn to the cope flaps or hooked on so they could be removed and cared for separately. That care mattered when a clasp was heavy or costly. Usually round or square in gilded silver, they bore pearls, stones, enamel, niello and figures of saints, ranking among the goldsmith's finest work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orense:
Orense, a Galician diocese suffragan to Compostela, covers nearly all its civil province plus parts of Lugo and Zamora. Its capital, a city of 14,168 on the Miño famed since antiquity for hot springs, holds a see dating certainly before the fifth century.

Braga's first council in 561 created four dioceses whose bishops signed below Orense's, and Idacius names Pastor and Siagrius consecrated at Lugo in 433, one of them for Orense. Suevians turned Arian in 464 and Catholic under Chararic about 560, and the entry follows bishops through later centuries. Suevians embraced Arianism in 464 and returned to Catholicism under King Chararic about 560.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ortolano-ferr:
Giovanni Battista Benvenuti, called Ortolano Ferrarese because his father was a gardener, painted for the Ferrara school. He was born about 1490 and dead by about 1525. Little is known of his life beyond diligent study of Raphael and Bagnacavallo at Bologna in 1512 and 1513. His work is so close to Garofalo's that critics have argued endlessly over which hand painted which picture.

His master work, rich in colour and fine in drawing, shows Saints Sebastian, Roch, and Demetrius. It now hangs in the National Gallery in London. The gallery bought it in 1861, after it left the church at Bondeno in 1844. Other pictures linked to him stand in Ferrara cathedral and its smaller churches. Further works sit in galleries at Ferrara, Naples, and Berlin, with more in private hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philosophy-of:
The philosophy of common sense was the Scottish answer to Berkeley and Hume, the phase of reaction Kant matched in Germany. Common sense here means the original principles found in all normal minds, in Fénelon's phrase the notions one can neither contradict nor examine but by which one judges everything. Locke's doctrine of ideas, borrowed from Descartes, had let Berkeley dissolve the outer world into ideas and Hume dissolve the mind into a succession of states.

Between them, subject and object vanished into scepticism. Thomas Reid, dissenting from Locke, rebuilt philosophy on principles every mind shares: the senses truly report an outer world, and the self truly endures behind its states. Later sections follow Reid's successors through the Scottish school, weighing its appeal to universal judgment against the charge that it merely baptizes prejudice. The entry treats a school, not a faculty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-buse:
Pierre Busée, also called Buys, was a Jesuit theologian born at Nijmegen in 1540. Entering the Society at Cologne at twenty-two, he became master of novices there in 1567 and taught religion to the college's higher classes. His great labour was completing Canisius's large catechism by supplying the full text of every scriptural and patristic reference the author had cited, a project Canisius himself encouraged.

The first volume appeared at Cologne in 1569 as Authoritates sacrae Scripturae. The work was complete in 1570 in four volumes, and a fine Manutius edition of 1571 lacked only the last volume for unknown reasons. A revised one-volume Opus catechisticum followed in 1577. Busée left Cologne for Vienna, lectured on Scripture at the university, and taught Hebrew at the Jesuit college. He joined the commission drafting the Ratio Studiorum at Rome in 1584 and died rector of Vienna's College of Nobles in 1587.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relation-of-g:
The relation of God to the universe is the world's essential dependence on God, in creation and in conservation. Developing the First Cause argument, the entry holds that the world depends on God first as Creator, the producer of its whole being or substance. Once produced, its continuance at every moment rests on his sustaining power. Creation means producing a being wholly out of nothing, replacing absolute nonexistence with existence.

The Creator relation, the entry argues, is the sole way the Infinite can relate to the finite. Pantheist theories fail here: they turn the varieties of being into determinations, emanations, or phases of one eternal reality, Substance in Spinoza's system. Knowledge gained through revelation, guaranteed by infinite Truth himself, closes the discussion as the most certain knowledge we can possess.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-self-defense:
A private person who faces an unjust attack may use force in reply, and this entry sets out the moral rules that govern that right. It covers attacks on life, on the body, on property, and on good name. Catholic moralists, the entry says, agree on the main principles even where they differ on finer points. Defense of life comes first. A person may use whatever force is needed, even taking the attacker's life.

Force must stay within what is needed to defeat the attack. A slight wound or a call for help, if enough, forbids killing. The attack must have actually begun, not merely been planned. A person may also give up the right out of charity, unless duty binds him to defend himself fully. The entry goes on to defense of others, of property, and of reputation, with the same measure of restraint throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sister-louise:
Sister Louise, born Josephine Susanna Vanderschriek at Bergen-op-Zoom, Holland, on 14 November 1813, died at Cincinnati, Ohio, on 3 December 1886. Tenth of twelve children of an Antwerp advocate turned woolen-cloth manufacturer, she inherited from her father skill in managing affairs, firmness on principle, and unswerving fidelity to duty. From her mother she gained a gentle disposition that endeared her to all. 

Clothed in the habit on 15 October 1837 as Sister Louise, her fervor shortened her probation. She professed vows on 7 May 1839. That same year Sister Louise joined seven others as volunteers when Bishop Purcell of Cincinnati, visiting Namur, sought sisters for his diocese. Landing at New York on 19 October 1840, they reached Cincinnati and built a province that grew to nearly twelve hundred members. A novitiate opened in America in 1846, and a second at Roxbury near Boston in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ambrose:
St. Ambrose was bishop of Milan from 374 to 397, born probably in 340 at Trier, Arles, or Lyons. He died on 4 April 397, one of the most illustrious Fathers and Doctors of the Church. This long entry sets him beside Augustine, Chrysostom, and Athanasius as upholders of St. Peter's chair. It notes that his biography must be pieced together from his own writings, since the Life by his secretary Paulinus, written at Augustine's suggestion, disappoints.

Descended from an ancient Roman family that had long embraced Christianity, counting martyrs and high officials among its members. Ambrose was born while his father, also Ambrosius, served as prefect of Gaul, ruling France, Britain, and Spain. The entry follows his rise from governor to bishop and his battles with emperors and heretics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-blaise:
St. Blaise was bishop and martyr, whose name the ninth-century martyrologies of Europe list on 15 February as Blasius, bishop of Sebaste and martyr. This entry follows the evidence with care. The Greek synaxaria list him under 11 February. The oldest known recension of the so-called martyrology of St. Jerome lacks his name, and only in the later, enlarged catalogues is he mentioned.

The historical notices about him in those martyrologies and synaxaria rest on the legendary Acts. All the statements agree that Blasius was bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, and most accounts place his martyrdom in the reign of Licinius, about 316. Those reports may rest on old traditions bound up with the saint's veneration in the Church liturgy, so they should not be absolutely rejected. Perhaps it can be assumed that Blasius was a bishop and suffered martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-louis-of-t:
Louis of Toulouse, bishop who died at twenty-three, spent seven years a hostage prince learning from Franciscans. Born at Brignoles in February 1274, he was second son of Charles II of Anjou, the Lame, king of Naples, and Mary of Hungary. Mary was great-niece of Elizabeth of Hungary, and Louis was nephew of Louis IX of France. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Brignoles to 19 August 1297.

Some early sources call him firstborn only because he succeeded to his brother Charles Martel's rights after Martel died in 1295. Louis went with two brothers to Aragon in 1288 as hostage for his father, captured in a naval battle off Naples in 1284. During seven years' captivity, 1288 to 1295, at Sciurana castle and partly at Barcelona, Franciscan friars educated the three princes. Among them were Ponzius Carbonelli, Peter of Falgar, and Richard of Middleton. From that schooling grew a bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syracuse:
Syracuse in Sicily is an archdiocese whose city stands on a peninsula reaching into the Ionian Sea near the Anapus, where papyrus still grows. Its chief harbour is Sicily's largest and among the Mediterranean's finest, guarded by two islets without blocking entry, and exports now exceed imports. The cathedral rises on a temple of Minerva that once held thirty-six columns, of which twenty-two remain.

Inside, Scilla's pictures and frescoes share space with a silver statue of Lucy and a font carved from a Greek crater on seven bronze lions from the San Giovanni catacombs. Other churches hold works by Caravaggio, Minniti, and Marabitti, civic buildings show Gothic and Moorish styles, and the museum is rich in Christian inscriptions. Ancient ruins and a full archaeology bibliography round out the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarentaise:
Tarentaise, also called Moutiers en Tarentaise, is a diocese of the Moutiers arrondissement in Savoie, suffragan of Chambéry. Legend says James the Assyrian, secretary to Honoratus of Arles, evangelized the Centrones in the fifth century. He became first bishop of Darantasia and named Marcellus his successor. The first reliable document is Leo the Great's letter of May 450, assigning Tarentaise to Vienne.

Sanctius, at Epaon in 517, is the first historically known bishop. Frankfort in 794 heard a plea against Leo's settlement. Leo III made Darantasia a metropolis over Aosta, Sion, and Maurienne while keeping Vienne's primacy. That quarrel lasted four centuries. Saracens wrecked Darantasia in the tenth century, and archbishops moved across the Isère. Moutiers grew there, and in 1186 Barbarossa made the archbishop a prince of the empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-telese:
Telese is a small town in Benevento province, southern Italy, in the valley of the Calore, famed for hot sulfur springs. Ruins of ancient Telesia, the Tedis of Oscan coins, still stand on Monte Acerro. Hannibal captured the city in 207 BC, and Scipio founded a colony there. Fallen into decay, it was rebuilt in the ninth century. Its first bishop appears in Agnellus in 487, and by the tenth century it answered to the Archbishop of Benevento.

Bishop Gian Francesco Leoni moved the episcopal residence to Cerreto Sannita in 1612. The see later joined Piedimonte d'Alife, but was re-established in 1852. Among its bishops, Alberico Giacquinto of 1540 was famed for learning and piety. Angelo Massarelli of 1567 served as secretary of Trent and wrote its acts and a diary. Vincenzo Lupoli of 1792 was a distinguished jurisconsult. The diocese holds 24 parishes, 60,600 people, and fifty priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tenebrae-hear:
The Tenebrae hearse is the triangular candlestick used in the Tenebrae service. Its name comes through French herse from Latin herpex, a harrow, the same word now used for funeral processions. The funeral hearse was first a frame over the bier, holding the pall. It bore many prickets for burning tapers, and their likeness to harrow teeth gave it the name. Later it meant any coffin receptacle, then the vehicle carrying the dead.

The Tenebrae hearse takes its name the same way, from prickets like harrow teeth. It dates at least to the seventh century, in an ordo published by Mabillon. Candle numbers varied: Amalarius speaks of twenty-four, others of thirty, twelve, nine, or seven. Today it bears fifteen candles, all unbleached wax, though some churches put a white candle at the apex. During the service candles die one by one after each psalm, leaving only the highest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-calas-cas:
A Toulouse merchant's fate became a cause célèbre of religious tolerance, and this entry tells it plainly. Jean Calas, a French Calvinist born in 1698 near Castres, had lived some forty years in Toulouse when his son Marc-Antoine was found hanged in the family warehouse on 13 October 1761. A crowd cry turned suspected suicide into alleged murder by a father bent on blocking a conversion.

Capitouls, the city's chief magistrates, seized on the charge. Calas was tried, condemned, and executed on 10 March 1762. Voltaire took up the case, exposed the flimsy evidence, and won rehabilitation for the family. The entry follows the trial, the pamphlet war, and the verdict's reversal with sober detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-dease:
Thomas Dease, Bishop of Meath, was born in Ireland in 1568 and died at Galway in 1651. From an old landed family in Cavan and Westmeath, he learned Irish well enough to write poems in it, then trained at Paris, where he became rector of the Irish Seminary. Consecrated Bishop of Meath in 1622, he returned to Ireland under the penal laws.

Dease stayed loyal to England and preached loyalty to his flock, refusing to join the Confederation of Kilkenny despite pressure from the primate. That stance won him toleration from the government but angered fellow Catholics and the papal nuncio Rinuccini, who blamed him for sowing strife between the Confederate generals Preston and O'Neill. A false report of his death in 1648 drew little regret from the nuncio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-toulouse:
Toulouse is an archdiocese covering the department of Haute-Garonne in southern France. Re-established by the Concordat of 1802, it first held Haute-Garonne and Ariege, with the archbishop styling himself also of Auch, Narbonne and Albi. Later creations cut it back, and the bull Paternae Caritatis of July 1822 fixed it almost wholly within the old dioceses of Toulouse, Rieux and Comminges.

The city itself, chief town of the Tectosagi, resisted Rome in the Cimbric invasion, then flourished as a Roman town with famous schools. Taken by the Goths in 413, it later passed through Frankish, Visigothic and French hands. In 1295 Boniface VIII cut off Pamiers from it, and in 1319 John XXII made Toulouse a metropolitan see, with Montauban, Saint-Papoul, Rieux and Lombez as suffragans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-universe:
Universe is taken here in the astronomical sense, from our own planet out to the starry realm. The entry treats systems of the world in the widest sense, covering the structure and motions of the heavenly bodies across past, present, and future ages. Its present system forms the subject of universal cosmography, as described by Lambert, the Herschels, Laplace, Newcomb, and others. The section at hand deals only with the solar system, and in particular with the rival theories of Ptolemy and Copernicus.

Greek astronomy opens the story, with the earliest planetary schemes of the Greek schools. The entry then sets out the Ptolemaic system, earth at the centre, and the Copernican answer, sun at the centre, with the proofs that at last favoured Copernicus. Readers get a compact history of how men mapped the heavens, from ancient spheres to the modern picture of a sun-ruled system.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-henry-mor:
Henry Morse was a martyr born in Norfolk in 1595 who died at Tyburn on 1 February 1644. Received into the church at Douai on 5 June 1614, he was ordained at Rome after various journeys and left for the mission on 19 June 1624. Admitted to the Society of Jesus at Heaton, he was arrested and jailed three years in York Castle. There he made his novitiate under fellow prisoner Father John Robinson and took simple vows.

Later he served as missionary to English regiments in the Low Countries. Returning to England late in 1633, he laboured in London, and in 1636 he is reported to have received about ninety Protestant families into the church. He caught the plague himself but recovered. Arrested again in February 1636 and jailed in Newgate, he was tried for his priesthood and suffered at Tyburn.
chantry-house:
Charlotte M. Yonge's novel was illustrated by W. J. Hennessy and issued by Macmillan at New York. It opens in a nursery of memory. The narrator recalls his mother reading aloud as he lay in his crib. A feeble water-coloured drawing of a trio stays with him. Family history, told backward from childhood, is the book's method from its first chapter, A Nursery Prose.

Forty-eight chapters follow the family of Chantry House through purposes, discoveries, and a midnight chase. Wills old and new are compared, a price is set and then paid, and restitution closes one long account. Lady Margaret's ghost haunts the house's past, her portrait met on the stairs of the story. Yonge writes domestic duty and old wrongs with patient, churchly care.
china-and-the-chinese:
Herbert Allen Giles, professor of Chinese at Cambridge, delivered six lectures at Columbia University on the Dean Lung foundation, published in 1902. The Chinese language comes first, in all its difficulty. Giles covers dialects, tones, the written characters, and pidgin-English. He finds no grammar where Europeans expect it, and says so cheerfully.

A Chinese library fills the second lecture, from the Confucian canon to novels and dictionaries. Democratic China, the third, walks through magistrates, taxation, and village rule. China and ancient Greece are then compared, coincidence by coincidence — counting-boards, olives, and musical systems among them. Taoism takes the fifth lecture, from Lao Tzu to the elixir of life. Giles writes as a scholar who expects his audience to be surprised.
christmas-tales-and-christmas-verse:
Eugene Field's Christmas pieces were gathered by Scribner's Sons in 1912, with illustrations by Florence Storer, some in colour. A hymn opens the book: bells ring and children sing because a star once stopped above a manger. Tales and poems then alternate, as the title promises, in Field's gentle register.

Joel's Talk with Santa Claus gives the prose its humour. The Three Kings of Cologne and The First Christmas Tree retell old legends. A mauve mouse named Squeaknibble stars in The Mouse and the Moonbeam. She turns double somersaults on a stump of tail, then is fooled by a white-furred ghost promising cheese. Mistress Merciless, The Symbol and the Saint, and a Chrystmasse of Olde widen the set. Field writes Christmas for the nursery without leaving adults outside.
claverhouse:
Claverhouse, by Mowbray Morris, is a biography of John Graham of Claverhouse, the soldier remembered as Viscount Dundee. Its bibliography shows the ground the life stands on. Balcarres' Memoirs, Burnet's History of My Own Time, and the letters of Dundee himself, printed for the Bannatyne Club, head a long list of Scottish sources.

Morris tests famous charges against that record. On the deaths of two women honored in the martyrology of the Scottish Covenant, he argues the evidence clears his subject. Claverhouse was present, he shows, neither at their trial nor their execution. He had no more to do with those deaths than men already in their graves or boys at the time.
cock-lane-and-common-sense:
Cock Lane and Common-Sense, by Andrew Lang, first published in 1894, argues that modern ghost reports deserve study, not dismissal. Its preface complains of a split. Folklorists gladly record wraiths, corpse-lights, and fire-walking as savage or rural belief. First-hand testimony from living men and women, they refuse to touch.

The Society for Psychical Research makes the opposite error, Lang argues, by neglecting history and tradition. His introduction ranges from animistic beliefs in every stage of culture to Dr. Carpenter's theory of unconscious cerebration. Cases include Nicolai, who studied the false figures that beset him. The Cock Lane ghost of the title stands for the old, famous haunting at the book's heart.
common-sense:
Thomas Paine, a recent English immigrant to America, fired the colonies toward independence with Common Sense in early 1776. Philadelphia readers passed the pamphlet hand to hand while war with Britain already burned. Paine argues in plain, hard sentences that America must cut loose from king and Parliament. His postscript of February 14, 1776 notes that no answer had yet appeared.

Four parts divide the case, starting with the origin and design of government in general. Paine separates society, born of human wants, from government, born of human wickedness. Monarchy and hereditary succession take a beating as absurd and insulting systems. Thoughts on the present state of American affairs then urge a clean break and a new union. A final section rates America's present ability, counting ships, men, and resources for war. Few pamphlets have moved a nation faster; readers still study Paine's mix of Bible talk, street logic, and moral heat.
cord-and-creese:
Cord and Creese, by James De Mille, opens in a port town on the morning a ship brings the English mail. Ocean steam navigation had not yet reached so far, and the crowd besets the post office while knots at the street corners trade hints of news. At the lower end of King Street stands the warehouse of Compton & Brandon, commission merchants, its sign newly gilded.

The partners contrast. Brandon, the junior, has an olive complexion, regular features, and dark hazel eyes with a peculiarity seen, the narrator says, in the gipsy and in successful spiritual mediums. Adventure follows the firm seaward. A diving scene finds Louis rising freed from his weight, helmet off, smiling at Frank's ashen face: pull up the signal line and see for yourself.
de-libris-prose-and-verse:
Prose and verse about books fill Austin Dobson's De Libris, issued by Macmillan of London in 1908. A merry prologue in verse opens the book. Dobson tells the kind reader he cannot make him read, and has no hope to please the town.

He slipped scraps of verse in among the prose, he says, to make things less monotonous. One essay weighs an artist who drew the world of Pride and Prejudice, down to the furniture of Longbourn and Rosings. Other pieces treat books and their associations, and an epistle to an editor. Publishers who let him reprint pieces are thanked by name. The book is a bookman's miscellany, light in tone and deep in reading.
denslow-s-mother-goose:
The old nursery rhymes, edited and drawn by W. W. Denslow, fill this picture book of 1901. McClure, Phillips and Company of New York published it, under copyright by William Wallace Denslow. Denslow inscribes it to Ann Waters Denslow, with love and thanks for her help.

Humpty Dumpty sits on his wall on an early page, with a note that he is an egg. Mistress Mary, Bye Baby Bunting, and Little Jack Horner follow in bold type. Each rhyme stands with Denslow's flat, poster-like pictures, marked as illustrations through the text. Words are few and large, made for a child on a lap. The book is a famed American picture book of its year, more drawn than written.
divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-paradis:
Dante Alighieri's Paradise, the Paradiso, closes his Divine Comedy in H F Cary's translation, with thirty-three cantos of ascent. Beatrice guides Dante through the spheres of heaven, each planet holding souls whose earthly loves ordered them toward God. The opening canto confesses that heaven's glory exceeds telling.

Dante meets Saint Dominic's and Saint Francis's orders, warrior spirits forming a cross in Mars, and his own ancestor Cacciaguida, who prophesies his exile and bids him stand apart. Saint Peter examines his faith, and the final cantos rise past angels to the vision of the Trinity. Cary's blank verse, the standard English Dante of the nineteenth century, carries the theology in stately lines.
doe-osti-17034390-c-page-manual-version-:
Manual for C-PAGE, version 1.0, was released in May 2026 by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory staff, led by Michael Abdelmalak and Pavel Etingov. C-PAGE turns production cost model results into working power flow cases that obey alternating current physics. Power planners use such cases to test whether a planned grid can really carry the flows a cost model predicts.

The workflow standardizes GridView output, samples key hours, builds direct current cases in PowerWorld, then converts them for a two stage AC solver in EGRET. Benchmark tools compare each stage against the last, and mapping tools in QGIS display results. Tested commands and setup templates target users with limited software background.
doe-osti-2584648-langevin-dynamics-model:
Final technical report DE-SC0021206, from Ranganathan Gopalakrishnan at the University of Memphis and covering September 2020 to August 2024, builds a predictive theory for gas-phase ion-ion recombination. When a positive and a negative ion meet, they can neutralize each other. That rate shapes flames, plasmas, and even interplanetary clouds, yet no robust model existed. The team's answer couples classical trajectory simulations with a Monte Carlo operator for the electron transfer itself, its probability from two-state Landau-Zener theory.

Quantum chemistry calculations fed the theory, and a Langevin treatment folded in the neutral gas. For hydrogen and lithium hydride pairs, predicted cross-sections matched measurement up to about 100,000 meters per second. Other pairs landed close: neon-chloride rates ran two to three times high near one torr, while xenon-fluoride came in about twenty percent low at high pressure. A quaternion method extended the trajectories to non-spherical ions.
doe-osti-2586394-port-authority-of-new-y:
Jonathan Morgenstein and Akhil Magal of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory are the technical contacts on this final report, NREL/TP-7A40-95614, issued in August 2025 for CRADA number CRD-21-18244. Benjamin Cuozzo shares credit for the work. The project supported a New York Power Authority feasibility study advising the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey on future distributed energy deployments at its facilities.

NREL's main product was a high-level literature review of commercially viable distributed energy technologies in New York City and New York State. A spreadsheet compares each option by use case and ownership model, with levelized cost of energy, operating costs, installed costs, benefits, and drawbacks. Technologies covered include solar photovoltaics, lithium-ion and other battery storage, kinetic and thermal storage, natural gas and hydrogen fuel cells, and small wind turbines.
doe-osti-2587070-2016-u-s-petroleum-fuel:
Joseph Chou, Matthew Jamieson, and Michelle Krynock of the National Energy Technology Laboratory produced this baseline study, DOE/NETL-2025/4944, dated August 28, 2025. It fixes a reference point for the life cycle impacts of United States petroleum fuels in the year 2016. Later studies of fuels and emissions policy can measure themselves against this frozen baseline.

Chou led the methods, analysis, and data work, with Jamieson supervising and Krynock reviewing. The study leans on OPGEE, an engineering model of oil fields. OPGEE estimates the energy use and emissions of producing crude oil. Inputs span the full fuel path, from oil field work through refining and transport to the finished fuels. Data sources include Canadian crude export statistics, since imported oil feeds United States refineries. The report documents each assumption so the baseline can be reproduced or challenged.
doe-osti-2588410-enabling-the-next-gener:
Jay Wilhelm of Ohio University led this final report for federal grant DE-FE0032078, submitted to the National Energy Technology Laboratory. The project asked whether cellular 5G could carry the next generation of smart sensors inside coal-fired power plants. Wiring there is expensive, conditions are harsh, and wireless coverage is spotty.

The team built and tested sensor links in the 3.5 to 4.5 gigahertz range, working with a 4.0 gigahertz sensor. Calibration used the standard short-open-load-through method. Testing revolved around what the report calls a resolution triangle. Three variables in the frequency scans were traded against each other to optimize system performance. Raising scan resolution costs speed or range, so the balance matters. The full hosted text carries the engineering detail, from task list through methods. The goal is plant health data streamed without new cable runs.
doe-osti-2588509-ai-accelerated-optimiza:
Lilo Pozzo of the University of Washington led this final report for award DE-SC0019911, covering June 2022 through June 2025. The materials are organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors, polymers that carry both ions and electrons. They matter for high-capacity batteries, bio-electronic interfaces, and neuromorphic computing, but their two conduction modes usually fight each other during optimization.

Pozzo's team tried to decouple them through structure. Blends of ion-conducting block copolymers with electronic conducting polymers self-assemble into ordered nanostructures, the block copolymers guiding the conjugated parts into place. Artificial intelligence methods, coupled to neutron and X-ray scattering, mapped the phase diagrams of these blends with far less human trial and error. Small-angle neutron scattering, including rheo-SANS under shear at ANSTO and contrast variation work at HFIR, pinned down where the conjugated polymer sits inside the assemblies. The methods transfer to other soft materials.
doe-osti-2588785-developing-partnership-:
Minghui Diao of San Jose State University led this final report for grant DE-SC0023155, covering September 2022 through May 2025 and submitted September 18, 2025. Adam Kochanski was co-investigator, and Shaocheng Xie of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory collaborated without funding. The project's first goal was the partnership itself: linking a public university's faculty and students to a national laboratory's climate data and models, with equity and inclusion in the frame.

The science ran through the Department of Energy's Atmospheric Radiation Measurement program. Analyses of the MICRE and AWARE field campaigns used a cyclone compositing method to quantify how synoptic dynamics shape clouds. Observations showed stronger asymmetry in cloud and radiative properties between western and eastern cyclone sectors at McMurdo than at Macquarie Island. The E3SM version 1 model consistently underestimated ice water in the comparison, a concrete target for model improvement handed back to the laboratory side of the partnership.
doe-osti-2589594-sierra-code-coupling-mo:
Sandia National Laboratories manual SAND2025-11826, by Samuel Subia, James Overfelt, David Baur, and co-authors, teaches Arpeggio, the coupling module of the SIERRA simulation family. Version 5.26 is dated September 2025. Engineers use coupling when one physics problem feeds another, such as heat flow changing how a part bends.

Opening chapters explain coupled physics styles, how SIERRA codes pass data through transfer services, and how a run is steered. Later chapters give the full input language, command by command, with defaults and value rules. Setup notes differ for Sandia users and outside users. Analysts setting up multi-physics runs can work from this single reference instead of hunting through code notes.
doe-osti-2997112-adoption-of-ai-in-the-u:
Idaho National Laboratory white paper INL/RPT-25-87526, by Emma Stewart, Patience Yockey, Remy Stolworthy, and Megan Culler, dated September 2025, surveys artificial intelligence adoption in utility transmission and distribution work. Grid operators face more data than staff can read, from smart meters to feeder sensors. The paper sorts real uses from hype and weighs what each use risks.

AI tasks are grouped into detection of faults and odd behavior, prediction such as load and storm forecasting, optimization and control, and customer-facing business tools. Deployment stories show how utilities actually start: audit the data, assign an owner to each source, and stream meter flags together with feeder telemetry and weather feeds. Model choice guidance stresses physics context, since a grid model that ignores how power flows can mislead operators.
doe-osti-2997610-the-user-guide-for-the-:
Savannah River National Laboratory user guide SRNL-STI-2009-00093, Revision 2, by Madison Hsieh and Fabienne Johnson, dated September 2025, explains the ComPro glass database. ComPro, in its Revision 3, holds 14,134 rows and 125 columns of glass composition, durability, and fabrication data. Durability is measured by the Product Consistency Test, the standard leach check for waste glass.

Of those rows, 8,484 count as model data and 5,650 as non-model data, a split the guide explains. Chapters map which source data sets make up each part and define the terms a user will meet. Glass scientists designing waste forms can search the library for a composition near their target and read off its tested durability. The guide keeps outside users from misreading columns that carry decades of shorthand.
doe-osti-3005569-24-1-3-4-upgraded-fixed:
Duc Ta Vo of Los Alamos files the fiscal 2025 annual report for project 24.1.3.4, LA-UR-25-31302, issued November 17, 2025. The project maintains FRAM, the Fixed Energy Response Function Analysis with Multiple Efficiencies software. FRAM reads gamma-ray spectra to weigh uranium, plutonium, and mixed oxide material without destroying it. Safeguards inspectors and plant accountants rely on it worldwide.

The annual report bundles three documents: a capability review of FRAM version 7.1, a study of that version's measurement bias, and version 2 of the user manual. The manual runs long, through detector setup and the handling of irregular source shapes. Bundling them under one cover makes the fiscal year's upgrade citable as a unit. The support address printed in the appendix is the author's own group at Los Alamos.
doe-osti-3010192-new-molecular-mechanism:
Final technical report from Cornell University, by principal investigator Phillip Milner, dated December 23, 2025, covers greenhouse gas capture in metal-organic frameworks under award DE-SC002100, funded at 750,000 dollars. The aim is sorptive separations that use far less energy than current gas separation plants.

Hydroxide and amine N-oxide groups built into the frameworks bind carbon dioxide with high affinity, even straight from air, with unusual resistance to oxidation. Other materials recover fluorinated greenhouse gases from refrigerator and Teflon plant emissions for reuse as chemical building blocks. A third line charged hydroxide into cheap porous carbon, making charge sorbents stable to oxidation up to 150 degrees Celsius that still pull carbon dioxide from air.
doe-osti-3012132-ranking-biological-feat:
Biological features in soil microbial multi omics data are ranked by integration modelling in a December 2025 Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report. The authors are David Degnan, Ryan McClure, Daniel Claborne, Lisa Bramer, and Javier Flores. Several integration methods, including DIABLO, MOFA, and SLIDE, were run on the combined dataset. Feature weights were cut where a kneedle algorithm bends the ranked curve.

A neural net fitted to MOFA returned one dominant component. Its Shapley value was 0.162, against under 0.001 for all others. Models separated week zero samples from later weeks without being given collection times. MOFA and SLIDE even separated the 4, 8, and 12 week groups. Features span 16S, metabolomics, and other omic types.
doe-osti-3012508-computational-materials:
Oak Ridge CRADA final report ORNL/TM-2025/4014, by Patxi Fernandez-Zelaia, Jiahao Cheng, Jason Mayeur, and four co-authors, dated April 2025, builds a computer framework for judging the reliability of hydrogen-fueled gas turbine parts. Burning blended fuels changes the heat and pressure profiles inside engines, and small differences in how parts are made change their metal structure. Both effects bear on how long hot parts last.

The framework judges high-temperature creep, the slow stretching of metal under load, in nickel-based superalloys used in hot engine sections. A physics model captures grain-boundary effects, the weak seams between metal crystals, and a probabilistic calibration folds in uncertainty from both microstructure and operating conditions. Fleet operators could use such models to set inspection and upkeep schedules with less wasted caution.
doe-osti-3013844-financing-storage-as-a-:
Financing storage as a transmission asset is the topic of this Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report. Daniel Boff, Jay Barlow, and Jeremy Twitchell wrote it. Batteries and other storage can sometimes relieve grid congestion more cheaply than new lines. That use case is called storage as a transmission asset, or SATA. Regulators are still working out who may own such storage and how it gets paid for.

The report lays out the questions now emerging. How should planners compare a battery against a line in transmission planning? How would cost recovery through transmission rates work? And how does a dual-use asset avoid double payment when it also plays in energy markets? The paper maps the decision space for regulators and transmission organizations. It is an initial-considerations paper, not a settlement of the issue.
doe-osti-3018735-sierra-code-coupling-mo:
Sandia's SIERRA Thermal/Fluid Development Team issued this user manual, SAND2026-16588, printed January 28, 2026. Its subject is Arpeggio, the coupling module for the Sierra Mechanics suite. Sierra's applications each simulate one physics well. Real problems couple several at once. Arpeggio provides loose coupling between the applications. It gives them access to shared framework services, and it orchestrates their joint execution. Analysts use it to run, for example, a thermal code and a fluids code as one scenario.

The manual describes Arpeggio's components and how they operate. Command reference entries fill most of the book: assigning start times, suppressing output from the nonlinear loop, setting termination times. Simple examples lead, so a new analyst can reach a working coupled run quickly. Version 5.28 is the release documented. For multiphysics teams, Arpeggio is the conductor, and this manual is its score.
doe-osti-3021993-ice-calculator-2-final-:
LBNL final report by Peter Larsen, Kyle Carney, Joseph H. Eto, and co-authors, dated February 27, 2026, reports Phases 1 and 2 of the national effort to rebuild the Interruption Cost Estimate (ICE) Calculator. The ICE Calculator is a public online tool, first built over fifteen years ago, that gauges what power outages cost electricity users. Power firms use it to value reliability and resilience spending.

The update rests on fresh surveys. Sponsoring power firms gave identical, thorough outage cost questionnaires to statistically representative customer samples. Eight firms sponsored Phase 1. Berkeley Lab pooled the replies and rebuilt the calculator's math engines, including customer damage functions anchored at momentary, 2-hour, 8-hour, and 24-hour outage lengths. Separate functions were built for home and non-home customers. The report records the survey process and what the new data changed.
doe-osti-3022726-summary-of-potential-in:
ANL report ANL-25/24 Volume 2, by Mark Grippo and Erna Grelle, examines what could go wrong with carbon dioxide pipelines and geologic storage. It also asks what the consequences would be for people and ecosystems. It covers the project life cycle from construction through operation, including routine disturbances such as land clearing and the accident cases that dominate public concern.

Impact tables trace release scenarios. Carbon dioxide or co-transported gases reaching the atmosphere can cause acute physiological stress and, at high concentrations, death. Contaminants mobilized by injected carbon dioxide can reach water and soil. Case studies of notable accidental releases and natural analogues, places where carbon dioxide has leaked from the ground for centuries, ground the analysis in observed behavior. Worker safety during construction and drilling is treated alongside public impacts.
doe-osti-3028320-fast-outer-loop-solutio:
Adrian Sandu of Virginia Tech reports award DE-SC0021313, which ran September 2020 through August 2023, on faster outer loop algorithms. Outer loops are the repeated simulation campaigns behind uncertainty quantification, inverse problems, and data assimilation. Each campaign reruns a big multiphysics model many times, and the report notes the outer problem can cost at least ten times the already large inner simulation cost.

The project's answer couples physical models and machine learning models coherently, so the cheap learned model carries part of the load without drifting away from the physics. Publications listed include physics-informed neural networks for PDE-constrained optimization and control, ensemble variational Fokker-Planck methods, and a 2025 Computational Geosciences paper on preserving nonlinear constraints in variational flow filtering for data assimilation.
doe-osti-3030153-reliable-protection-for:
ConEdison closes award DE-EE0010655 in this final report, for a project that ran from October 2023 to March 2025. Patricia Jacques served as principal investigator, with Zheyuan Cheng of Quanta Technology as program manager. The problem is grid protection as solar, wind, and batteries take over. These inverter-based resources feed faults very differently from spinning generators, so the relays and software tuned for the old grid can misjudge a fault.

The team ran a large check of common short-circuit programs, ASPEN, CAPE, and CYME, against detailed vendor models across 1,000 automated fault cases. Standard models held errors under 5 percent when inverter behavior was predictable. They also failed to converge on close-in faults at high inverter shares, and static tables could not capture pre-fault operating states.
doe-osti-3031283-one-earth-energy-static:
Fang Yang, Oladipupo Babarinde, and Roland Okwen of the Prairie Research Institute model a carbon storage site in this report. It is DOE-UIUC-31892-13, issued April 27, 2026. The site belongs to One Earth Energy, near Gibson City in McLean County, Illinois. Under the CarbonSAFE Phase III Illinois Storage Corridor project, the firm would bury captured carbon dioxide in the Mt. Simon Sandstone. The target is over 50 million tonnes.

A fresh stratigraphic well, OEE number 1, fed the models. Two older wells and 2-D seismic lines helped. Static models built in Petrel software map the rock layers and their traits. Flow runs then tested the program yardstick of 50 million tonnes over 30 years. Faster cases ran 20 to 50 million tonnes over 12 to 20 years, tied to tax credit timing.
doe-osti-3363255-applications-of-federat: Lauren Danielle Ortiz of the University of Arizona presents this August 2025 Idaho National Laboratory poster (INL/EXP-25-86459), mentored by Wayne Austad under CyManII. Chip makers guard their process data closely, which starves the data hungry models they want to train. The poster reviews federated learning, where sites train a shared model by exchanging model weights instead of raw data, and surveys tools such as TensorFlow Federated, Flower, and PySyft. It flags gaps in cross company models, predictive maintenance studies, and joint privacy and performance metrics.
doe-osti-3367084-sierra-code-coupling-mo:
Sandia National Laboratories manual SAND2026-21786, by Samuel Subia, James Overfelt, and David Baur, documents Arpeggio version 5.30, the coupling module for the Sierra mechanics code suite. Sierra's specialized applications each solve part of a multiphysics problem. Arpeggio passes data between them. A thermal code and a structural code can then advance together instead of in separate runs stitched by hand.

The manual is a command-by-command reference. Time step controls get detailed treatment. Steps can clip or overrun at a transient loop's end. A snap option quantizes time values to multiples of a quantum 12 orders of magnitude below the loop span. Defaults are stated for every parameter. Analysts coupling Sierra applications consult it to configure runs that stay synchronized.
doe-osti-3374727-neams-technical-area-su:
INL/RPT-25-87963, an Idaho National Laboratory report, dated September 2025, is a milestone account of support work on the MOOSE simulation framework. Six members of the lab's Computational Frameworks group wrote it. Guillaume Giudicelli heads the printed author list. Alexander Lindsay closes it. MOOSE is the base code under many Nuclear Energy Advanced Modeling and Simulation tools. The report logs a year of fixes and upgrades made for those users.

One fix concerns mesh stitching. Names set for subdomains in later inputs were once dropped without warning. MOOSE now keeps every name and remaps numeric ids when names clash. A second fix attacks slow table output. The old FormattedTable cost grew with the square of the step count. That hurt small equation models run by the Griffin code over tens of thousands of steps.
doe-osti-3377459-greenhouse-gas-life-cyc:
Technical report NLR/TP-6A20-96533, dated June 2026, documents the GLEAM model built at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Garvin Heath heads the five-author team. GLEAM stands for Greenhouse Gas Life Cycle Emissions Assessment Model. It sums the emissions of energy systems from raw inputs to end use. Analysts use such sums to compare power and fuel options on one scale. The volume is the model's full record: inputs, sources, and worked tables.

Coal and gas get long treatment. Tables list plant types from fluidized bed to integrated gasification with carbon capture. Each row carries cost and emissions marks per unit of output. The gas chapter notes its weight in the grid: natural gas made a plurality, 43 percent, of United States electricity in 2023. Data lean on Energy Information Administration figures. The aim is a tool whose numbers users can trace back to named sources, not a black box.
doe-osti-3520291-direct-transfer-trip-te:
In September 2025, Oak Ridge National Laboratory released report ORNL/TM-2026/4770, which covers serial-based Direct Transfer Trip testing under the SPaRC program. David Cotten, Matthew DeMorat, and Emilio Piesciorovsky are among the authors. Serial links are an older, common way for relays to talk.

The testbed syncs to a time source so relay events carry timestamps. Those stamps let staff compute Mirrored Bits message delay between relays. Fault clearing time comes from the same stamps. Tests then vary channel conditions on purpose. Protection teams learn how serial links behave under stress before trusting them in service.
earth-s-holocaust-from-mosses-from-an-ol:
Nathaniel Hawthorne imagines the world burning its rubbish in Earth's Holocaust, a sketch from Mosses from an Old Manse. One day, past or future, mankind tires of its worn-out trumpery and builds a general bonfire on a broad western prairie. The narrator journeys out to watch, hoping the flames will light up some hidden moral truth.

Wagons, wheelbarrows, and women with full aprons stream in with goods judged fit only for fire. Titles, weapons, and the tools of punishment go on the heap. In one debate, even the consecrated guardians of benevolence take the hangman's view of his own trade. Hawthorne lets reformers cheer each new load, then asks the cold question the fire cannot answer. The heart itself, he hints, must change, or the world will rebuild all it burned.
edward-barnett-a-neglected-child-of-sout:
Tobias Aconite, styling himself Mayor of Hole cum Corner, tells a sensation tale in a book dated 1855. The title promises a neglected child of South Carolina. The boy rose to be a peer of Great Britain. The book adds his grandfather Captain Williams's stormy life, the terrible end of the proud Earl de Montford, and a shadow's punishment. Truth is stranger than fiction, the title page boasts.

Chapter one sits the Earl in a plain business room of his mansion. Hard benches, game law abstracts, and oak presses of old papers fill the room. Later scenes plunge into a cave. A captain there warms a cold heart with brandy and curses the stuff as poison. He starts at a bat in the smoke. Kidnapping, hidden birth, and revenge drive the plot in the dime-novel manner. The hosted text comes from the Wright American Fiction files at Indiana University.
ethel-morton-at-rose-house:
Mabell S. C. Smith's Ethel Morton at Rose House came out in 1915 from the World Syndicate Publishing Company of Cleveland and New York, in the Juvenile Library Girls Series. It opens on a hot May Day in Rosemont, New Jersey. Ethel Brown Morton and her cousin Ethel Blue are untangling maypole garlands for the town's first community Maypole, helped by their United Service Club.

Club work fills the book. The girls plan events at Rose House and look for ways their skills can serve the town. One plan grows from talk of peasant embroidery seen in Petrograd: local women who know fine needlework could teach classes, earn a fee, and enjoy the company. Scenes move between dances, gardens, and club meetings. Readers get a warm story about girls turning spare time and hand skills into shared community life.
ethel-morton-s-enterprise:
Mabell S. C. Smith returns to the two cousins named Ethel Morton, told apart by eye color as Ethel Blue and Ethel Brown. Ethel Morton's Enterprise opens in January snow, with the girls looking out at falling flakes and talking over seed catalogues. From that winter start the cousins and their friends in the United Service Club plan gardens, study color schemes, and hunt wild flowers for Helen's garden.

The contents trace the venture as it grows: a flower festival, produce enough to give away, and then a step into business. Roger takes a share in planting and working three gardens, and their grandfather backs a wider community plan with money, seeds, and help. Readers get a bright story about young people learning to plan, plant, and run a small shared enterprise.
eulogy-on-chief-justice-chase:
William M. Evarts delivered his eulogy on Chief Justice Chase before the alumni of Dartmouth College at Hanover on June 24, 1874, and D. Appleton and Company published it in New York that year. Evarts opens with his own close ties: work beside Chase in his later years, and personal friendship. Chase, he says, was a man living a whole nation admired and dead a whole nation laments.

The address traces a career that ran through lawyer, orator, senator, minister, and magistrate. Evarts meets one doubt head-on: some lawyers had questioned Chase's training for private cases, yet his patient, careful work on the bench settled it. Readers get a first-hand memorial of the Chief Justice by a leading lawyer who knew him, given at the college that claimed him as a son.
fifty-bab-ballads-much-sound-and-little-:
W S Gilbert subtitled his Fifty Bab Ballads 'much sound and little sense,' collecting comic verses he first printed in the magazine Fun under editor Tom Hood. The 1884 Routledge edition reprints two earlier volumes together, with Gilbert's own illustrations. His preface explains the ballads' magazine origins under the signature Bab.

Captain Reece, the Rival Curates, the Bishop of Rum-Ti-Foo, and the Precocious Baby lead a cast of sailors, curates, and ghosts behaving absurdly in perfect rhyme. A shocking old vagabond who dresses like a Guy Fawkes shows the method: politeness describing outrage. These verses trained the wit Gilbert later poured into the Savoy operas with Sullivan, and many pieces read like miniature comic operas.
flint-and-feather-collected-verse:
Flint and Feather gathers the collected verse of E Pauline Johnson, the Canadian poet of Mohawk and English descent who performed her work across Canada and England. Johnson inscribed the book, by permission, to the Duke of Connaught as Head Chief of the Six Nations. A memorial introduction recalls her deathbed wish, her London recital tours of 1906, and a gratitude her friends describe as a passion rather than a sentiment.

Inside, the poems speak in the two voices that made her famous. Some take up Indigenous legend, land, and grievance in strong narrative lines. Others give lyrics of the Canadian woods, rivers, and seasons. A producer's note warns that later printings added a misleading subtitle claiming completeness, and that claim is dropped here. What remains is the verse collection as Johnson shaped it, framed by those who knew her.
fun-and-nonsense:
Bonte's Fun and Nonsense is a small book of comic verse for children, drawn with many illustrations. Willard Bonte gives speech and feeling to common things. A chocolate drop works as a barber and seeks a peppermint stick for his pole. A lady cracker scorns Judge Wafer for lacking dough. A whitewash brush despairs of its pompadour hair. A lettuce loses its head and its way.

Each piece is a page or two, built on one pun or one absurd scene. Old Mr. Match scratches his head and lights the dark. A pretzel pilot turns out to owe his tan to a baking pan, not the sea. The humor is gentle and quick.
good-sense:
Baron d'Holbach's Good Sense, subtitled Freethoughts Opposed to Supernatural Ideas, is an English translation of his French Le Bon Sens. The undated translation names no translator, and a Bacon epigraph sets its theme: atheism leaves men to sense, philosophy and laws, while superstition erects an absolute monarchy in men's minds.

Contents ask what theology is, whether man is born with religious ideas, whether belief in God is necessary, and whether all religion is absurdity. Holbach argues plainly and polemically, in short chapters meant to be read and passed on. Readers interested in Enlightenment freethought will find Good Sense one of its bluntest, most readable statements.
govdocs-archive_org-nMonroeByCapellFranc:
A second copy of Frank A. Capell's 1964 booklet on the death of Marilyn Monroe sits in the archive beside the first. Capell was an anti-Communist investigator and the editor of the Herald of Freedom, and the booklet became his best-known work.

Monroe had been found dead in 1962, officially of an overdose, and Capell argued the case was stranger than the ruling allowed. His booklet worked over the evidence and pointed readers toward darker explanations. Duplicate captures are kept so a damaged page in one copy can be checked against the other; the text is an early landmark of Monroe conspiracy writing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAEuropeSecret:
Clare Pedrick reported for the Washington Post from Rome on November 13, on a disclosure that embarrassed governments across Western Europe. Operation Gladio, a clandestine network organized with the CIA, had maintained secret armies meant to resist a Soviet invasion.

The stay-behind networks had hidden weapons and agents in NATO countries for decades, and their exposure in 1990 raised hard questions about what they had actually done in peacetime. Pedrick's dispatch carried the story to American readers as the scandal broke. The article is preserved as first-day journalism on one of the Cold War's deepest secrets.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAPressSelf-Pr:
Bill Richards, a Washington Post staff writer, reported on a proposal to give the CIA what the FBI already had: its own weekly television series. The hit show The FBI had burnished that agency's image for years, and backers wanted the same service for the spies.

The proposal was backed by Dallas millionaire Gordon McLendon and by David Phillips, a former CIA officer who led an association of retired intelligence officers. Director Stansfield Turner was approached, and the agency's response was 'totally noncommittal.' The article survives as a curiosity of the CIA's image problem in the exposure years, when even its publicity plans made news.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrankShirleyRos:
An FBI memorandum from Savannah, dated September 30, 1964, reports a contact by Shirley Rose Frank. Frank had approached immigration authorities with a plain statement: she wanted to go to Russia because she is a Communist. The Bureau wrote her words into a memorandum.

In 1964, an American asking to leave for Russia drew official attention by reflex. Defections ran the other way in the public mind, and Oswald's own years in Russia were fresh history. The memo preserves one woman's request and the file it created, a small record of Cold War movement and suspicion.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JacksonJesse_Ja:
John Pekkanen profiled Jesse Jackson for a magazine on January 21, 1969, when Jackson was twenty-eight. The profile follows his Operation Breadbasket broadcasts in Chicago. It notes his honorary Doctor of Divinity degree from Lincoln College and names his style in its title: militant but nonviolent.

Jackson was then a young lieutenant of the slain Martin Luther King Jr., building his own pulpit of economic protest. Breadbasket used boycotts and broadcasts to press employers. A profile from 1969 catches him at the start of a public life that would run for decades, already fully formed in method.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JamesRosemaryWa:
C. D. DeLoach, a senior FBI official, wrote a memorandum on March 20, 1967 concerning the assassination of President Kennedy. Its subject was an attempt to involve Walter Jenkins in the matter. Jenkins had been President Johnson's closest aide before resigning in scandal in 1964.

Dragging a president's man toward the assassination story was the kind of claim the Bureau tracked carefully. DeLoach's memo put the attempt on headquarters paper. The record shows the FBI watching the story's edges, where rumor reached toward the White House itself, and writing down what it found.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ODanielWLeeSena: nsia-ODanielWLeeSenator ODaniel W Lee Senator: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TrialDefense_Tr: George Lardner Jr. covered the Watergate cover-up trial for the Washington Post. His article reports the prosecution's claim that the defense strategy was simply to blame John Dean, the former White House counsel who had turned against Nixon. Trials turn on stories juries can follow, and Lardner's piece shows both sides fighting over theirs. It is courtroom reporting from the scandal that ended a presidency.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
In 1997 the Defense Department ran Eligible Receiver, an early classified exercise on cyber attack against the United States. This briefing book, posted in August 2018, draws on recently declassified documents and an NSA video. The exercise went well beyond computers, its papers show.

Testers staged mock terror attacks, hostage seizures, and special operations raids. Those physical scenes demonstrated how wide the damage from a cyber-domain attack could spread. The exercise is now called seminal because it woke senior officials to the threat. Its documents let readers see the moment American defense planning started taking cyber war seriously.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_The: The Bolton Book Saga: Anatomy of a White House Cover-Up - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: In 1958 the United States and China fought a crisis over Taiwan and its offshore islands, and American planners weighed nuclear weapons in that fight. This briefing-book page revisits the 1958 Taiwan Strait Crisis as modern tensions over Taiwan raise its profile. A companion Archive report concluded that America came fairly close to using tactical nuclear weapons in 1958. The evidence here is the title alone. The page's point is the parallel: an old island crisis, read again under new pressure.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Government_a: After lawsuits and public pressure over its records practices, the government agreed to preserve White House records, and a National Security Archive briefing book page carries that agreement under a short headline. Such agreements bind an administration to keep the papers, messages, and call records the Presidential Records Act covers, so release can be fought over later with the evidence intact. Only the page capture survives here. It marks a checkpoint in the contest over whether a president's record belongs to the president or the public.
hanshu-ban-gu-chinese:
Ban Gu, a court scholar of the Eastern Han, wrote the Hanshu, the Book of Han, in the first century CE. It tells the story of the Western Han house, from its founding to the fall of Wang Mang. The text here is the full work in its original classical Chinese, drawn from Chinese Wikisource.

Annals of the emperors come first, then tables, then treatises on rites, law, food and goods, rivers, and the heavens. Biographies of ministers, rebels, scholars, and envoys fill the rest. The Hanshu set the form that all later Chinese dynastic histories would follow. It stays the base source for two centuries of China.
heartbreak-house:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Heartbreak House between 1913 and 1916, calling it a fantasia in the Russian manner on English themes.
